title: Aboriginal Australians

title: Ancestral Puebloans

title: Anglo-Saxons

title: Ayutthaya Kingdom

title: Buddhism

search: buddhism buddhism began in northeastern india between the sixth and fourth centuries bce with the teaching of siddhartha gautama, the buddha, and spread across asia into several major traditions, teaching a path out of suffering through insight and practice rather than through a creator god. siddhartha gautama, born a member of a ruling family in the region of present-day nepal and india, is said to have reached enlightenment and began teaching in his mid-thirties. his core teaching, the four noble truths, describes suffering, its cause in craving, its end, and a path to that end, aiming at release from the cycle of rebirth, called nirvana. the faith spread through missionary activity, trade routes and royal patronage, notably under the mauryan emperor ashoka. it developed into three major living traditions: theravada, dominant in sri lanka and mainland southeast asia; mahayana, dominant in china, japan, korea and vietnam; and vajrayana, dominant in tibet, bhutan and mongolia. buddhism has roughly 500 million adherents today, about 6 percent of the world's population.

title: Casarabe Culture

title: Celts

search: celts the celts were related peoples across iron age europe, sharing related languages and, later, the la tène artistic style, without forming a single state. rome absorbed most continental celts, and celtic language and culture lasted longest in ireland and parts of britain. the celts were many related tribal groups, including the gauls of mainland europe, speaking branches of the celtic language family such as gaulish. the la tène culture, known for swirling metalwork, flourished from about 450 bce until roman conquest, following the earlier hallstatt culture. druids held major religious and political influence in many celtic societies before roman conquest, though their role varied by region and period. rome attacked the arverni in 125 bce, and julius caesar completed the conquest of gaul by 50 bce despite resistance under leaders such as vercingetorix. rome targeted the druids directly, and continental and southern british celts were largely assimilated, while celtic culture lasted longer in ireland and northern britain.

title: Champa

title: Cherokee

search: cherokee the cherokee are a people native to the southeastern united states whose nation adopted a written syllabary in the 1820s and survived the forced removal known as the trail of tears, continuing today as several federally recognized nations including the eastern band in north carolina. at european contact in the sixteenth century the cherokee held a homeland spanning parts of present-day north carolina, south carolina, georgia, alabama and tennessee. sequoyah completed an 85-character syllabary for cherokee in 1821, after twelve years of work, enabling mass literacy within a short time. in 1838 and 1839 united states troops under general winfield scott forcibly removed most cherokee to territory west of the mississippi, a journey remembered as the trail of tears, in which many died. some cherokee avoided removal by hiding in the north carolina mountains or claiming state citizenship. their descendants formed the eastern band of cherokee indians, based on the qualla boundary. the cherokee nation in oklahoma and the eastern band are among the largest native american nations in the united states today.

title: Chinchorro Culture

title: Chola Dynasty

title: Christianity

title: Confucianism

search: confucianism confucianism is a chinese tradition of ethics and social order built on the teaching of confucius (551 to 479 bce), which became the official ideology of imperial china under the han dynasty and shaped government and family life across east asia. confucius was an itinerant teacher during china's warring states period who sought but largely failed to gain lasting influence as a government adviser in his own lifetime. his disciples compiled his sayings after his death as the analects, the central text of the tradition. a key teaching, filial piety, extends genuine respect and care for parents into a model for loyalty within the wider political order. under the han dynasty, confucianism became the state's official ideology, and an imperial examination system tested officials on confucian texts, a practice that shaped chinese government for centuries. the tradition spread beyond china to vietnam, korea and japan, shaping their systems of government and social norms, including their own examination systems modeled on china's.

title: Daoism

search: daoism daoism is a chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in harmony with the dao, "the way," traditionally traced to the sage laozi and later developed into organized religious movements alongside its philosophical school. laozi, traditionally placed in the sixth century bce, is credited as the founding figure, though modern scholars think the text attributed to him, the dao de jing, was likely compiled by multiple hands after his time. zhuangzi (about 369 to 286 bce) was a major later interpreter, and the book bearing his name is considered even more wide-ranging than the dao de jing. its central principle, wuwei, "nonaction," describes spontaneity and noninterference with the natural order rather than passive idleness. organized religious daoism began later, marked by the celestial masters movement founded when zhang daoling reported revelations from a deified laozi in 142 ce. daoist philosophy and religious practice both continued alongside confucianism in chinese life, sometimes overlapping with folk religion, making a precise adherent count difficult to give.

title: Etruscans

search: franks the franks were a germanic people who moved into roman gaul and built one of early medieval europe's most powerful kingdoms, first under the merovingian dynasty of clovis i and later under the carolingians, whose most famous ruler was charlemagne. the franks appear in roman records in the third century ce on the lower rhine and expanded into gaul as roman power weakened. clovis i of the merovingian dynasty defeated the last major roman official in gaul in 486 and had united the frankish tribes by about 501. clovis converted to catholic christianity, and his people's adoption of it helped unite the franks and set them apart from neighboring germanic kingdoms that followed other christian traditions. the merovingians ruled until the eighth century, when pepin the short, with papal support, founded the carolingian dynasty. the carolingian kingdom peaked under charlemagne and later divided among his descendants. its territories became the basis of medieval france, germany and the holy roman empire (not yet a vault note).

title: Funan

title: Garifuna

title: Ghana Empire

search: ghana empire the ghana empire, called wagadu by its own people, was a soninke state in the western sahel whose wealth rested on the trans-saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory. its exact extent, its end, and the role of outside conquest are debated. the empire lay in what is now southeastern mauritania, western mali, and eastern senegal. most scholars accept an origin in the 8th or 9th century. the soninke people formed its foundation. its wealth was linked to the growth of regular trans-saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory, which supported larger towns and territorial expansion to control trade routes. the capital is believed to have been at koumbi saleh, on the edge of the sahara. the description left by al-bakri in 1067 or 1068 says the capital consisted of two towns joined by continuous habitations. some accounts say the capital was sacked about 1076 by the almoravids of north africa, perhaps in retaliation for ghana's attempt to control trade held by saharan commercial centres. the empire declined in the 12th century, when competing trade routes opened further east and a prolonged dry spell hurt agriculture. tradition says the city was destroyed by sundiata in 1240 and what remained was absorbed into the mali empire.

title: Gupta Empire

search: gupta empire the gupta empire ruled much of northern india from about 320 to 550 ce and is often associated with a flowering of mathematics, astronomy, and the arts. the astronomer and mathematician aryabhata (born 476) worked in this period and gave an accurate value of pi. the decimal place-value system with zero as a digit was developed in india; see  zero and place-value notation . nalanda, a major buddhist center of learning, flourished. 'golden age' is a later label; historians debate how far it applies.

title: Göktürk Khaganate

title: Han Dynasty

title: Haudenosaunee Confederacy

search: haudenosaunee confederacy the haudenosaunee (iroquois) confederacy is a political union of indigenous nations in the northeastern woodlands of north america, formed centuries before european contact. the original five nations were the mohawk, oneida, onondaga, cayuga, and seneca; the tuscarora joined in the 18th century. the great law of peace is the oral constitution of the confederacy. clan mothers have the power to appoint and remove chiefs. estimates of the founding date range from about 1142 to the 15th century; scholars disagree.

title: Hawaiian Kingdom
sum: The Hawaiian Kingdom was a Native Hawaiian monarchy united by Kamehameha I between about 1795 and 1810 and overthrown in 1893. The United States annexed the islands in 1898; the annexation's legality remains disputed.
search: hawaiian kingdom the hawaiian kingdom was a native hawaiian monarchy united by kamehameha i between about 1795 and 1810 and overthrown in 1893. the united states annexed the islands in 1898; the annexation's legality remains disputed. kamehameha i conquered oʻahu in 1795 and gained kauaʻi and niʻihau by negotiation in 1810; sources differ on the founding year. the hawaiian kingdom's farmers worked taro terraces and fishponds in mountain-to-sea ahupuaʻa; exports shifted from sandalwood to sugar, boosted by an 1875 united states treaty. the kapu system of taboos ended in 1819, a written constitution followed in 1840, and britain and france recognized independence in 1843. introduced diseases cut the native hawaiian population to about 71,000 by 1853. after the 1848 great māhele, commoners' successful claims under the 1850 kuleana act covered under one percent of the land. an armed militia forced the 1887 bayonet constitution on kalākaua. in 1893 a committee of safety, with united states marines ashore, deposed liliuokalani. about 21,000 petitioned against annexation in 1897; congress annexed the islands in 1898.

title: Hinduism

title: Kalinago

title: Ordovician Period

search: ordovician period the ordovician period, from 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, is the second period of the paleozoic era. it is the interval of a great rise in marine biodiversity, the first evidence of plants on land, and, at its close, the first of the "big five" mass extinctions. the ordovician period spans 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago. its base is defined at green point, newfoundland, by the conodont iapetognathus fluctivagus, and its top at dob's linn in scotland by a graptolite. the great ordovician biodiversification, running for tens of millions of years from the early period, greatly increased the diversity of marine animals. sea level was very high, and warm shallow seas held reefs, brachiopods, trilobites, crinoids and graptolites. straight-shelled nautiloid cephalopods, some several metres long, were large predators. the earliest evidence of land plants, spores about 470 million years old, comes from this period; see  colonization of land . the climate cooled late in the period, and an ice age centred on gondwana set in during the hirnantian. the  late ordovician extinction , about 445 to 443 million years ago, removed an estimated 85 percent of species, mostly marine.

title: Paleogene Period
sum: The Paleogene Period, from 66 to 23.03 million years ago, is the first period of the Cenozoic Era. It is the interval in which mammals expanded after the end-Cretaceous extinction and the world moved from a warm, largely ice-free state…

title: Paleolithic

title: Paleoproterozoic Era

title: Permian Period

title: Pleistocene Epoch
sum: The Pleistocene Epoch (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago) is the age of recurring ice sheets. The genus Homo evolved and spread during it.

title: Silurian Period

title: Tonian Period

title: Triassic Period

title: Upper Paleolithic

title: 1918 Influenza Pandemic

title: African Humid Period

search: african humid period the african humid period, or green sahara, ran from about 14,800 to between 5,500 and 5,000 years ago, when the sahara held lakes, rivers, and savanna instead of desert, driven by a stronger monsoon. its end is debated: marine records show an abrupt collapse, archaeological records a slower, staggered desiccation. a marine sediment core off mauritania shows a low-dust interval from about 14,800 to 5,500 years ago, read as an abrupt onset and end. radiocarbon dating of roughly 150 sites across the eastern sahara instead shows humid conditions beginning suddenly around 8,500 bce, then drying out gradually, region by region, over thousands of years. a later synthesis proposed the end was locally abrupt but happened progressively later toward lower latitudes, reconciling the two pictures. onset and end occurred at similar levels of northern hemisphere summer sunlight, consistent with a threshold set by the precession cycle, one of the milankovitch cycles, amplified by vegetation and soil-moisture feedbacks. evidence for the wetter sahara includes rock art at tassili n'ajjer showing hippopotamuses and giraffes, lakeside cemeteries at gobero, niger, and fossil river networks visible only under satellite radar. similar episodes recurred over at least 800,000 years. a 2025 ancient-dna study at takarkori, libya, found a largely isolated north african ancestry, complicating the idea that the green sahara was always an open migration corridor.

title: Assembly of Pangaea

title: Banded Iron Formations
sum: Banded iron formations are ancient sedimentary rocks of alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers, deposited mostly between about 3.8 and 1.8 billion years ago. They are a major source of the world's iron ore.
search: banded iron formations banded iron formations are ancient sedimentary rocks of alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers, deposited mostly between about 3.8 and 1.8 billion years ago. they are a major source of the world's iron ore. the layers are usually millimetres to centimetres thick. the oldest are about 3.8 billion years old, in greenland, and deposition peaked about 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, with great deposits in western australia, south africa and the lake superior region of north america. the leading explanation is that oxygen-poor seawater held dissolved iron, which was oxidized and settled out when oxygen or other oxidants appeared. whether oxygen-producing bacteria or iron-using photosynthetic bacteria did most of the work is debated. deposition largely ended about 1.8 billion years ago, probably as the deeper ocean lost its dissolved iron, and a few late formations appear during the cryogenian ice ages; see  snowball earth . ore derived from these rocks is a major source of the iron used in steelmaking today.

title: Bantu Expansion
sum: Bantu-speaking peoples spread from a homeland in West-Central Africa (present-day Nigeria and Cameroon) across central, eastern, and southern Africa over about four thousand years.
search: bantu expansion bantu-speaking peoples spread from a homeland in west-central africa (present-day nigeria and cameroon) across central, eastern, and southern africa over about four thousand years. today about 350 million people speak one of roughly 500 bantu languages; estimates of the number of languages range from about 440 to 680, depending on how languages are counted. linguistic and archaeological evidence trace the spread from about 3000 bce. the expansion is associated with farming and, in places, iron working. it involved migration, intermarriage, and language shift, not only population replacement.

title: Battle of Adwa
sum: The Battle of Adwa, fought on 1 March 1896, saw the Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeat an invading Italian force, securing Ethiopia's independence.
search: battle of adwa the battle of adwa, fought on 1 march 1896, saw the ethiopian army under emperor menelik ii decisively defeat an invading italian force, securing ethiopia's independence. ethiopian forces numbered roughly 73,000 to over 100,000 against about 14,500 to 18,000 italian and colonial troops. more than 6,000 of the italian army were killed, slightly more than half of them italians and the rest african askari, and between 3,000 and 4,000 of those fighting under italian command were taken prisoner. the war arose from a dispute over article 17 of the treaty of wuchale, which read differently in amharic and italian. in october 1896 italy signed the treaty of addis ababa, abrogating wuchale.

title: Battle of Kadesh
sum: The Battle of Kadesh, fought around 1274 BCE near the Orontes River in what is now Syria, pitted Ramesses II of Egypt against Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire in one of the largest chariot battles on record.
search: battle of kadesh the battle of kadesh, fought around 1274 bce near the orontes river in what is now syria, pitted ramesses ii of egypt against muwatalli ii of the hittite empire in one of the largest chariot battles on record. ancient and modern estimates put the number of chariots involved in the thousands on both sides. the outcome was indecisive, and both sides claimed victory. ramesses commemorated the battle in temple reliefs and texts at abu simbel, karnak, and other sites. hittite and egyptian accounts both survive, which is unusual for the period. about fifteen years later the two powers concluded a peace treaty, around 1259 bce, of which versions survive in both egyptian and hittite archives.

title: Battle of Talas
sum: The Battle of Talas in 751 CE, near the Talas River in present-day Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, pitted a Tang Chinese army against an Abbasid army, and ended in Tang defeat.
search: battle of talas the battle of talas in 751 ce, near the talas river in present-day kyrgyzstan and kazakhstan, pitted a tang chinese army against an abbasid army, and ended in tang defeat. the tang army was led by gao xianzhi, and karluk mercenaries in the tang army are reported to have defected, though sources differ on whether the karluks were abbasid allies from the start. the defeat, followed by the an lushan rebellion beginning in 755, ended tang expansion in central asia. a tradition holds that chinese captives taught papermaking to the islamic world at samarkand; historians debate the role of the battle in the transfer of the technology. paper mills were operating in samarkand and baghdad by the later 8th century. it is often used as a symbolic marker of islamic influence in central asia.

title: Bengal Famine of 1943
sum: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people in British-ruled Bengal during World War II. Historians debate its causes, but agree that it was not simply a shortage of food and that wartime policy played a large part.
search: bengal famine of 1943 the bengal famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people in british-ruled bengal during world war ii. historians debate its causes, but agree that it was not simply a shortage of food and that wartime policy played a large part. estimates of deaths from starvation, malaria, and other disease range widely, from about 800,000 to 3.8 million. a scholarly consensus is often given as about 2.1 million, with some estimates of 2.7 to 3 million. the economist amartya sen argued that the famine was an entitlement failure: food supply in bengal did not fall sharply, but economic pressures prevented certain groups from buying it. after burma and singapore fell to japan in 1942, rice imports from those countries stopped, which worsened bengal's food crisis. british prime minister winston churchill has been criticized for war priorities and refusal to divert food to bengal. the war cabinet discussed requests for more grain shipments to india several times in late 1943 and early 1944, citing limited shipping and the need to keep reserves for military operations.

title: Black Death
sum: The Black Death was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that swept through Eurasia and North Africa from 1346 to 1353.
search: black death the black death was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium yersinia pestis that swept through eurasia and north africa from 1346 to 1353. it likely killed 30 to 60 percent of europe's population, and estimates for eurasia as a whole run to tens of millions of deaths, with some as high as 75 to 200 million. it spread along trade routes, via fleas on rodents and on people. labor shortages after the pandemic raised wages in parts of europe. plague returned in waves for centuries.

title: Boxer Rebellion
sum: The Boxer Rebellion (1899 to 1901) was an anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in northern China, supported by the Qing court, that ended with defeat by an eight-nation alliance.
search: boxer rebellion the boxer rebellion (1899 to 1901) was an anti-foreign, anti-christian uprising in northern china, supported by the qing court, that ended with defeat by an eight-nation alliance. the boxers (the 'righteous and harmonious fists') attacked foreign missionaries and chinese christians. the empress dowager cixi eventually backed the movement and declared war on foreign powers. an eight-nation alliance relieved the besieged legations in beijing. the boxer protocol of 1901 imposed a large indemnity on china.

title: Breakup of Pangaea
sum: Pangaea, the supercontinent that had assembled by about 300 million years ago, began to split about 200 million years ago, opening the Atlantic Ocean and reshaping the map of the world.
search: breakup of pangaea pangaea, the supercontinent that had assembled by about 300 million years ago, began to split about 200 million years ago, opening the atlantic ocean and reshaping the map of the world. rifting began in the late triassic to early jurassic, and the central atlantic opened first. large volcanic outpourings, the central atlantic magmatic province, coincided with the triassic-jurassic extinction, about 200 million years ago. the south atlantic opened much later, in the early cretaceous. alfred wegener proposed continental drift in 1912; plate tectonics gained wide acceptance in the 1960s. continental motion continues today.

title: British Raj
sum: The British Raj was the period of direct British rule over the Indian subcontinent, from 1858 to 1947. It began when the Crown took over from the East India Company after the Rebellion of 1857 and ended with the independence and partition…
search: british raj the british raj was the period of direct british rule over the indian subcontinent, from 1858 to 1947. it began when the crown took over from the east india company after the rebellion of 1857 and ended with the independence and partition of india and pakistan. the government of india act, passed on 2 august 1858, transferred authority over india from the east india company to the british crown, as a response to the indian rebellion of 1857. the company lost all its administrative powers, and its territories and armed forces passed to the crown. the company itself was formally dissolved by an act of parliament in 1874. the act created a cabinet-level secretary of state for india and a fifteen-member council of india in london. in calcutta the governor-general became head of the government of india and was called the viceroy. the raj lasted until the independence of india and pakistan in 1947.

title: Bronze Age Collapse
sum: Around 1200 BCE, many states of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East collapsed within a few decades, ending the Late Bronze Age palace economies.
search: bronze age collapse around 1200 bce, many states of the eastern mediterranean and near east collapsed within a few decades, ending the late bronze age palace economies. the hittite empire fell, mycenaean palaces were destroyed, and ugarit was burned. egyptian inscriptions record attacks by the 'sea peoples', around 1177 bce. proposed causes include drought, earthquakes, migrations, and the breakdown of trade networks. egypt survived but was weakened.

title: Bølling-Allerød Warming
sum: The Bølling-Allerød was an abrupt warm interval from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago, the first major warming after the Last Glacial Maximum. It ended just as abruptly with the onset of the Younger Dryas.
search: bølling-allerød warming the bølling-allerød was an abrupt warm interval from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago, the first major warming after the last glacial maximum. it ended just as abruptly with the onset of the younger dryas. the interval ran from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago, following the oldest dryas, the final cold stage of the retreat from the last glacial maximum. warming was abrupt and large in the northern hemisphere, while the southern hemisphere cooled slightly at the same time, a pattern seen in other rapid climate shifts. boreal forest and birch woodland spread across western europe and the north european plain, including doggerland, replacing tundra vegetation. a pulse of rapid sea-level rise, meltwater pulse 1a, began within the interval as the laurentide and eurasian ice sheets lost mass quickly; estimates of the rise range from roughly 10 to 20 meters over a few centuries. the interval was briefly interrupted by the older dryas, a cold spell of one to two centuries whose evidence is strongest in northern europe, leading some to debate whether it was global or regional. it ended abruptly with the onset of the  younger dryas , which itself lasted until about 11,700 years ago, when the holocene began.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic
sum: The COVID-19 pandemic was a global outbreak of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first identified in late 2019.
search: covid-19 pandemic the covid-19 pandemic was a global outbreak of the coronavirus sars-cov-2, first identified in late 2019. the world health organization declared a pandemic on 11 march 2020 and ended the global health emergency on 5 may 2023. more than 7 million deaths were officially reported; who estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 (range 13.3 to 16.6 million), nearly three times the reported covid deaths for that period. vaccines using mrna technology were developed and authorized within about a year. lockdowns, remote work, and supply-chain disruption affected economies worldwide.

title: Cambrian Explosion
sum: The Cambrian Explosion is the relatively rapid appearance, over roughly 13 to 25 million years starting 538.8 million years ago, of most major animal body plans in the fossil record.
search: cambrian explosion the cambrian explosion is the relatively rapid appearance, over roughly 13 to 25 million years starting 538.8 million years ago, of most major animal body plans in the fossil record. animals with hard parts, such as shells and exoskeletons, appear widely. famous fossil sites include the burgess shale in canada and chengjiang in china. ediacaran precursors show that animals existed before the cambrian. oxygen levels, ecological arms races, and developmental genetics are all proposed contributors.

title: Campanian Ignimbrite Eruption
sum: The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption of the Campi Flegrei caldera near Naples, Italy, about 39,850 years ago, was the largest explosive eruption in Europe in roughly the last 200,000 years. Its ash spread across the Mediterranean and Eastern…
search: campanian ignimbrite eruption the campanian ignimbrite eruption of the campi flegrei caldera near naples, italy, about 39,850 years ago, was the largest explosive eruption in europe in roughly the last 200,000 years. its ash spread across the mediterranean and eastern europe, and its role in neanderthal decline around the same time is debated. a 2017 study combining radiocarbon and argon dating with a synchronized varve chronology dated the eruption precisely to about 39,850 years ago. the eruption released roughly 181 to 265 cubic kilometers of magma, a volcanic explosivity index of 7, the largest in europe in about 200,000 years. its ash, the y-5 layer, dispersed over about 3 million square kilometers and is used as a dated marker in sediment cores from the mediterranean to the russian plain. the eruption fell close to the onset of heinrich event 4, a severe cold phase, but records show the ash postdates that onset by roughly 700 to 800 years, complicating a simple eruption-triggers-cooling account. climate modeling found the cooling and acid deposition lasted only one to two years and that the most intense cooling largely missed the western european areas where late neanderthal populations lived. at several italian sites, modern-human-associated stone tools appear stratigraphically before the ash layer, and some recalibrated neanderthal extinction dates predate the eruption too; some researchers still argue it shaped cultural change further east, where modeled cooling was stronger.

title: Carboniferous Coal Forests
sum: The Carboniferous coal forests were swamp forests of wet tropical lowlands, mostly in the later Carboniferous, about 323 to 299 million years ago. Their buried plant matter became much of the world's coal.
search: carboniferous coal forests the carboniferous coal forests were swamp forests of wet tropical lowlands, mostly in the later carboniferous, about 323 to 299 million years ago. their buried plant matter became much of the world's coal. the forests grew mainly on the lowlands of the northern continent of euramerica and in parts of china, and included tree-sized club-mosses such as lepidodendron, tree ferns, giant horsetails and early conifers. repeated rises and falls of sea level, linked to the late paleozoic ice age, drowned and re-exposed the swamps and stacked many separate coal seams. at joggins in nova scotia, hollow fossil tree stumps contain remains of early amphibians and reptiles. burial of plant carbon lowered atmospheric carbon dioxide and probably raised oxygen. coal from these rocks fuelled the  industrial revolution  in britain and other regions. about 305 million years ago the wet tropical forests collapsed into isolated patches as the climate became drier and cooler, an event linked to declines among amphibians and the rise of reptiles.

title: Chinese Reform and Opening
sum: Beginning in December 1978, China under Deng Xiaoping introduced market reforms and opened to foreign trade, and over the following decades the economy grew rapidly.
search: chinese reform and opening beginning in december 1978, china under deng xiaoping introduced market reforms and opened to foreign trade, and over the following decades the economy grew rapidly. the reforms were launched at the third plenum of the 11th central committee in december 1978. agricultural reforms, the household responsibility system, replaced collective farming in the early 1980s. special economic zones, including shenzhen, were established starting in 1980. china's economy grew at high rates, averaging roughly nine to ten percent a year for several decades. hundreds of millions of people were lifted out of extreme poverty.

title: Classic Maya Collapse
sum: Between about 800 and 950 CE, many Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands were abandoned or stopped building monuments, while Maya communities elsewhere continued.
search: classic maya collapse between about 800 and 950 ce, many classic maya cities of the southern lowlands were abandoned or stopped building monuments, while maya communities elsewhere continued. the last dated monument in the long count calendar, at tonina, is from 909 ce. populations in the southern lowlands fell sharply, but the maya did not disappear: several million people speak mayan languages today. cities of the northern yucatan, such as chichen itza, flourished afterwards. proposed causes include severe droughts, shown in cave and lake records, warfare, political fragmentation, and environmental degradation. no single cause is accepted.

title: Closure of the Isthmus of Panama
sum: The Isthmus of Panama, traditionally dated to about 3 million years ago, joined North and South America, closed a sea passage between the Pacific and Atlantic, and triggered a major exchange of land animals.
search: closure of the isthmus of panama the isthmus of panama, traditionally dated to about 3 million years ago, joined north and south america, closed a sea passage between the pacific and atlantic, and triggered a major exchange of land animals. the land bridge allowed the great american biotic interchange, in which mammals crossed between the continents. ground sloths, armadillos, and opossums moved north; cats, dogs, horses, and other groups moved south. the closure ended the exchange of pacific and atlantic waters at low latitudes and is thought to have strengthened atlantic circulation. the timing is debated: some studies argue for a much earlier start to the land connection, while others support about 3 million years ago. northern glaciation began at about the same time.

title: Cold War
sum: The Cold War (about 1947 to 1991) was a global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, fought mainly through arms races, alliances, and proxy wars.
search: cold war the cold war (about 1947 to 1991) was a global rivalry between the united states and the soviet union and their allies, fought mainly through arms races, alliances, and proxy wars. the rivals formed alliances (nato in 1949, the warsaw pact in 1955) and stockpiled nuclear weapons. the cuban missile crisis of october 1962 is often called the closest approach to nuclear war. proxy wars included korea (1950 to 1953) and vietnam. the berlin wall stood from 1961 to 1989; the soviet union dissolved in december 1991.

title: Collapse of the Soviet Union
sum: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991 after the revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe and a failed coup in August 1991, ending the Cold War.
search: collapse of the soviet union the soviet union dissolved on 26 december 1991 after the revolutions of 1989 in eastern europe and a failed coup in august 1991, ending the cold war. the berlin wall opened on 9 november 1989. mikhail gorbachev's reforms of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) began in the mid-1980s. hardliners attempted a coup from 18 to 22 august 1991 and failed. russia, ukraine, and belarus agreed to dissolve the union on 8 december 1991. fifteen successor states emerged.

title: Collision of India and Asia
sum: The Indian plate collided with Eurasia beginning about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, and the convergence continues today.
search: collision of india and asia the indian plate collided with eurasia beginning about 50 million years ago, raising the himalaya and the tibetan plateau, and the convergence continues today. india separated from gondwana and drifted north, unusually fast for a continental plate. most estimates place the start of collision at about 50 to 55 million years ago, and the final closure of the tethys ocean between about 50 and 60 million years ago. the collision built the himalaya, whose highest peak, mount everest, is 8,848.86 meters by the 2020 china-nepal survey. india still converges on asia at a few centimeters a year. the uplift shaped the south asian monsoon and the sources of the indus, ganges, and brahmaputra rivers.

title: Colonization of Land
sum: Plants, then arthropods and vertebrates, moved onto land beginning about 470 million years ago, transforming the planet's surface.
search: colonization of land plants, then arthropods and vertebrates, moved onto land beginning about 470 million years ago, transforming the planet's surface. the earliest land plant spores are found in ordovician rocks (about 470 million years old). forests appeared in the devonian, and vast swamp forests in the carboniferous formed coal. early tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fishes; see  tiktaalik . land plants changed soils, rivers, and the carbon cycle.

title: Columbian Exchange
sum: The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492.
search: columbian exchange the columbian exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the americas and the rest of the world after 1492. the term was coined by historian alfred crosby in 1972. old world diseases such as smallpox caused catastrophic mortality among indigenous peoples of the americas; estimates of the loss vary widely, from about 50 to 95 percent of the population by 1650. maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and cassava spread worldwide, and horses, cattle, and wheat spread to the americas. the exchange underpinned the growth of european empires and the  atlantic slave trade .

title: Congo Free State
sum: The Congo Free State (1885 to 1908) was a vast territory in Central Africa ruled as the personal possession of King Leopold II of Belgium, notorious for forced labor in rubber and ivory collection and for mass deaths.
search: congo free state the congo free state (1885 to 1908) was a vast territory in central africa ruled as the personal possession of king leopold ii of belgium, notorious for forced labor in rubber and ivory collection and for mass deaths. the berlin conference recognized leopold's claim to most of the congo basin in 1884 to 1885, on the pretext of philanthropy. forced labor quotas, hostage-taking, and mutilation were used to force rubber collection. estimates of the decline in the congolese population range from about 1 million to 15 million, with about 10 million the most commonly cited central figure; the numbers are contested. international outcry led belgium to take over the colony in 1908.

title: Control of Fire
sum: Human ancestors began controlling fire at least around a million years ago, and habitual fire use is well established by about 400,000 years ago.
search: control of fire human ancestors began controlling fire at least around a million years ago, and habitual fire use is well established by about 400,000 years ago. evidence at wonderwerk cave in south africa dates to about one million years ago. burned seeds, wood, and flint at gesher benot ya'aqov in israel suggest human control of fire nearly 790,000 years ago. earlier claims, at about 1.5 million years, are disputed. cooked food is easier to chew and digest, and may have supported larger brains.

title: Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction
sum: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) extinction, about 66 million years ago, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and about three-quarters of species after an asteroid struck what is now Mexico.
search: cretaceous-paleogene extinction the cretaceous-paleogene (k-pg) extinction, about 66 million years ago, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and about three-quarters of species after an asteroid struck what is now mexico. the chicxulub impact crater lies beneath the yucatan peninsula. a global layer rich in iridium, an element common in asteroids, was reported by luis and walter alvarez and colleagues in 1980. volcanism in the deccan traps probably contributed to the stress on ecosystems. birds, descended from small feathered dinosaurs, survived; see  dinosaurs .

title: Crusades
sum: The Crusades were a series of religiously sanctioned military expeditions launched by Western European Christians from 1095, largely to capture and hold Jerusalem and other holy sites in the Levant.
search: crusades the crusades were a series of religiously sanctioned military expeditions launched by western european christians from 1095, largely to capture and hold jerusalem and other holy sites in the levant. pope urban ii called for the first crusade at the council of clermont in 1095. the first crusade captured jerusalem in 1099 and established crusader states. saladin retook jerusalem in 1187. the fourth crusade sacked the christian city of constantinople in 1204. the last crusader stronghold on the mainland, acre, fell to the mamluks on 28 may 1291.

title: Deccan Traps Eruptions
sum: The Deccan Traps eruptions were a huge outpouring of lava in west-central India, with the main phases at about 66.3 to 65.5 million years ago. They overlap the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, and their role in it is debated.
search: deccan traps eruptions the deccan traps eruptions were a huge outpouring of lava in west-central india, with the main phases at about 66.3 to 65.5 million years ago. they overlap the end-cretaceous mass extinction, and their role in it is debated. the deccan traps are among the largest volcanic provinces on earth; the lava flows pile up to more than two kilometres thick in the western ghats and once covered well over a million square kilometres. radiometric dating places most of the volume within about a million years around the cretaceous-paleogene boundary, with large pulses both before and after the chicxulub impact. the relative timing is debated. the eruptions released carbon dioxide and sulfur gases, which could have caused warming, cooling episodes and acid rain, and stressed ecosystems before the impact. some recent studies conclude that the impact, not the volcanism, was the main driver of the extinction; the question remains open. the eruptions are linked to the réunion hotspot, which india passed over as it drifted north.

title: Decolonization
sum: Decolonization was the process by which most colonies of European empires became independent states, mainly between 1945 and 1975.
search: decolonization decolonization was the process by which most colonies of european empires became independent states, mainly between 1945 and 1975. the united nations began with 51 members in 1945 and has 193 today, largely from decolonization. india and pakistan became independent in 1947; ghana, in 1957, was the first sub-saharan african colony to gain independence; 17 african states became independent in 1960. independence was won through both negotiation and war, for example in algeria (1962). the portuguese colonial empire in africa ended in 1974 to 1975, after the carnation revolution of april 1974 overthrew the regime in lisbon.

title: Devonian Forests and the Rise of Trees
sum: The Devonian forests were the first forests on Earth, appearing about 385 million years ago and spreading through the rest of the period. Trees evolved independently in several plant lineages, and their roots and litter changed soils,…
search: devonian forests and the rise of trees the devonian forests were the first forests on earth, appearing about 385 million years ago and spreading through the rest of the period. trees evolved independently in several plant lineages, and their roots and litter changed soils, rivers and the carbon cycle. the gilboa fossil forest in new york, about 385 million years old, holds some of the oldest known fossil trees, including cladoxylopsids with hollow trunks. archaeopteris, a tree with woody trunks and fern-like foliage that grew more than ten metres tall, formed forests across several continents in the late devonian. trees arose independently in several plant lineages during the devonian and carboniferous, including club-mosses, relatives of horsetails and ancestors of seed plants. deep roots speeded the chemical weathering of rock and built soils, and atmospheric carbon dioxide fell over the devonian, which may have contributed to later cooling. some researchers link the spread of forests to nutrient runoff and ocean oxygen loss at the time of the  late devonian extinction ; the link is debated.

title: Digital Revolution
sum: The Digital Revolution is the spread of digital computing and networks from the mid-20th century on, including the internet (from 1969) and the World Wide Web (from 1989 to 1991).
search: digital revolution the digital revolution is the spread of digital computing and networks from the mid-20th century on, including the internet (from 1969) and the world wide web (from 1989 to 1991). the first message on arpanet, a precursor of the internet, was sent in 1969. tim berners-lee proposed the world wide web in 1989 and it became public in 1991. smartphones, from about 2007, put networked computers in billions of pockets. more than five billion people now use the internet.

title: Divergence of the Hominin Lineage
sum: The hominin lineage, the line leading to humans, split from the line leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago in Africa.
search: divergence of the hominin lineage the hominin lineage, the line leading to humans, split from the line leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago in africa. genetic estimates of the split depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times: one 2006 study placed it no earlier than about 6.3 million years ago, while studies using longer generation times imply earlier dates. early candidate hominins include  sahelanthropus tchadensis  (about 7 million years ago). upright walking (bipedalism) is a key early trait; see  australopithecus afarensis . a 2006 genetic study proposed that the split was gradual, with interbreeding between the lineages for a time, though this model is disputed.

title: Domestication of Maize
sum: Maize (corn) was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, and became a staple crop across the Americas.
search: domestication of maize maize (corn) was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in southwestern mexico about 9,000 years ago, and became a staple crop across the americas. genetic studies trace maize to the wild teosinte zea mays subsp. parviglumis. five major morphological differences separate maize from teosinte, and regions throughout the genome contributed to the change. early maize had tiny cobs; selection over thousands of years produced large ears. the maya and aztecs treated maize as sacred; cooking it with lime (nixtamalization) makes its nutrients available. maize is now among the world's most-produced crops by volume.

title: Domestication of Rice
sum: Rice (Oryza sativa) was domesticated from wild rice in the Yangtze River region of China beginning around 9,000 to 7,000 years ago, over a long process rather than a single event.
search: domestication of rice rice (oryza sativa) was domesticated from wild rice in the yangtze river region of china beginning around 9,000 to 7,000 years ago, over a long process rather than a single event. wild ancestor populations of rice are usually identified as oryza rufipogon. early evidence for rice use and cultivation comes from yangtze valley sites such as shangshan, where rice phytoliths date to about 9,000 years ago, and later kuahuqiao and hemudu. domestication traits such as non-shattering seed heads appeared gradually over thousands of years. the japonica subspecies is generally traced to the yangtze region; the indica subspecies is thought to have arisen through later crossing with other rice populations, an origin that is debated. rice is a staple for more than half of the world's population.

title: Domestication of the Dog
sum: Dogs descend from a now-extinct population of Pleistocene wolves, but when and where domestication happened is one of the most disputed dates in the whole domestication record. Genetic studies place the split from the nearest known wolf…
search: domestication of the dog dogs descend from a now-extinct population of pleistocene wolves, but when and where domestication happened is one of the most disputed dates in the whole domestication record. genetic studies place the split from the nearest known wolf relatives at roughly 40,000 to 20,000 years ago; the oldest widely accepted dog remains, from bonn-oberkassel in germany, are about 14,200 years old. a 2020 study of 27 ancient dog genomes found all dogs share ancestry distinct from any wolf population sampled today, descending from a single extinct pleistocene lineage. the same and related studies place the genetic divergence at roughly 40,000 to 27,000 years ago, with some estimates extending to about 20,000; no tighter date is agreed. whether domestication happened once or twice, in separate eurasian wolf populations that later merged, is argued both ways; a large 2020 study favors a single origin, but other ancient-wolf-genome work has reopened the dual-origin question. the bonn-oberkassel dog, buried with two humans about 14,200 years ago, is one of the first remains universally agreed to be a dog rather than a wolf. older candidate "paleolithic dogs" from goyet cave, belgium, and předmostí, czech republic, roughly 30,000 years or more, remain disputed: their skulls do not clearly exclude wolves, and one předmostí specimen is genetically closer to wolves. evidence points to an origin somewhere in eurasia, often argued to be siberia, though the region is unsettled.

title: Dutch East India Company

title: Eocene-Oligocene Transition

title: Milankovitch Cycles and the Ice Ages

search: amanitore amanitore was a queen of the kingdom of kush who co-ruled from the capital meroe alongside a king, natakamani, usually thought to be her son, during a prosperous period in the middle of the 1st century ce. kushite royal women held the title kandake, often rendered "candace"; inscriptions and temple reliefs show amanitore depicted with the same royal regalia and war imagery as natakamani, suggesting genuinely shared rule rather than a purely ceremonial role. the pair sponsored a major building program, including temples at meroe, naqa and amara, among the best-preserved kushite monuments to survive. a relief at the lion temple at naqa shows amanitore, like natakamani, smiting bound captives, an image of royal power normally reserved for kings elsewhere in the nile valley tradition. her exact reign dates are not fixed by any king list; estimates for the coregency center on the middle of the 1st century ce, though some run earlier, and it is sometimes placed as contemporary with the roman emperor nero.

title: Ambiorix
sum: Ambiorix (active 54 to 53 BCE) was co-ruler of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe in what is now eastern Belgium, remembered for destroying a Roman legion during a revolt against Julius Caesar's occupation of Gaul.
search: ambiorix ambiorix (active 54 to 53 bce) was co-ruler of the eburones, a belgic tribe in what is now eastern belgium, remembered for destroying a roman legion during a revolt against julius caesar's occupation of gaul. he shared kingship of the eburones with an older co-ruler, cativolcus, an arrangement caesar's own account describes but does not fully explain. in the winter of 54 bce he lured a roman force under quintus titurius sabinus and lucius aurunculeius cotta out of its fortified camp with false promises of safe passage, then ambushed and destroyed it, killing both commanders. caesar responded with a campaign of deliberate devastation against the eburones intended to eliminate the tribe entirely, but ambiorix himself escaped capture and vanishes from the historical record after 53 bce. nearly everything known about him comes from caesar's own commentarii de bello gallico, written to justify caesar's conduct of the war to a roman audience.

title: Amir Khusrau
sum: Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) was the leading court poet of the Delhi Sultanate, writing in Persian while drawing on the Indian world around him. He is regarded as the founding figure of Indo-Persian literature and is traditionally credited…

title: Amrita Sher-Gil

title: Anacaona

title: Andrea Palladio
sum: Andrea Palladio (1508 to 1580) was a Renaissance architect from the Republic of Venice whose villas and churches, and an illustrated treatise, turned Roman classicism into a portable style. His influence is arguably the widest of any…
search: andrea palladio andrea palladio (1508 to 1580) was a renaissance architect from the republic of venice whose villas and churches, and an illustrated treatise, turned roman classicism into a portable style. his influence is arguably the widest of any single architect in western history. palladio was born andrea di pietro della gondola in padua in 1508. he was apprenticed to a stonemasons' guild and moved to vicenza to work as a carver. the nobleman gian giorgio trissino gave him a classical education, renamed him "palladio" after pallas athena, and took him to rome to measure and draw ancient ruins. his remodelling of the medieval basilica of vicenza, dated to 1546 in some sources, made his name. for three decades he designed country villas for the venetian nobility and churches in venice. in 1570 he published i quattro libri dell'architettura, part treatise and part illustrated catalogue of his buildings. he died in 1580, at either vicenza or maser. key works include the villa rotonda (1566 to about 1592), the teatro olimpico (1580 to about 1585) and san giorgio maggiore in venice (1566 to 1610). he worked out room proportions using simple musical ratios he believed produced harmony, and built in brick with stucco finished to imitate stone to keep costs down. the four books carried his style to england, where inigo jones and lord burlington built a palladian movement, and to colonial america. thomas jefferson owned and annotated a copy and drew on it for monticello and the rotunda of the university of virginia. vicenza's historic centre and the palladian villas of the veneto are a unesco world heritage site.

title: Antoni Gaudí
sum: Antoni Gaudí (25 June 1852 to 10 June 1926) was the leading architect of Catalan Modernisme, the regional cousin of Art Nouveau. Almost all his mature work stands in Barcelona, and it culminates in the still-unfinished Sagrada Família.
search: antoni gaudí antoni gaudí (25 june 1852 to 10 june 1926) was the leading architect of catalan modernisme, the regional cousin of art nouveau. almost all his mature work stands in barcelona, and it culminates in the still-unfinished sagrada família. gaudí was born in reus or possibly the neighbouring riudoms, catalonia (sources differ, and from 1915 he himself said riudoms), the youngest son of a coppersmith. he credited his father's workshop with teaching him to see three-dimensional space. he graduated from the barcelona school of architecture in 1878. the industrialist eusebi güell noticed a display case he designed for a glove-maker at the paris world's fair and became his patron for the rest of his career. he never married, grew increasingly devout, and by his sixties lived an almost monastic life devoted to the sagrada família. on 7 june 1926 he was struck by a tram while walking to church in shabby clothes. mistaken for a beggar, he received delayed care and died on 10 june. he was buried in the crypt of his unfinished basilica. he modelled forms on nature and hung scale models of chains and sandbags, photographed upside down, to find the ideal shape for a compression-only arch. he revived trencadís, mosaic of broken tile, as a cheap weatherproof skin. key works include casa vicens (1883 to 1885), palau güell (1886 to 1888), park güell (1900 to 1914), casa batlló (about 1904 to 1906) and casa milà (about 1906 to 1912; sources differ, and one gives both as built between 1904 and 1910). modernist critics dismissed him after his death; salvador dalí and the surrealists were early champions. seven of his works are a unesco world heritage site. the sagrada família is funded by ticket sales and donations, and its main towers are targeted for completion around the centenary of his death.

title: Aristotle
sum: Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist who studied logic, ethics, politics, physics, and biology, and tutored Alexander of Macedon.

title: Artemisia Gentileschi
sum: Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1654) was an Italian Baroque painter, known for powerful heroines painted with Caravaggesque drama. She was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing.
search: artemisia gentileschi artemisia gentileschi (1593 to about 1654) was an italian baroque painter, known for powerful heroines painted with caravaggesque drama. she was the first woman admitted to florence's academy of the arts of drawing. artemisia was born in rome on 8 july 1593, the eldest child of the painter orazio gentileschi, a friend and follower of caravaggio. she trained in his workshop and painted susanna and the elders by the age of 17. in 1611 she was raped by agostino tassi, a painter working with her father. at the seven-month trial in 1612 she was tortured with thumbscrews to test her testimony. tassi was convicted and sentenced to exile from rome, but the exile was never carried out and he spent less than a year in prison. she married the florentine painter pierantonio stiattesi and moved to florence, where she won the patronage of grand duke cosimo ii de' medici, befriended galileo galilei and in 1616 was admitted to the accademia delle arti del disegno. she learned to read and write in these years. from about 1630 she settled in naples. about 1638 she travelled to london to join her father at the court of charles i. she is thought to have died in naples about 1654, though some have speculated she died in the naples plague of 1656. she specialised in strong women from the bible and ancient history: judith, susanna, jael, cleopatra and lucretia. she often lent her own features to saints and allegories. key works include susanna and the elders (1610), judith slaying holofernes (first version about 1612 to 1613, second version about 1614 to 1620) and self-portrait as the allegory of painting (about 1638 to 1639). after her death many works were credited to her father or others. the art historian roberto longhi wrote about her in 1916, and from the 1970s feminist scholars, notably mary d. garrard, made her a central figure. the national gallery, london, held an exhibition in 2020.

title: Ashoka
sum: Ashoka (about 304 to 232 BCE) was a Mauryan emperor who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent and became a patron of Buddhism after a bloody war.

title: Ashurbanipal
sum: Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE. He is known for his conquests, for the royal library at Nineveh, and for palace reliefs showing war and lion hunts.

title: Attila

title: Augustus

title: Ba Trieu

title: Ban Zhao

search: ban zhao ban zhao (about 45 to about 117 ce) was a chinese historian and scholar of the eastern han dynasty who helped complete the book of han after her brother's death and wrote lessons for women. she was also a tutor and adviser at court. ban zhao was born about 45 ce (some sources say about 49) into a scholarly family. her father ban biao and her brother ban gu wrote much of the book of han (hanshu), a history of the western han dynasty. ban gu died in prison in 92 ce with the history unfinished, and ban zhao helped complete it by supplying the missing part of the eight tables. she served at the imperial court as a tutor to the empress and her ladies and, from about 106 ce, as an adviser to the regent empress deng. she is believed to have written lessons for women (nüjie), in seven chapters, about 106 ce, though the date is not firmly established. it argues that girls should be educated and sets out rules of conduct for wives. later writers used lessons for women as a standard text for teaching girls obedience, and modern scholars disagree on whether it reinforced or challenged limits on women. she died about 117 ce; some sources say about 120.

title: Basawan

title: Basil II
sum: Basil II (958 to 1025) was Byzantine emperor for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in Roman or Byzantine imperial history, remembered above all for his decades-long war against the First Bulgarian Empire.
search: basil ii basil ii (958 to 1025) was byzantine emperor for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in roman or byzantine imperial history, remembered above all for his decades-long war against the first bulgarian empire. he became co-emperor as a child in 960 but did not gain full personal control of the government until about 989, when he was in his thirties, after suppressing rebellions by powerful aristocratic generals including bardas skleros and bardas phokas. his long campaigns against bulgaria culminated in the decisive battle of kleidion in 1014, after which bulgaria was absorbed into the byzantine empire by 1018, earning him the later epithet "bulgar-slayer" (boulgaroktonos). a story recorded by later chroniclers claims he blinded thousands of bulgarian prisoners after kleidion, leaving one eye to each of every hundredth man to lead the rest home; modern historians debate how literally this account should be taken. he left the imperial treasury full and the empire at its greatest territorial extent since the 7th century, but died without an heir, and the strong central rule he had imposed did not survive his less capable successors.

title: Behzad
sum: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād (also spelled Bihzad, born about 1455 to 1460 and died about 1535) is the most celebrated painter in the Persian tradition. He led the royal manuscript workshops at Herat and later Tabriz, and many works are attributed…
search: behzad kamāl ud-dīn behzād (also spelled bihzad, born about 1455 to 1460 and died about 1535) is the most celebrated painter in the persian tradition. he led the royal manuscript workshops at herat and later tabriz, and many works are attributed to him on grounds of style. behzād was probably born about 1455 to 1460 in herat, capital of the timurid dynasty founded by  timur . orphaned young, he was brought up by the painter mirak naqqash, head of the royal library, and was protected by the poet and minister mir ali-shir nava'i. under sultan husayn bayqara, who ruled herat from 1469 to 1506, he became the leading artist of the royal kitabkhana, the library workshop. his most famous surviving works date from this period, including paintings in a bustan of sa'di (1488) and a khamsa of nizami (1494 to 1495). after herat fell to the uzbeks in 1506 and then to the safavid shah ismail i in about 1510, he moved to tabriz, where in 1522 ismail appointed him director of the royal library. he died about 1535. a legend says that during the battle of chaldiran in 1514 the shah hid behzād in a cave, in some tellings together with a famous calligrapher, because he valued him more than his army. his figures have individual faces and gestures and are often busy with everyday tasks. he often hid his signature discreetly in the architecture of a painting. his followers mir sayyid ali and abd al-samad trained in his tradition and went on to found the mughal imperial workshop under humayun and akbar. his name became a byword for excellence, which led to many false attributions. scholars debate which works are by his own hand.

title: Buster Keaton

search: buster keaton buster keaton (1895 to 1966) was an american silent-film comedian, writer and director known as the deadpan "great stone face," who built his comedy on engineered physical stunts he performed himself. ranked with charlie chaplin among silent comedy's defining stars, he made the general (1926), now considered among the greatest films ever made. born in 1895 into a vaudeville family, keaton performed from age three in the act the three keatons, taking falls that built his later physical control. he entered film in 1917 under roscoe "fatty" arbuckle, and by 1920 was writing, directing and starring in his own comedies, moving into features with  our hospitality  (1923).  sherlock jr. title: Caravaggio
sum: Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio (1571 to 1610), was an Italian painter who transformed European painting around 1600 with harsh theatrical light and street-level realism. His turbulent life ended at 38, but his influence spread…
search: caravaggio michelangelo merisi, called caravaggio (1571 to 1610), was an italian painter who transformed european painting around 1600 with harsh theatrical light and street-level realism. his turbulent life ended at 38, but his influence spread across europe within a generation. caravaggio was born in milan in september 1571. his name comes from the nearby town his family came from. he trained in milan with simone peterzano and arrived in rome about 1592. cardinal francesco maria del monte took him into his household. his first public commission, two large paintings of st matthew for the contarelli chapel in san luigi dei francesi (1599 to 1600), caused a sensation. several later altarpieces were rejected as indecorous. police records list brawls, assaults and insults. in 1606 he killed a man, ranuccio tomassoni, and fled rome under sentence of death. he then lived in naples, malta and sicily. he died in july 1610 at porto ercole in tuscany, on his way to rome hoping for a papal pardon. he painted directly on the canvas, apparently without preparatory drawings, from live models posed under a single strong light. his backgrounds are dark and bare (tenebrism). key works include judith beheading holofernes (about 1599 to 1602, sources differ), the calling of saint matthew (1599 to 1600) and supper at emmaus (1601). the "caravaggisti" included orazio and artemisia gentileschi, jusepe de ribera, georges de la tour and the utrecht painters, and through them his influence reached  diego velázquez  and  rembrandt van rijn . a 1951 exhibition in milan came within the twentieth-century revival of a reputation that had faded, though sources do not name it as the cause.

title: Catherine de' Medici

search: catherine de' medici catherine de' medici (1519 to 1589) was queen of france and, as mother to three kings, one of the most powerful figures in france during the wars of religion between catholics and huguenots. born into the powerful medici banking family of florence, she married the future henry ii of france in 1533 and became queen in 1547. after henry's death in 1559 she was the chief political influence for her sons francis ii, charles ix and henry iii, though she was not formally regent under francis ii or henry iii and held the regency only for charles ix (as gouvernante de france from december 1560 until august 1563), during a period of escalating conflict between catholics and protestant huguenots. she is widely held responsible, though the exact extent of her role is debated, for approving the assassination of huguenot leaders, which began with the shooting of admiral coligny on 22 august 1572 (he survived, then was killed two days later as the massacre began) and triggered the st. bartholomew's day massacre in august 1572, in which about 2,000 to 3,000 huguenots were killed in paris and more in other cities. she pursued marriage alliances and diplomacy across europe to secure the valois dynasty's position, though her efforts did not prevent the eventual extinction of the valois line with the death of her last son in 1589.

title: Chandragupta Maurya
sum: Chandragupta Maurya (about 340 to 297 BCE) founded the Maurya Empire, the first political power to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 321 BCE.
search: chandragupta maurya chandragupta maurya (about 340 to 297 bce) founded the maurya empire, the first political power to unite most of the indian subcontinent, after overthrowing the nanda dynasty of magadha around 321 bce. with guidance from the strategist chanakya (kautilya), chandragupta seized the throne of magadha and took the throne of magadha. the arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to chanakya, was long linked to his administration, but most scholars now date it to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries ce and doubt that it describes his reign. between about 305 and 303 bce he fought the diadoch ruler seleucus i nicator; the resulting settlement ceded territory in the northwest to the maurya and included a marriage alliance, while seleucus received war elephants in return. the greek ambassador megasthenes, sent to chandragupta's court at pataliputra, wrote the indica, a major but now fragmentary source on mauryan india. later jain tradition holds that chandragupta abdicated, became an ascetic under bhadrabahu, and died by ritual fasting (sallekhana) at shravanabelagola in karnataka, though this account survives mainly in sources written well after his reign.

title: Charlemagne
sum: Charlemagne (c. 748 to 814) was king of the Franks who conquered much of western and central Europe and was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome on Christmas Day 800.
search: charlemagne charlemagne (c. 748 to 814) was king of the franks who conquered much of western and central europe and was crowned emperor by the pope in rome on christmas day 800. he became sole king of the franks in 771. he conquered the lombards in italy, the saxons, and parts of spain's northern border. pope leo iii crowned him emperor on 25 december 800. his court promoted a revival of learning, the carolingian renaissance, and the spread of a clear minuscule script. his empire was divided among his descendants after his death in 814 and, under the treaty of verdun in 843, split into three kingdoms.

title: Charles Darwin
sum: Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) was an English naturalist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection, published in 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.

'the descent of man' (1871) applied the theory to human origins. modern genetics later provided the mechanism of inheritance that darwin lacked.

title: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
sum: Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868 to 1928) was a Glasgow architect-designer who led the "Glasgow Style" of Art Nouveau, treating buildings, furniture and interiors as one unified art. His Glasgow School of Art and total interior schemes made…
search: charles rennie mackintosh charles rennie mackintosh (1868 to 1928) was a glasgow architect-designer who led the "glasgow style" of art nouveau, treating buildings, furniture and interiors as one unified art. his glasgow school of art and total interior schemes made him a major influence on european design, though home recognition came only after his death. born in glasgow in 1868, mackintosh trained as an architect while attending evening classes at the glasgow school of art, where he met his future wife, artist margaret macdonald. with macdonald, her sister frances and herbert macnair, he formed "the four," a symbolist group whose style became the glasgow style. at honeyman and keppie he won an anonymous 1896 competition for his own art school's new building; its 1909 completion made his reputation. he then designed houses, tearooms and a school around glasgow, including hill house (1902-1904), the willow tearooms (1903) and scotland street school (1903-1906), with macdonald designing the furnishings throughout. his towering ladder-back chairs, shaped as much to define a room as to be sat in, became his best-known design. commissions dried up after 1910, through changing taste and his own difficult manner with clients; by 1914 he had left glasgow for england. in the 1920s he and macdonald settled in southern france, where he turned to watercolours; he returned to london for cancer treatment and died there in 1928, in obscurity and hardship. though nearly forgotten in britain by his death, his work had already shaped josef hoffmann and the wiener werkstätte via the 1900 vienna secession, and now ranks among the era's most important architect-designers.

title: Chico Mendes
sum: Chico Mendes (Francisco Alves Mendes Filho, 1944 to 1988) was a Brazilian rubber tapper, union leader and environmental activist in the state of Acre. He organized rubber tappers to defend the forest against clearing for cattle ranching…

title: Christopher Dresser
sum: Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and…
search: christopher dresser christopher dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. he worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism. dresser was born in glasgow in 1834 and trained at the government school of design in london. he lectured on botany and in 1859 received a doctorate from the university of jena for research into plant structure. he moved into design from about 1858, with ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onwards (sources differ on the start), and published the art of decorative design (1862) and principles of decorative design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface. in 1876 and 1877 he travelled to japan, one of the first western designers to do so, partly on commission from tiffany & co. to report on japanese art and manufacturing. he designed for minton, wedgwood, coalbrookdale, hukin & heath and james dixon & sons, and was art superintendent of the linthorpe art pottery. he died in 1904. he reduced plants and shells to underlying geometry and embraced industrial methods, electroplating and moulded earthenware, that many reformers rejected. key works include an electroplated teapot (1879), a toast rack (about 1880) and the linthorpe "sea urchin" vase. he was long overshadowed by william morris and the craft wing of the aesthetic movement and has been substantially rediscovered since the late 20th century. his insistence that a mass-made object could be both functional and beautiful anticipated principles usually credited to the bauhaus.

title: Christopher Wren
