title: Saladin
sum: Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
search: saladin saladin (salah ad-din yusuf ibn ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a kurdish-born muslim commander who founded the ayyubid dynasty, ruled egypt and much of syria, and recaptured jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187. saladin was born about 1137 in tikrit, in present-day iraq, to a kurdish family, and died in damascus on 4 march 1193. he rose in the service of the zengid ruler nur ad-din and became vizier of fatimid egypt in 1169. in 1171 he ended the fatimid caliphate and restored egypt's allegiance to the abbasid caliph; his family, the ayyubids, went on to rule egypt and syria. after nur ad-din died in 1174 he took damascus and brought much of syria and northern mesopotamia under his rule. on 4 july 1187 his army destroyed a crusader army at the battle of hattin. jerusalem surrendered on 2 october 1187, and its latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved. in the third crusade he fought richard i of england. the treaty of ramla (september 1192) left the crusaders a coastal strip and allowed christian pilgrims to visit jerusalem.

title: Sappho
sum: Sappho (about 630 to about 570 BCE) was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos whose songs of love, longing and ritual were collected in at least eight books, possibly nine, in antiquity. Only fragments survive, plus one complete…
search: sappho sappho (about 630 to about 570 bce) was a greek lyric poet from the island of lesbos whose songs of love, longing and ritual were collected in at least eight books, possibly nine, in antiquity. only fragments survive, plus one complete poem. sappho was born about 630 bce on lesbos in the eastern aegean, in mytilene or eresos according to ancient sources; her dates are approximate. she composed songs in aeolic greek to be sung with a lyre, and the sapphic stanza is named after her. ancient scholars gathered her poems in at least eight books, possibly nine. only fragments survive, apart from one complete poem, a prayer to aphrodite (fragment 1). new papyrus fragments published in 2004 and 2014 added lines, including a poem that mentions her brothers. many surviving poems express desire for women. scholars debate whether her circle on lesbos was a religious association, a school for girls, or a social group. ancient sources say she spent time in exile in sicily and had a daughter, cleis. the biography is largely unreliable. the words "sapphic" and "lesbian" derive from her name and her island.

title: Savitribai Phule
sum: Savitribai Phule (1831 to 1897) was an Indian educator, poet and social reformer in Maharashtra who, with her husband Jyotirao Phule, opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848. She died of plague in 1897 after nursing…
search: savitribai phule savitribai phule (1831 to 1897) was an indian educator, poet and social reformer in maharashtra who, with her husband jyotirao phule, opened one of the first schools for girls in pune in 1848. she died of plague in 1897 after nursing patients. savitribai phule was born on 3 january 1831 in naigaon, maharashtra, and married jyotirao phule in 1840 as a child. he taught her to read. in 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in pune. she is often called india's first woman teacher; earlier girls' schools existed, so the "first" claim is contested, and historians also credit fatima sheikh as a co-worker. accounts say she was harassed with stones and dung on her way to teach. she and jyotirao later opened further schools, including for children of lower castes, and in 1863 they founded a home for the prevention of infanticide. she published a book of poetry,  kavya phule , in 1854. she died on 10 march 1897 in pune after catching plague while nursing patients during an outbreak.

title: Seondeok
sum: Queen Seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 CE) ruled the Korean kingdom of Silla as its first reigning queen, a period marked by Buddhist temple building, early astronomical observation and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of…
search: seondeok queen seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 ce) ruled the korean kingdom of silla as its first reigning queen, a period marked by buddhist temple building, early astronomical observation and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of baekje and goguryeo. she succeeded her father, king jinpyeong, in 632 after he left no surviving son, becoming silla's first female monarch in her own right. her reign saw the construction of cheomseongdae, often described as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in east asia, and the hwangnyongsa nine-story pagoda, built to help protect the kingdom according to buddhist belief. silla faced repeated attacks from baekje during her reign, including the loss of border fortresses, and she decided to form a military alliance with tang china, with her general kim yushin and diplomat kim chunchu, later king muyeol, traditionally credited with the negotiations. a rebellion by the noble bidam against her rule broke out in 647 and was suppressed by kim yushin and kim alcheon shortly after her death that same year, which some accounts link to the unrest.

title: Sequoyah
sum: Sequoyah (about 1770 to 1843) was a Cherokee silversmith who created the Cherokee syllabary, a writing system for the Cherokee language, completed by 1821. It is one of the few writing systems whose invention by a single known person is…
search: sequoyah sequoyah (about 1770 to 1843) was a cherokee silversmith who created the cherokee syllabary, a writing system for the cherokee language, completed by 1821. it is one of the few writing systems whose invention by a single known person is well documented. sequoyah was born about 1770 in the cherokee town of tuskegee, in present-day tennessee; the birth year is approximate. he did not read or write english. he began work on a writing system for cherokee about 1809 and completed it by 1821. the syllabary has 85 characters (86 in early versions), each standing for a syllable. the system spread rapidly among the cherokee. the cherokee phoenix, a newspaper printed in cherokee and english, began publication in 1828 and was the first native newspaper in the united states. he later lived among cherokee who had moved west of the mississippi river. he died in august 1843 in mexico while searching for a group of cherokee said to have settled there.

title: Sergei Eisenstein
sum: Sergei Eisenstein (1898 to 1948) was a Soviet film director and theorist, born in Riga, who argued that meaning came from the collision between shots rather than any single image. His Odessa Steps massacre sequence in Battleship Potemkin…
search: sergei eisenstein sergei eisenstein (1898 to 1948) was a soviet film director and theorist, born in riga, who argued that meaning came from the collision between shots rather than any single image. his odessa steps massacre sequence in battleship potemkin (1925) remains one of cinema's most studied passages. eisenstein was born in riga in 1898, son of an architect and civil engineer, and trained in engineering and architecture before turning to the arts. the russian revolution pushed him into theatre; he joined meyerhold's proletkult theatre before moving into film in the early 1920s. his second feature,  battleship potemkin  (1925), made for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 revolution, brought him international fame. in  strike  (1925) he pioneered "intellectual montage," cutting colliding images together and favoring crowds and non-professional "types" over trained stars. invited to hollywood then mexico in the early 1930s, both projects went unfinished, and his 1937 soviet film  bezhin meadow  was suppressed and reportedly destroyed. he regained official favor with  alexander nevsky  (1938), scored by sergei prokofiev, extending his editing style to sound and mass combat. he spent his final years on  ivan the terrible ; part i won a stalin prize, but part ii, completed in 1946, was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958; eisenstein died of a heart attack in moscow in 1948. his writings, including  film form  and  the film sense , became foundational film-studies texts, and he is ranked among cinema's most important directors and theorists.

title: Sesshū Tōyō
sum: Sesshū Tōyō (1420 to 1506) was a Japanese Zen monk and painter who studied Chinese ink painting in Ming China and made it a Japanese art. He is regarded as the greatest master of Japanese ink painting.
search: sesshū tōyō sesshū tōyō (1420 to 1506) was a japanese zen monk and painter who studied chinese ink painting in ming china and made it a japanese art. he is regarded as the greatest master of japanese ink painting. sesshū was born in 1420 in bitchū province (present-day okayama prefecture) and entered a zen temple as a boy. he studied painting at shōkoku-ji in kyoto with the monk-painter tenshō shūbun. about the 1460s he took the name sesshū ("snow boat") and settled in yamaguchi under the patronage of the ōuchi family. in 1467 he joined a trade mission to ming china and spent about two to three years there (sources differ), travelling to beijing and receiving an honorary title at the tiantong monastery near ningbo. he returned to japan about 1469, as the ōnin war was tearing kyoto apart, and worked in the provinces from his studio, the unkoku-an, in yamaguchi. he is credited with designing several temple gardens and died in 1506. he painted in suibokuga, black ink and water on paper or silk, including the loose haboku ("broken ink") manner. key works include haboku landscape (1495), huike offering his arm to bodhidharma (1496) and view of ama-no-hashidate (about 1501 to 1506). six of his works are designated national treasures of japan, more than any other painter. the unkoku school continued his studio, and hasegawa tōhaku styled himself sesshū's fifth-generation heir. in 1956 the world peace council named him one of its "great cultural figures".

title: Shaka
sum: Shaka kaSenzangakhona (about 1787 to 1828) was the founder of the Zulu Kingdom, who transformed its military and political organization.
search: shaka shaka kasenzangakhona (about 1787 to 1828) was the founder of the zulu kingdom, who transformed its military and political organization. he came to power around 1816 and expanded the zulu state quickly. he is credited with new weapons and tactics, including the short stabbing spear and a 'buffalo horns' formation. he was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brothers. much of what is told about him comes from colonial-era european accounts and oral tradition, and is debated.

title: Shen Zhou
sum: Shen Zhou (1427 to 1509) was a scholar-painter of Ming-dynasty China who founded the Wu School in Suzhou. He never held office, and his landscapes combine painting, poetry and calligraphy as a record of friendship and quiet life.
search: shen zhou shen zhou (1427 to 1509) was a scholar-painter of ming-dynasty china who founded the wu school in suzhou. he never held office, and his landscapes combine painting, poetry and calligraphy as a record of friendship and quiet life. shen zhou was born in 1427 near suzhou in the jiangnan region, into a wealthy family of scholars, poets and collectors. his grandfather and father were painters, and the family avoided government service. he never sat the civil service examinations. when local officials recommended him for office he declined, saying he had to care for his widowed mother, who lived to almost 100. his home became a meeting place for suzhou's intellectual elite, and many paintings were made as gifts for friends, marking birthdays, farewells or shared outings. he painted "in the manner of" the four great yuan masters, huang gongwang, wu zhen, ni zan and wang meng. almost every painting carries his own poem in his calligraphy. he was one of the first chinese painters to make albums of real local places around suzhou. key works include lofty mount lu (1467), night vigil (1492) and poet on a mountaintop (about 1500). through his pupil wen zhengming the wu school dominated chinese painting in the 16th century. with wen zhengming, tang yin and qiu ying he is counted among the "four masters of the ming dynasty". according to one story, when forgers sold fake shen zhou paintings, he sometimes signed them to help them earn a living. he died in 1509, aged 82. later theorists such as dong qichang placed him in the "southern school" of literati painters, whom they judged superior to professional court artists.

title: Siddhartha Gautama
sum: Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher in northern India whose teachings founded Buddhism. Traditional dates are about 563 to 483 BCE, but modern scholarship suggests a somewhat later range.
search: siddhartha gautama siddhartha gautama, known as the buddha, was a spiritual teacher in northern india whose teachings founded buddhism. traditional dates are about 563 to 483 bce, but modern scholarship suggests a somewhat later range. buddhist tradition holds that he left a princely life and attained awakening at bodh gaya. his teachings include the four noble truths and the eightfold path. the exact dates of his life are debated among scholars. buddhism later spread across asia via monks and trade routes.

title: Sitting Bull

title: Sofonisba Anguissola

title: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

title: Sukarno

search: sukarno sukarno (1901 to 1970) was the leader of indonesia's independence movement and its first president. he proclaimed independence in 1945, ruled until 1967, and was removed from power after the killings of 1965 and 1966. sukarno was born on 6 june 1901 in surabaya, in the dutch east indies, and died on 21 june 1970 in jakarta, under house arrest. he founded the indonesian national party in 1927. the dutch arrested him in 1929 and released him in 1931, then exiled him to flores in 1934 and to sumatra in 1938. he cooperated with the japanese occupation from 1942 to 1945, which forced millions into labor and whose food requisitions contributed to a famine that killed over a million people in java in 1944 and 1945. on 1 june 1945 he presented pancasila, five founding principles for the state, and on 17 august 1945 he proclaimed independence, becoming president the next day. he hosted the bandung conference of asian and african states in 1955 and introduced "guided democracy" in 1959, ending parliamentary rule. after the 30 september movement of 1965, an army-led campaign killed between 500,000 and over a million people, mostly communists and alleged sympathizers. general suharto took power in 1966 and 1967.

title: Suleiman the Magnificent

search: suleiman the magnificent suleiman the magnificent (1494 to 1566) was ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent, military power, and legal and cultural achievement. his armies captured belgrade in 1521 and rhodes in 1522, then advanced deep into central europe, defeating and killing the king of hungary at the battle of mohacs in 1526, though a first siege of vienna in 1529 failed to take the city. known by the epithet kanuni (the lawgiver), which is absent from sixteenth and seventeenth-century ottoman sources and may date only from the early 18th century, he issued a major legal code harmonizing ottoman civil law with islamic religious law across the empire's diverse territories. his navies under admirals such as barbarossa hayreddin pasha contested mediterranean control with spain and its allies, and ottoman forces also pushed into persia and mesopotamia, capturing baghdad in 1534. his reign saw a major flourishing of ottoman architecture under the chief architect  mimar sinan , and of court poetry, painting, and decorative arts, centered on istanbul.

title: Sun Tzu
sum: Sun Tzu (traditionally about 544 to 496 BCE) is the name attached to The Art of War, the most influential text on military strategy from ancient China, said to have served the state of Wu. Whether he was one historical person is disputed.
search: sun tzu sun tzu (traditionally about 544 to 496 bce) is the name attached to the art of war, the most influential text on military strategy from ancient china, said to have served the state of wu. whether he was one historical person is disputed. tradition places sun tzu, personal name sun wu, as a general who advised king helü of wu in the late 6th century bce. the art of war is organized in about 13 short chapters. the historian sima qian, writing centuries later, told a story of sun tzu proving his discipline by drilling the king's concubines, executing two who disobeyed. scholars treat this as legend. his name appears in no text earlier than sima qian's history, and one theory holds "sun wu" was a made-up title, with the art of war actually the work of his supposed descendant sun bin. in 1972 bamboo strips from a han tomb at yinqueshan included versions of both the art of war and a separate text by sun bin, confirming the art of war circulated early and that sun bin was a distinct author. the text has shaped military and business thought for over two thousand years, and is translated worldwide.

title: Sun Yat-sen

search: sun yat-sen sun yat-sen (1866 to 1925) was a chinese revolutionary and physician who worked for decades to overthrow the qing dynasty and became the first provisional president of the republic of china in 1912. both mainland china and taiwan honor him as a founder. sun yat-sen was born on 12 november 1866 in cuiheng, guangdong, and died on 12 march 1925 in beijing. he was educated in hawaii and trained as a doctor in hong kong, graduating in 1892. he founded the revive china society in 1894, after an earlier reform petition was rejected, and organized several failed uprisings against the qing from 1895 onward. in tokyo in 1905 he founded the tongmenghui, which grew to about a thousand members, and set out his three principles of the people: nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood. the wuchang uprising of 10 october 1911, which he did not lead in person, began the revolution that ended the qing dynasty. he returned from abroad and served as provisional president from 1 january 1912, resigning that march to yuan shikai. he rebuilt his kuomintang party in 1919, and in 1923 allied it with the soviet union and the small chinese communist party. in 1904 he obtained a certificate claiming birth in hawaii in 1870, later renounced; his standard birth year and place are not in doubt.

title: Sundiata Keita

title: Sunni Ali

search: sunni ali sunni ali (ruled about 1464 to 1492) was the ruler who turned songhai from a small state on the niger river into a west african empire, taking timbuktu in 1468 as the mali empire declined. his birth year is unknown. sunni ali became ruler of songhai about 1464, the fifteenth in the sunni dynasty. he conquered timbuktu in 1468 and, after a long siege, the trading city of djenné, taking advantage of the weakening mali empire. he was nominally muslim but tolerated older local religious practice, and this drew tension with muslim scholars in timbuktu, whose chronicles remember him harshly. he died in 1492; accounts differ on whether he drowned crossing a river or died another way. his son sunni baru succeeded him but was overthrown in 1493 by askia muhammad, a general who accused sunni baru of insufficient devotion to islam and founded a new dynasty.

title: Tamar of Georgia

search: tamar of georgia tamar (born about 1160 or 1166, died 1213) ruled the kingdom of georgia from 1184 to 1213, presiding over its political and cultural high point, later called the georgian golden age. she was crowned co-ruler with her father, george iii, in 1178 to secure her succession, then became sole monarch on his death in 1184, ruling with the formal title "king of kings" rather than a feminine equivalent. her armies won major victories against regional muslim powers, including the battle of shamkor in 1195 and the battle of basian (dated to 1202, 1203 or 1204 depending on the source), expanding georgian influence across much of the south caucasus and into parts of armenia and anatolia. her reign saw significant patronage of georgian literature and architecture, including the era's most celebrated work, shota rustaveli's epic poem "the knight in the panther's skin," traditionally associated with her as its inspiration. she was canonized as a saint by the georgian orthodox church, and centuries of later georgian tradition remember her reign as the kingdom's greatest period of security and cultural achievement.

title: Teddy Roosevelt
sum: Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt (1858 to 1919) was the 26th President of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909, known for trust-busting antitrust policy, an assertive foreign policy, and a major expansion of federal land conservation.
search: teddy roosevelt theodore "teddy" roosevelt (1858 to 1919) was the 26th president of the united states, serving from 1901 to 1909, known for trust-busting antitrust policy, an assertive foreign policy, and a major expansion of federal land conservation. he became president in 1901 after the assassination of william mckinley, at 42 the youngest person to hold the office, and was elected in his own right in 1904. he pursued antitrust action against major corporate combinations, including a successful suit against the northern securities company railroad trust in 1904, and mediated the 1902 coal strike partly by threatening to send in federal troops to run the mines. he established the united states forest service and used his executive authority to create national forests, wildlife refuges, and national monuments, protecting roughly 230 million acres of land during his presidency. after leaving office he attempted a comeback in the 1912 election on a progressive "bull moose" third-party ticket, splitting the republican vote and helping elect woodrow wilson instead.

title: Timur

title: Tokugawa Ieyasu

search: tokugawa ieyasu tokugawa ieyasu (1543 to 1616) unified japan after decades of civil war and founded the tokugawa shogunate, a military government that ruled japan for over two and a half centuries. he rose through alliance and conflict with the era's other major warlords, oda nobunaga and toyotomi hideyoshi, before defeating a rival coalition at the battle of sekigahara in 1600. he was appointed shogun by the emperor in 1603, then formally passed the title to his son hidetada in 1605 while continuing to hold real power as retired shogun until his death. he destroyed the remaining toyotomi family stronghold at the siege of osaka castle in 1615, removing the last major rival claim to national authority. his government issued regulations restricting christianity and foreign trade that his successors expanded into the sakoku ("closed country") policy, limiting most foreign contact for over two centuries.

title: Tomyris
sum: Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people east of the Caspian Sea, who according to the Greek historian Herodotus defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE. She is known only from Herodotus, and other ancient…
search: tomyris tomyris was a queen of the massagetae, a nomadic people east of the caspian sea, who according to the greek historian herodotus defeated and killed cyrus the great of persia in 530 bce. she is known only from herodotus, and other ancient accounts of cyrus's death differ. tomyris appears only in book 1 of herodotus's histories, written about a century after the events. her dates are unknown; the date given here is that of the battle in his account. herodotus says she ruled the massagetae, who lived east of the caspian sea near the araxes river, and rejected cyrus's offer of marriage, which he saw as a way to gain her kingdom. in his account the persians captured her son spargapises by trickery, and he killed himself in captivity. tomyris then defeated the persian army in battle. herodotus says she had cyrus's body found and his head put in a wineskin filled with blood. other ancient accounts differ: xenophon has cyrus die peacefully in his palace, and ctesias has him die of a wound in a war on the eastern frontier that the persians won. herodotus compares the massagetae's customs with those of the scythians.

title: Toussaint Louverture
sum: Toussaint Louverture was a formerly enslaved man who became the principal military and political leader of the Haitian Revolution, and died in a French prison in 1803.
search: toussaint louverture toussaint louverture was a formerly enslaved man who became the principal military and political leader of the haitian revolution, and died in a french prison in 1803. he was born into slavery on saint-domingue around 1743 (20 may 1743 in one account) and was freed in 1776 or 1777, depending on the source, before the revolution began in 1791. he began as a lieutenant in the 1791 uprising and at first allied with the spanish of neighboring santo domingo. in 1794 he switched to the french republic, which had abolished slavery, and in 1798 he negotiated the withdrawal of british forces under a treaty with general thomas maitland. on 7 july 1801 he promulgated a constitution asserting his authority over the whole island of hispaniola, which made him governor-general for life. napoleon sent an expedition in 1802; toussaint was arrested by deception and deported to france, where he died at fort de joux in april 1803. jean-jacques dessalines proclaimed haiti's independence on 1 january 1804.

title: Trajan
sum: Trajan (53 to 117 CE) was Roman emperor from 98 to 117, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent and a major program of public building and infrastructure across the Roman world.
search: trajan trajan (53 to 117 ce) was roman emperor from 98 to 117, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent and a major program of public building and infrastructure across the roman world. born in hispania, in present-day spain, he was the first roman emperor born outside italy, adopted as heir by the emperor nerva in 97 after a career as a successful general. his conquest of dacia, commemorated in the reliefs of trajan's column in rome, added a wealthy new province rich in gold mines north of the danube. he extended roman territory to its largest extent by annexing armenia and parts of mesopotamia after a campaign against the parthian empire late in his reign, gains his successor hadrian largely abandoned as unsustainable. his building programs included trajan's forum and market in rome, a new harbor at ostia, and an extensive network of roads and bridges across the provinces, funded substantially by dacian gold.

title: Truganini
sum: Truganini (about 1812 to 1876) was a Tasmanian Aboriginal woman of the Nuenonne people who grew up on Bruny Island and lived through the British colonization of Tasmania and died in Hobart. She was later widely called "the last Tasmanian…
search: truganini truganini (about 1812 to 1876) was a tasmanian aboriginal woman of the nuenonne people who grew up on bruny island and lived through the british colonization of tasmania and died in hobart. she was later widely called "the last tasmanian aboriginal," a label that tasmanian aboriginal people reject. truganini was born about 1812, reportedly at recherche bay in southern tasmania, as a member of the nuenonne people, and she grew up on bruny island. accounts say members of her family were killed or abducted by colonists during the black war of the 1820s and early 1830s. in the 1830s she worked with george augustus robinson, a government-appointed conciliator who persuaded surviving aboriginal people to move to flinders island, where disease and hardship were severe. she later lived at oyster cove, south of hobart, and died on 8 may 1876. her skeleton was exhumed in 1878 and displayed in the tasmanian museum from 1904 until 1947, despite her reported fear of mutilation. in 1976 her remains were cremated and the ashes scattered in the d'entrecasteaux channel. tasmanian aboriginal people today descend from other women, such as fanny cochrane smith, and the community continues.

title: Trưng Sisters
sum: The Trưng Sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị (Chinese Zheng Ce and Zheng Er), led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in northern Vietnam from 40 to 43 CE. Their birth years are unknown; the dates given here are those of the revolt.
search: trưng sisters the trưng sisters, trưng trắc and trưng nhị (chinese zheng ce and zheng er), led a revolt against han chinese rule in northern vietnam from 40 to 43 ce. their birth years are unknown; the dates given here are those of the revolt. the trưng sisters came from mê linh in the red river region, then part of the han commandery of jiaozhi. they began the revolt in 40 ce. chinese sources link it to harsh rule by the han governor su ding, and vietnamese tradition adds that he executed trưng trắc's husband, thi sách. they took towns in several southern commanderies and are recorded as ruling as queens for about three years. the han general ma yuan led an army south and defeated them by 43 ce. the chinese history  hou hanshu  says they were captured and beheaded, while vietnamese tradition says they drowned themselves in a river; this second account is traditional. temples in vietnam honor the sisters today, and streets are named for them (hai bà trưng).

title: Tupaia
sum: Tupaia (about 1725 to 1770) was a priest and navigator from Ra'iatea in the Society Islands who sailed with James Cook on the Endeavour in 1769 and drew a chart of Pacific islands. He died at Batavia in 1770.
search: tupaia tupaia (about 1725 to 1770) was a priest and navigator from ra'iatea in the society islands who sailed with james cook on the endeavour in 1769 and drew a chart of pacific islands. he died at batavia in 1770. tupaia was born about 1725 on ra'iatea and became a priest and navigator. after warriors from borabora took ra'iatea, he took refuge on tahiti. in july 1769 he joined cook's endeavour, usually said to be at tahiti (sources differ on the place), as a guide and interpreter, with a young servant, taiata. in august 1769 he began a chart of the pacific with cook, joseph banks and other officers. sources differ: it is said to show about 130 islands, of which he could name about 74, and it is often described as centered on ra'iatea. the chart did not match european map conventions, and modern scholars have argued that it follows a polynesian way of organizing islands by voyages and directions. on reaching new zealand in october 1769 he could speak with māori, whose language is closely related to tahitian, and he interpreted for the crew. he died at batavia on 20 december 1770, of illness, and taiata died there in the same month.

title: Túpac Amaru II
sum: Túpac Amaru II (José Gabriel Condorcanqui, born 1738 or about 1742, died 1781) was a hereditary Indigenous chief and trader who led a large rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in the Andes in 1780 and 1781. He was executed in Cusco.
search: túpac amaru ii túpac amaru ii (josé gabriel condorcanqui, born 1738 or about 1742, died 1781) was a hereditary indigenous chief and trader who led a large rebellion against spanish colonial rule in the andes in 1780 and 1781. he was executed in cusco. josé gabriel condorcanqui was born in 1738 (some sources say about 1742) in the highlands near cusco. he became a kuraka (hereditary local chief) and a successful muleteer and trader. he took the name túpac amaru, claiming descent from the inca ruler túpac amaru, whom the spanish executed in 1572. grievances behind the rebellion included higher spanish taxes, forced sales of goods to indigenous communities, and the mita, forced labor in mines. on 4 november 1780 he seized a local spanish official, antonio de arriaga, who was executed shortly after (10 november 1780 per two sources), which began the rebellion. he issued proclamations ending the mita and other abuses, and the rebellion spread across the southern highlands. spanish forces captured him in april 1781, and he was executed in cusco on 18 may 1781 together with his wife micaela bastidas, who had helped lead the rebellion.

title: Ulugh Beg
sum: Ulugh Beg (1394 to 1449) was a Timurid ruler and astronomer who built an observatory at Samarkand and produced one of the most accurate star catalogues before the telescope.
search: ulugh beg ulugh beg (1394 to 1449) was a timurid ruler and astronomer who built an observatory at samarkand and produced one of the most accurate star catalogues before the telescope. he became governor of samarkand in 1409, at about sixteen. he built a madrasa (1417 to 1420) and, in 1420, an observatory. his star catalogue, completed by about 1437, lists at least 1,018 stars. he died in 1449 and was buried in the gur-e-amir mausoleum in samarkand, beside his grandfather timur.

title: Usman dan Fodio
sum: Usman dan Fodio (1754 to 1817) was a Fulani scholar and religious leader who led the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate.
search: usman dan fodio usman dan fodio (1754 to 1817) was a fulani scholar and religious leader who led the jihad that created the sokoto caliphate. he taught and preached in the hausa state of gobir and wrote widely in arabic and fulfulde. in 1804 he and his followers left gobir, and the jihad began in february of that year. he is regarded as the founder of the sokoto caliphate and its first sultan or caliph. his brother and his son helped to administer the new state.

title: Utagawa Hiroshige
sum: Utagawa Hiroshige (1797 to 1858) was the last great master of the ukiyo-e woodblock print, a lyrical designer of rain, snow, moonlight and travellers on the road. His series on the Tōkaidō highway and on Edo were huge commercial successes…
search: utagawa hiroshige utagawa hiroshige (1797 to 1858) was the last great master of the ukiyo-e woodblock print, a lyrical designer of rain, snow, moonlight and travellers on the road. his series on the tōkaidō highway and on edo were huge commercial successes and later inspired european artists. hiroshige was born in edo in 1797 into the andō samurai family, whose hereditary job was fire warden at edo castle. both parents died when he was about 12, and he inherited the post. about 1811 he became a pupil of the print designer utagawa toyohiro, who gave him the name hiroshige. he handed the fire warden post to his son in 1823 and turned to landscape after hokusai's fuji series opened a new market. according to tradition he travelled the tōkaidō in 1832 with an official delegation. the prints he published in 1833 to 1834 made him the most popular landscape artist in japan. in 1856 he became a buddhist monk but kept working on one hundred famous views of edo. he died in edo on 12 october 1858, probably in a cholera epidemic. he designed the prints; carvers and printers made them. he used soft colour gradations (bokashi) and, in the edo series, a vertical format with a large foreground object framing a distant view. "hiroshige blue" was made with imported prussian blue. van gogh painted copies of two of his edo prints. whistler's thames nocturnes, monet's japanese bridge at giverny and 1890s art nouveau posters show his influence, and  frank lloyd wright  was a major collector and dealer of his prints.

title: Vincent van Gogh
sum: Vincent van Gogh (30 March 1853 to 29 July 1890) was a Dutch painter who worked in France. He painted for only about ten years, produced around 2,100 works, and sold almost nothing, yet his vivid colour and expressive brushwork made him…
search: vincent van gogh vincent van gogh (30 march 1853 to 29 july 1890) was a dutch painter who worked in france. he painted for only about ten years, produced around 2,100 works, and sold almost nothing, yet his vivid colour and expressive brushwork made him the most famous artist of modern times. van gogh was born in zundert in the southern netherlands, the son of a protestant minister. at 16 he joined the art dealers goupil & cie and was dismissed in 1876. he then tried teaching and preaching among coal miners in the borinage. in 1880 he decided to become an artist. his younger brother theo, an art dealer, supported him for the rest of his life. his letters, mainly to theo, are among the most moving documents of any artist's life. in 1886 he moved to paris, where he met pissarro, toulouse-lautrec, émile bernard and gauguin and discovered impressionist colour and japanese prints. he painted copies of two hiroshige prints. in 1888 he moved to arles. gauguin joined him in october, and the partnership collapsed in december after van gogh cut off part of his own ear. he entered the asylum at saint-rémy in may 1889, where he painted the starry night. in may 1890 he moved to auvers-sur-oise and painted about one canvas a day. he shot himself on 27 july 1890 and died two days later, aged 37. his work comprises around 2,100 pieces, including some 860 oil paintings. key works include the potato eaters (1885), sunflowers (1888) and wheatfield with crows (1890). theo died six months after vincent. theo's widow, johanna van gogh-bonger, promoted the work and published the letters in 1914. the van gogh museum in amsterdam opened in 1973.

title: Vitus Bering
sum: Vitus Bering (1681 to 1741) was a Danish-born officer in the Russian navy who led two expeditions across Siberia to chart the waters between Asia and North America. The strait and sea between the continents carry his name.
search: vitus bering vitus bering (1681 to 1741) was a danish-born officer in the russian navy who led two expeditions across siberia to chart the waters between asia and north america. the strait and sea between the continents carry his name. bering was baptized on 5 august 1681 in horsens, denmark, and joined the russian navy in 1704 under peter the great. he died on 19 december 1741 on the island now named for him. on the first kamchatka expedition (1725 to 1730) he sailed through the strait between siberia and alaska in 1728 without sighting the american coast, though some historians think it was visible. the great northern expedition (1733 to 1743) grew to about 3,000 people, one of the largest scientific undertakings of its time. in 1741 his ship, the st. peter, and a second ship under aleksei chirikov, the st. paul, sailed separately toward america. chirikov's crew sighted land about a day earlier, on 15 july by the dates given in the sources; bering's crew sighted mount saint elias on 16 july. on the return voyage the st. peter wrecked on an uninhabited island. bering died there, a death traditionally put down to scurvy and exposure, though a 1991 analysis of his remains judged heart failure the likely cause; of 77 men aboard, 46 survived to reach kamchatka the next year. the cossack semyon dezhnev had already passed through the strait in 1648, but bering's voyages brought it to european attention, and james cook named it for him in 1778.

title: Wangari Maathai
sum: Wangari Maathai (1940 to 2011) was a Kenyan environmental and political activist who founded the Green Belt Movement, which organized women to plant trees, and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
search: wangari maathai wangari maathai (1940 to 2011) was a kenyan environmental and political activist who founded the green belt movement, which organized women to plant trees, and in 2004 became the first african woman to win the nobel peace prize. maathai was born on 1 april 1940 in ihithe, near nyeri, kenya. she studied biology in the united states and at the university of nairobi, where she received a doctorate in 1971; she is recorded as the first woman in east and central africa to earn one. in 1977 she founded the green belt movement, which organized women to plant tree seedlings against deforestation, soil loss and fuelwood shortage. her campaigns against building projects on public land in nairobi and against forest clearing brought clashes with the government of president daniel arap moi; she was arrested and at times injured. she was elected to parliament in 2002 and served as an assistant minister for the environment from 2003. she received the nobel peace prize in 2004. in the same year a kenyan newspaper reported that she had said hiv was deliberately created by scientists; she denied saying it and stated that she did not hold that belief. she died in nairobi on 25 september 2011.

title: Wassily Kandinsky
sum: Wassily Kandinsky (16 December 1866 to 13 December 1944) was a Russian painter and theorist, one of the first to create purely abstract works in Europe. He believed colours and forms, freed from depicting objects, could move the viewer as…
search: wassily kandinsky wassily kandinsky (16 december 1866 to 13 december 1944) was a russian painter and theorist, one of the first to create purely abstract works in europe. he believed colours and forms, freed from depicting objects, could move the viewer as directly as music. kandinsky was born in moscow and grew up in odessa. he studied law and economics and began an academic career. in 1896, having seen one of monet's haystacks and heard wagner's lohengrin, he gave up law and moved to munich to study painting. in 1911 he and franz marc founded der blaue reiter (the blue rider) and he published on the spiritual in art. about then he painted his first fully abstract works. the first world war forced him back to russia, where he took part in soviet cultural institutions after the 1917 revolution. he returned to germany in 1920 or 1921 (sources differ) and taught at the bauhaus from 1922 to 1933. when the nazis closed the bauhaus he moved to neuilly-sur-seine near paris, becoming a french citizen in 1939, and died there. he sorted his works into impressions, improvisations and compositions, and made only ten compositions over 30 years. he probably experienced synaesthesia and assigned musical qualities to colours: yellow like a trumpet, blue like a deep cello. compositions i to iii were destroyed in the second world war. the guggenheim museum holds more than 150 of his works. his work influenced the abstract expressionists. in 2023 murnau with church ii sold for £37.2 million.

title: Wilfrid Laurier
sum: Wilfrid Laurier (1841 to 1919) was the first French-Canadian Prime Minister of Canada, serving from 1896 to 1911 during a period of rapid western settlement and economic growth.
search: wilfrid laurier wilfrid laurier (1841 to 1919) was the first french-canadian prime minister of canada, serving from 1896 to 1911 during a period of rapid western settlement and economic growth. a lawyer from quebec, he became liberal party leader in 1887 and prime minister in 1896, holding the office for over fifteen years, then the longest unbroken term in canadian history. his government promoted immigration and settlement of the canadian prairies, a policy associated with his minister clifford sifton, that brought large numbers of european immigrant farmers to western canada. he worked to balance relations between english- and french-speaking canada, though his support for canadian participation in britain's boer war strained relations with quebec nationalists who opposed it. he lost the 1911 election over a proposed reciprocity (free trade) agreement with the united states, which opponents attacked as a threat to canada's ties with britain.

title: William Morris
sum: William Morris (1834 to 1896) was an English designer, writer and socialist, the central figure of the Arts and Crafts movement. He rejected cheap mechanised ornament in favour of patterns drawn from nature and made by traditional craft…
search: william morris william morris (1834 to 1896) was an english designer, writer and socialist, the central figure of the arts and crafts movement. he rejected cheap mechanised ornament in favour of patterns drawn from nature and made by traditional craft methods. morris was born in walthamstow in 1834 into a family that had grown wealthy through copper mining. at oxford he met the painter edward burne-jones and, through him, the circle around dante gabriel rossetti. he built red house (1859 to 1860) and, unable to find furnishings he considered well made, founded a decorative arts firm in 1861 with burne-jones, rossetti, philip webb and others. it was reorganised in 1875 as morris & co. he founded the socialist league in 1884 and wrote extensively on politics and utopian fiction. in 1891 he founded the kelmscott press; its illustrated chaucer was completed months before his death in 1896. he designed from real plants, disciplining them into flattened repeating patterns. he revived hand block-printing and indigo-discharge dyeing and letterpress printing from hand-cut type over faster industrial methods. his principle was "have nothing in your house that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful". his goods were luxuries that generally only the wealthy could afford. morris & co. wallpapers and textiles, including strawberry thief (1883) and willow bough (1887), remain in production. the kelmscott chaucer launched the private-press movement.

title: Wu Zetian
sum: Wu Zetian (624 to 705 CE) was the only woman to rule China in her own name as emperor, founding the short-lived Zhou dynasty (690 to 705).
search: wu zetian wu zetian (624 to 705 ce) was the only woman to rule china in her own name as emperor, founding the short-lived zhou dynasty (690 to 705). she entered the palace as a concubine of the tang emperor and later became empress consort. she ruled effectively for decades before taking the throne herself in 690. she expanded the civil service examination system to draw in talent from beyond the aristocracy. she supported buddhism.

title: Xuanzang
sum: Xuanzang (602 to 664) was a Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled overland to India from 629 to 645 in search of authentic scriptures, studied for years at the monastery of Nalanda, and returned to translate texts and record his journey.
search: xuanzang xuanzang (602 to 664) was a chinese buddhist monk who traveled overland to india from 629 to 645 in search of authentic scriptures, studied for years at the monastery of nalanda, and returned to translate texts and record his journey. xuanzang was born in 602 and ordained as a monk in his youth. in 629 he left china without imperial permission, traveling west through central asia toward india. he spent years studying at nalanda, a major center of buddhist learning, under the scholar silabhadra, and visited buddhist sites across the subcontinent. he returned to china in 645 with buddhist texts, images and relics, and was welcomed by the tang court despite his earlier unauthorized departure. with official support he led a translation effort that produced more than a thousand fascicles of buddhist texts rendered from sanskrit into chinese. he also wrote the great tang records on the western regions, a travel account whose distances and descriptions later helped archaeologists locate sites such as nalanda itself. centuries later his journey was reworked into the folk novel journey to the west, adding a fantastical cast around a lightly fictionalized version of him.

title: Yaa Asantewaa
sum: Yaa Asantewaa (about 1840 to 1921) was the queen mother of Ejisu in the Asante kingdom, in present-day Ghana, who led an Asante uprising against British rule in 1900. She died in exile in the Seychelles.
search: yaa asantewaa yaa asantewaa (about 1840 to 1921) was the queen mother of ejisu in the asante kingdom, in present-day ghana, who led an asante uprising against british rule in 1900. she died in exile in the seychelles. yaa asantewaa was born about 1840 and was queen mother (ohemaa) of ejisu, a title held by a woman who advises and helps choose the ruler. the british exiled the asante king prempeh i in 1896. in march 1900 the governor, frederick hodgson, demanded the golden stool, the asante symbol of national unity, so that he could sit on it. according to tradition, she then urged the asante chiefs at a council to resist and became a leader of the uprising sometimes called the war of the golden stool. asante forces besieged the british fort at kumasi for several months in 1900. british reinforcements relieved it, and the fighting ended that year with a british victory. she was captured and exiled to the seychelles in 1901, and died there on 17 october 1921. the british annexed asante in 1902 but did not obtain the golden stool itself.

title: Yermak Timofeyevich
sum: Yermak Timofeyevich (about 1532 to 1585) was a Cossack leader whose expedition across the Urals in 1581 and 1582 overthrew the Khanate of Sibir and began the Russian conquest of Siberia. His early life is poorly known.
search: yermak timofeyevich yermak timofeyevich (about 1532 to 1585) was a cossack leader whose expedition across the urals in 1581 and 1582 overthrew the khanate of sibir and began the russian conquest of siberia. his early life is poorly known. yermak's birth year is uncertain; about 1532 is often given. most accounts say he was a volga cossack, and some say he was wanted for piracy. in 1581 he set out from the ural lands of the stroganov merchant family with several hundred men armed with firearms. accounts of the year and the numbers vary. in 1582 his force defeated the army of khan kuchum of sibir and took the khanate's capital, qashliq (isker), on 26 october. he sent word of the conquest to tsar ivan iv, who reportedly pardoned him and sent gifts. yermak died in august 1585 (some sources say 1584) in an ambush by kuchum's forces. tradition says he drowned in the irtysh river, weighed down by chain mail sent by the tsar. russian forts followed, including tyumen in 1586 and tobolsk in 1587.

title: Yongle Emperor
sum: The Yongle Emperor (Zhu Di; 1360 to 1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty, whose reign moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored the ocean voyages of Zheng He.
search: yongle emperor the yongle emperor (zhu di; 1360 to 1424) was the third emperor of china's ming dynasty, whose reign moved the capital to beijing and sponsored the ocean voyages of zheng he. he seized the throne from his nephew, the jianwen emperor, in a civil war from 1399 to 1402, after his father, the dynasty's founder, had passed over him in the succession. he moved the imperial capital from nanjing to beijing and began construction of the forbidden city in 1405, with most palaces completed by the end of 1417; beijing was officially declared the principal capital in 1420. he commissioned  zheng he 's treasure-fleet voyages, six of the seven falling in his reign (the seventh came under the xuande emperor), the first of which departed in 1405, reaching as far as the coasts of east africa and arabia and projecting ming naval power across the indian ocean. he sponsored the yongle encyclopedia, an enormous compilation of chinese knowledge finished in 1408 that ran to over 11,000 volumes, most of which was later lost.

title: Zenobia
sum: Zenobia (Septimia Zenobia; about 240 to after 272) was queen of the caravan city of Palmyra in present-day Syria. She ruled for her young son and briefly extended Palmyrene control over Roman Egypt, Syria and much of Anatolia before the…
search: zenobia zenobia (septimia zenobia; about 240 to after 272) was queen of the caravan city of palmyra in present-day syria. she ruled for her young son and briefly extended palmyrene control over roman egypt, syria and much of anatolia before the emperor aurelian defeated her in 272. zenobia was the wife of odaenathus, the ruler of palmyra who had fought the sasanian persians for rome in the 260s. he was killed about 267, and she took power as regent for their son vaballathus. about 270 her forces took roman egypt and pushed into anatolia. by 271 she and her son used the titles augusta and augustus. some coins struck in 271 and 272 show aurelian on one side and vaballathus on the other, so her claim was for a time framed inside the roman order. aurelian defeated her armies in 272 at immae and emesa and captured her. palmyra was sacked in 273 after a revolt. her fate is unknown. one tradition says she was shown in aurelian's triumph in 274; its source, the  historia augusta , is often unreliable.

title: Zheng He
sum: Zheng He (1371 to 1433) was a Chinese admiral who led seven large naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa.
search: zheng he zheng he (1371 to 1433) was a chinese admiral who led seven large naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching southeast asia, india, arabia, and east africa. he served the ming emperor yongle and was a muslim of yunnan origin. his fleets included very large ships and thousands of crew members. the voyages displayed ming power and collected tribute; they were then stopped. they came decades before european ocean voyages of the same type.

title: Aksum
sum: Aksum is a town in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia that was the capital of the Kingdom of Aksum, a trading state active from about the 1st century CE to the 7th century and later, known for its stone stelae, coinage and early…
search: aksum aksum is a town in the tigray region of northern ethiopia that was the capital of the kingdom of aksum, a trading state active from about the 1st century ce to the 7th century and later, known for its stone stelae, coinage and early adoption of christianity. aksum lies in the highlands of northern ethiopia, and the periplus of the erythraean sea, a greek trade guide of about the 1st century ce, mentions aksum and its port adulis on the red sea. aksumite rulers minted gold, silver and bronze coins from about the late 3rd century ce, and king ezana adopted christianity around 330 ce; coins struck afterward bear the cross. ezana's inscriptions were written in ge'ez, sabaean and greek. aksum's monolithic stelae mark burial sites; the largest, about 33 meters high, fell and broke, and a 24-meter stele taken to rome by italian forces in 1937 was returned in 2005 and re-erected in 2008. ethiopian christian tradition holds that the church of our lady mary of zion at aksum houses the ark of the covenant; the claim cannot be examined. aksum declined from the 7th century, and proposed causes include changes in red sea trade after the rise of islam, environmental stress and internal conflict; the causes are debated. unesco inscribed aksum in 1980.

title: Amazon River
sum: The Amazon River flows about 6,575 kilometers through Peru, Colombia and Brazil and carries by far the largest volume of any river on Earth, draining a rainforest basin long settled by farming and fishing societies before European contact.
search: amazon river the amazon river flows about 6,575 kilometers through peru, colombia and brazil and carries by far the largest volume of any river on earth, draining a rainforest basin long settled by farming and fishing societies before european contact. the amazon's length, about 6,575 kilometers, and whether it or the nile is the world's longest river are disputed depending on which headwater and mouth channels are counted; its average discharge at the delta, about 224,000 cubic meters per second, is unmatched by any other river. communities along the river and its floodplains built raised fields, mounds and patches of enriched dark earth from at least the 1st millennium bce, evidence used to argue for larger and more settled pre-columbian populations than once assumed. the spanish expedition of francisco de orellana made the first recorded european descent of the river in 1541 to 1542, reaching its mouth on 24 august 1542; orellana's account of fighting women warriors is the traditional source of the river's name. rubber tapped from amazonian trees fed a boom from 1879 to 1912 that enriched cities such as manaus and iquitos and brought forced labor and violence against indigenous peoples, with estimates of about 100,000 deaths across the region in that period; the boom collapsed after rubber plantations in southeast asia entered the market in 1912. deforestation for agriculture, logging and mining has reduced parts of the rainforest, and large dams such as belo monte on a major tributary have displaced communities and altered river flow; the extent of long-term ecological damage is debated.

title: Angkor
sum: Angkor was the capital region of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia, including the temple of Angkor Wat, built in the early 12th century.
search: angkor angkor was the capital region of the khmer empire in present-day cambodia, including the temple of angkor wat, built in the early 12th century. angkor wat is the largest religious monument in the world by area. aerial laser surveys reveal a vast urban area of roughly a thousand square kilometers. a network of reservoirs (barays) and canals managed water. it was declared a unesco world heritage site in 1992. the traditional date of 1431 for the sack of angkor by ayutthaya and its abandonment is now disputed, and angkor wat itself was never abandoned.

title: Antarctica
sum: Antarctica is Earth's southernmost continent, with no indigenous population, first sighted by ships in 1820, reached at its geographic pole by Roald Amundsen in 1911, and governed since 1961 under a treaty that reserves it for peaceful,…
search: antarctica antarctica is earth's southernmost continent, with no indigenous population, first sighted by ships in 1820, reached at its geographic pole by roald amundsen in 1911, and governed since 1961 under a treaty that reserves it for peaceful, scientific use. antarctica covers about 14,200,000 square kilometers under an ice sheet averaging about 1.9 kilometers thick, holding roughly 70 percent of the world's fresh water. the continent's coast was probably first sighted in 1820 by a russian expedition under fabian von bellingshausen and mikhail lazarev, among rival claims from british and american sealers in the same years; the first confirmed landing came in 1895 by a norwegian party. roald amundsen's norwegian team reached the geographic south pole on 14 december 1911, weeks ahead of a british team led by robert falcon scott, whose party died on the return journey. the antarctic treaty, signed in 1959 and in force from 1961, bars military activity, mining, and nuclear testing or waste disposal, reserves the continent for peaceful and scientific use, and sets aside territorial claims among its parties. about 5,000 people work at research stations across antarctica in the southern summer, falling to about 1,000 in winter. warming has been recorded across the continent, with the antarctic peninsula's temperature rising by about 3 degrees celsius since the mid-20th century and the west antarctic ice sheet losing roughly 100 billion metric tons of ice a year since 2002, contributing to projected sea-level rise.

title: Arkaim
sum: Arkaim is a fortified Bronze Age settlement of the Sintashta culture in Chelyabinsk Oblast, in the southern Urals of Russia, occupied from about 2000 to 1700 BCE by older reckoning, with a current dating of about 2050 to 1900 BCE.
search: arkaim arkaim is a fortified bronze age settlement of the sintashta culture in chelyabinsk oblast, in the southern urals of russia, occupied from about 2000 to 1700 bce by older reckoning, with a current dating of about 2050 to 1900 bce. archaeologists identified arkaim in 1987 during surveys ahead of a planned reservoir; the reservoir was cancelled in april 1991 and the site was declared a historical and geographical museum. arkaim had a roughly circular plan, on the order of 160 meters across, with concentric walls of earth, timber and clay around houses set in a ring. arkaim shows evidence of copper and bronze metalworking, and sites of the same culture in the region are associated with graves holding horses and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots. arkaim appears to have been abandoned around 1700 bce, though sources differ on the date; some accounts describe it as burned, and whether by attack, accident or deliberate burning on departure is debated. since the 1990s arkaim has become a tourist and pilgrimage destination and a focus of popular claims that it was an "aryan" homeland or proto-city, claims that professional archaeologists do not accept as established.

title: Athens
sum: Athens is a Greek city that, in the 5th century BCE, became the leading city of the Greek world, with an early form of direct democracy and major achievements in philosophy, drama, and art.
search: athens athens is a greek city that, in the 5th century bce, became the leading city of the greek world, with an early form of direct democracy and major achievements in philosophy, drama, and art. cleisthenes' reforms of about 508 bce established democratic institutions. the parthenon was built between 447 and 432 bce. socrates, plato, and the tragedians worked in athens. athens lost to sparta in the peloponnesian war (431 to 404 bce).

title: Atlantic Ocean
sum: The Atlantic Ocean, the second largest of Earth's oceans at about 85 million square kilometers, became from around 1000 CE a corridor for transoceanic voyages that reshaped the connections among Europe, Africa and the Americas.
search: atlantic ocean the atlantic ocean, the second largest of earth's oceans at about 85 million square kilometers, became from around 1000 ce a corridor for transoceanic voyages that reshaped the connections among europe, africa and the americas. the atlantic covers about 85,133,000 square kilometers, has an average depth of about 3,646 meters, and reaches a maximum depth of 8,376 meters in the puerto rico trench. norse voyagers were the first people known to have crossed the north atlantic, reaching greenland and, around 1000 ce, north america. christopher columbus's 1492 voyage opened sustained, repeated crossings between europe and the americas, beginning an age of european exploration and colonization that the vault treats through the columbian exchange. from the 16th to the 19th centuries the ocean carried the atlantic slave trade; estimates for the number of enslaved africans embarked run to about 12.5 million, of whom roughly 10.7 million are estimated to have survived the crossing. the first transatlantic telegraph cable operated briefly from august to october 1858 before failing; a successful and lasting cable was laid by the ship great eastern in 1866, linking ireland and newfoundland by telegraph. the atlantic remains central to global shipping and fishing, and its western basin is the source of atlantic hurricanes that form there in summer and autumn.

title: Auschwitz-Birkenau
sum: Auschwitz-Birkenau was a complex of Nazi German concentration and extermination camps near the Polish town of Oświęcim, operated from 1940 to January 1945, where at least 1.1 million people, about 960,000 of them Jews, were murdered.
search: auschwitz-birkenau auschwitz-birkenau was a complex of nazi german concentration and extermination camps near the polish town of oświęcim, operated from 1940 to january 1945, where at least 1.1 million people, about 960,000 of them jews, were murdered. auschwitz was established in 1940 near oświęcim, in polish territory annexed by germany, first for polish political prisoners; the camp at birkenau (auschwitz ii) was built from 1941 and became a center of mass murder in gas chambers from 1942, and the monowitz camp (auschwitz iii) supplied forced labor to a chemical works of ig farben. about 1.3 million people were deported to auschwitz and at least 1.1 million of them died; about 960,000 were jews from across occupied europe, and other victims included about 74,000 non-jewish poles, about 21,000 roma and sinti, and about 15,000 soviet prisoners of war. most victims were killed on arrival after selection on the rail platform; others died of forced labor, starvation, disease, shootings and medical experiments. prisoners resisted: in october 1944 members of the sonderkommando revolted and destroyed a crematorium, and escapees, including witold pilecki in 1943 and rudolf vrba and alfred wetzler in 1944, carried reports of the killings to the outside. as soviet forces approached in january 1945, the ss forced tens of thousands of prisoners on death marches, and soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 january 1945, finding about 7,000 prisoners still there. auschwitz-birkenau became a state museum in 1947, and unesco inscribed the site in 1979; 27 january is observed as international holocaust remembrance day.

title: Ayutthaya
sum: Ayutthaya is a city on an island at the meeting of three rivers in central Thailand, traditionally founded in 1350, the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom until the Burmese army destroyed it in 1767, and a major trading port of Southeast…
search: ayutthaya ayutthaya is a city on an island at the meeting of three rivers in central thailand, traditionally founded in 1350, the capital of the ayutthaya kingdom until the burmese army destroyed it in 1767, and a major trading port of southeast asia. ayutthaya lies on an island at the confluence of the chao phraya, lopburi and pa sak rivers, and is traditionally said to have been founded in 1350 by king u thong (ramathibodi i). ayutthaya's forces took angkor in 1431, after which the khmer court moved away from angkor. chinese, japanese, persian, indian and malay merchants traded at ayutthaya; the portuguese, in 1511, were the first europeans to reach it, the dutch east india company opened a trading post in 1608, and king narai exchanged embassies with the french court in the 1680s. european visitors in the 17th century described a city of canals, palaces and many temples, and some estimates put its population at several hundred thousand at its height. a burmese army besieged ayutthaya for about 14 months and took it in april 1767, burning much of the city; many thousands of captives were taken to burma, and much of the kingdom's written record was lost. taksin re-established a siamese state after 1767 and the capital moved to thonburi and then to bangkok in 1782. unesco inscribed the historic city of ayutthaya in 1991.

title: Babylon
sum: Babylon was a city on the Euphrates River in present-day Iraq, first mentioned in the late 3rd millennium BCE, the capital of Hammurabi's kingdom and later of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and a center of astronomy, law and religion.
search: babylon babylon was a city on the euphrates river in present-day iraq, first mentioned in the late 3rd millennium bce, the capital of hammurabi's kingdom and later of the neo-babylonian empire, and a center of astronomy, law and religion. babylon lies near hillah, about 85 kilometers south of baghdad, and is first mentioned in a tablet from the late 3rd millennium bce. babylon rose under hammurabi (reigned about 1792 to 1750 bce), whose law code was inscribed on a stele found at susa and now held in the louvre. the hittite king mursili i sacked babylon about 1595 bce, after which the kassites ruled it for centuries; the assyrian king sennacherib destroyed it in 689 bce, and his son esarhaddon rebuilt it. under nebuchadnezzar ii (reigned 605 to 562 bce) babylon had the ishtar gate, a large ziggurat called etemenanki and palaces, and his armies destroyed jerusalem in 586 bce. cyrus the great of persia took babylon in 539 bce; the cyrus cylinder, a clay text found there in 1879, presents him as chosen by the god marduk, and claims that it is a charter of human rights are debated. alexander the great died at babylon in 323 bce; the city declined after the seleucids founded seleucia on the tigris. babylonian scribes kept the astronomical diaries from about 652 to 61 bce, one of the longest continuous records of celestial observation. no babylonian text or archaeological trace has confirmed the hanging gardens described by greek writers; some scholars have proposed that they were at nineveh. military bases of us-led forces at the site in 2003 to 2004 damaged ancient remains, and unesco inscribed babylon in 2019.

title: Bagan
sum: Bagan is an archaeological zone on the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar, the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from a traditional founding date of 849 CE until the kingdom's collapse in the late 13th century, and the site of thousands of…
search: bagan bagan is an archaeological zone on the irrawaddy river in central myanmar, the capital of the pagan kingdom from a traditional founding date of 849 ce until the kingdom's collapse in the late 13th century, and the site of thousands of buddhist monuments. bagan lies on the irrawaddy river in central myanmar; tradition dates its founding to 849 ce, and it flourished from the 11th to the 13th century. king anawrahta (reigned 1044 to 1077) expanded the kingdom and promoted theravada buddhism. more than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries are estimated to have been built on the plain, and about 2,200 survive. many monuments were funded by private donors as well as kings, and inscriptions record gifts of land, labor and goods to temples; some historians argue that tax-exempt land grants to religious institutions reduced state revenue, a view that is debated. mongol armies defeated pagan forces at ngasaunggyan in 1277 and invaded again in 1287, after which the pagan kingdom collapsed; bagan remained a religious center. earthquakes have damaged the monuments, including one in 2016 that damaged hundreds of them, and unesco inscribed bagan in 2019.

title: Baghdad
sum: Baghdad is a city on the Tigris River in Iraq, founded in 762 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur as a round capital and, for about five centuries, the seat of the Abbasid caliphs and a leading center of learning.
search: baghdad baghdad is a city on the tigris river in iraq, founded in 762 ce by the abbasid caliph al-mansur as a round capital and, for about five centuries, the seat of the abbasid caliphs and a leading center of learning. baghdad was founded in 762 by the caliph al-mansur as a round city called madinat al-salam ("city of peace"), near the older sasanian capital ctesiphon; no part of the round city survives above ground. baghdad became the center of the translation movement and the house of wisdom, and paper mills were operating there by the 790s. population estimates for baghdad in the 9th and 10th centuries run from several hundred thousand to over a million, which would have made it one of the largest cities in the world. baghdad remained the seat of the abbasid caliphs until 1258, when mongol forces under hulagu took the city after a siege and killed the caliph al-musta'sim; chronicles report 200,000 to a million dead, figures that modern historians regard as too high, though the massacre and destruction were severe. baghdad was under ottoman rule from 1534, with safavid periods before and after, until british forces captured it in 1917; it became the capital of the kingdom of iraq in 1921. in april 2003, after the us-led invasion, looting of the iraq national museum removed about 15,000 objects, some of which have since been recovered.

title: Beringia
sum: Beringia was the land region, including a broad land bridge, that joined northeastern Siberia and Alaska when sea levels were lower during the last ice age, and that later flooded to form the Bering Strait.
search: beringia beringia was the land region, including a broad land bridge, that joined northeastern siberia and alaska when sea levels were lower during the last ice age, and that later flooded to form the bering strait. lower sea level during glacial periods exposed the shallow floor of the bering and chukchi seas. at its widest, the exposed land was more than a thousand kilometers from north to south. much of beringia was cold, dry steppe-tundra that supported mammoths, bison, and horses, and was largely unglaciated. genetic evidence suggests ancestors of native americans may have been isolated in beringia for several thousand years before moving south; this is the beringian standstill hypothesis, still debated. rising seas began flooding the land bridge around 11,000 years ago, and it was fully submerged by roughly 10,000 to 9,000 years ago.

title: Borobudur
sum: Borobudur is a large Mahayana Buddhist monument in central Java, built around 800 CE under the Sailendra dynasty and often described as the world's largest Buddhist temple.
search: borobudur borobudur is a large mahayana buddhist monument in central java, built around 800 ce under the sailendra dynasty and often described as the world's largest buddhist temple. construction is dated to roughly the late 8th and early 9th centuries. the monument has nine stacked platforms and is decorated with 2,672 relief panels and originally 504 buddha statues. it was abandoned in the centuries after the shift of power in java and later covered by vegetation and volcanic ash. thomas stamford raffles's agent, hermann cornelius, cleared the site in 1814. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1991 after major restoration.

title: Botany Bay
sum: Botany Bay is an inlet on the coast of Sydney, Australia, where the Gweagal and Kamaygal peoples lived for thousands of years and where James Cook landed in 1770, though the British colony of 1788 was founded nearby at Port Jackson instead.
search: botany bay botany bay is an inlet on the coast of sydney, australia, where the gweagal and kamaygal peoples lived for thousands of years and where james cook landed in 1770, though the british colony of 1788 was founded nearby at port jackson instead. botany bay lies about 13 kilometers south of central sydney; the gweagal lived on its south shore and the kamaygal on its north, part of a wider set of at least 28 clans in the region, who call the bay kamay in the dharawal language, with archaeological evidence of occupation going back some 5,000 years. james cook landed at kurnell on 29 april 1770; he first called the site stingrays harbour, then renamed it botany bay for the many plants collected there by the naturalists joseph banks and daniel solander. cook's landing party had a brief and wary encounter with local aboriginal people; when the first fleet arrived in january 1788, aboriginal observers were reported as curious but suspicious of the newcomers. governor arthur phillip found botany bay unsuitable for the planned colony because of poor freshwater, shallow anchorage, weak soil and exposed, swampy ground, and on 26 january 1788 he moved the fleet to found the settlement at sydney cove on port jackson instead. sydney airport now occupies the northwestern shore of the bay, with runways extending into it, and port botany is a major container port.

title: Bukhara
sum: Bukhara is a city in the Zarafshan oasis of Uzbekistan, a Sogdian trading city, capital of the Samanid dynasty, and for more than a thousand years a center of Islamic learning on the Silk Roads.
search: bukhara bukhara is a city in the zarafshan oasis of uzbekistan, a sogdian trading city, capital of the samanid dynasty, and for more than a thousand years a center of islamic learning on the silk roads. bukhara has been settled for a long time; the city celebrated 2,500 years in 1997 on a traditional dating, while archaeological evidence for its walled center is generally placed several centuries bce. bukhara was a sogdian city when arab armies took it in 709 to 710, and the scholar muhammad al-bukhari, compiler of a major collection of hadith, was born there in 810. under the samanid dynasty (819 to 999), bukhara was a capital of learning and of persian literature; the physician and philosopher ibn sina was born near it in 980, and the samanid mausoleum was built in the late 9th to 10th century. the mongol army under chinggis khan took bukhara in 1220; the city was burned and many of its people were killed or enslaved, though the number is unknown. the kalyan minaret, built in 1127, still stands, and bukhara was the capital of the emirate of bukhara (1785 to 1920), a russian protectorate from 1868. the red army took bukhara in 1920, and the citadel (ark) was damaged in the assault. unesco inscribed the historic centre of bukhara in 1993.

title: Cahokia
sum: Cahokia was the largest city of the Mississippian culture, near present-day St. Louis, flourishing from about 1050 to 1350 CE.
search: cahokia cahokia was the largest city of the mississippian culture, near present-day st. louis, flourishing from about 1050 to 1350 ce. at its peak, about 1050 to 1150, it may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people, though some estimates are much higher. monks mound, about 30 meters high, is the largest earthen mound in the americas. a circle of posts, known as woodhenge, likely tracked the sun. its population relied on maize agriculture and declined after about 1250, for reasons that are debated. it was designated a unesco world heritage site in 1982.

title: Caral
sum: Caral is an ancient city in Peru's Supe Valley, occupied from about 2600 BCE, and one of the oldest known urban centers in the Americas.
search: caral caral is an ancient city in peru's supe valley, occupied from about 2600 bce, and one of the oldest known urban centers in the americas. its monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas date to the same era as the egyptian pyramids. the society had no pottery and no evidence of large-scale warfare. coastal fishing provided anchovies and sardines, and cotton for nets, while inland farming provided crops. knotted cords found at the site may be early relatives of the quipu; see  quipu . it was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 2009.

title: Carthage
sum: Carthage was a Phoenician colony on the coast of present-day Tunisia, traditionally founded in 814 BCE, which became a major Mediterranean power until Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE.
search: carthage carthage was a phoenician colony on the coast of present-day tunisia, traditionally founded in 814 bce, which became a major mediterranean power until rome destroyed it in 146 bce. it grew into a naval and commercial empire across the western mediterranean. three punic wars against rome were fought between 264 and 146 bce. hannibal crossed the alps with an army in 218 bce. rome destroyed the city in 146 bce and later refounded it as a roman colony. it was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 1979.

title: Chaco Canyon
sum: Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was the ceremonial and trade center of the Ancestral Puebloan world from about 850 to 1150 CE.
search: chaco canyon chaco canyon, in northwestern new mexico, was the ceremonial and trade center of the ancestral puebloan world from about 850 to 1150 ce. its 'great houses', such as pueblo bonito, had hundreds of rooms. a network of roads radiated from the canyon. buildings and rock carvings align with the sun and moon, such as the 'sun dagger' on fajada butte. chaco is considered sacred by modern pueblo peoples. it became a unesco world heritage site in 1987.

title: Chang'an
sum: Chang'an was the capital of the Western Han dynasty from 202 BCE and, in a rebuilt form, of the Sui and Tang dynasties, on the site of present-day Xi'an in Shaanxi, China, until it was dismantled in 904 CE.
