search: chang'an chang'an was the capital of the western han dynasty from 202 bce and, in a rebuilt form, of the sui and tang dynasties, on the site of present-day xi'an in shaanxi, china, until it was dismantled in 904 ce. chang'an was founded as the han capital after 202 bce, with the changle palace completed in 200 bce; the census of 2 ce recorded about 250,000 residents. the sui dynasty built a new planned city, daxing, southeast of the han site from 582, and the tang, from 618, kept its plan and the name chang'an. tang chang'an was a grid of walled wards, with gates closed at night, enclosing about 78 square kilometers, with a central avenue and two state-supervised markets. estimates of its population, with suburbs, vary by source, from several hundred thousand up to about one million. chang'an received envoys and merchants from central asia, persia, korea, japan and tibet. the monk xuanzang returned there in 645 with buddhist texts from india, and the nestorian stele, recording a christian community, was erected there in 781. chang'an fell to rebels in 756 during the an lushan rebellion and was briefly held by tibetan forces in 763. in 904 the warlord zhu wen forced the court to move to luoyang and had the city's palaces and houses pulled down. the plan of chang'an influenced the layout of the japanese capitals nara and kyoto.

title: Chauvet Cave
sum: Chauvet Cave in the Ardeche region of southern France contains some of the oldest known figurative paintings, made by early Homo sapiens about 36,000 years ago.
search: chauvet cave chauvet cave in the ardeche region of southern france contains some of the oldest known figurative paintings, made by early homo sapiens about 36,000 years ago. the cave was found in december 1994 by jean-marie chauvet, eliette brunel, and christian hillaire. it holds hundreds of paintings and engravings of animals including horses, lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bears. radiocarbon dates place the main painted phase at about 37,000 to 33,500 years ago, in the aurignacian, with a second phase of use about 31,000 to 28,000 years ago. a rockfall sealed the cave entrance, preserving the art until its discovery. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 2014; a full-scale replica, the caverne du pont d'arc, opened nearby in 2015.

title: Chichen Itza
sum: Chichen Itza is a major Maya-Toltec city on the Yucatan Peninsula that flourished from about 800 to 1100 CE and is known for its stepped pyramid, El Castillo.
search: chichen itza chichen itza is a major maya-toltec city on the yucatan peninsula that flourished from about 800 to 1100 ce and is known for its stepped pyramid, el castillo. it is in the northern yucatan, where it prospered after many southern lowland cities declined. el castillo, the temple of kukulcan, has 91 steps on each of its four stairways plus a top platform, totaling 365. at the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight creates a serpent-like shadow on the staircase. the site has the largest ball court in the americas, about 166 meters (545 feet) long, and a sacred cenote used for offerings. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1988.

title: Constantinople
sum: Constantinople was founded in 330 CE by Emperor Constantine on the site of Byzantium and served as the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.
search: constantinople constantinople was founded in 330 ce by emperor constantine on the site of byzantium and served as the capital of the eastern roman (byzantine) empire until the ottoman conquest in 1453. the hagia sophia was completed in 537 under emperor justinian. the city was sacked by the fourth crusade in 1204. it fell to mehmed ii on 29 may 1453. it sits on the bosphorus, between europe and asia; it is now istanbul.

title: Cusco
sum: Cusco is a city in the Andes of southern Peru, at about 3,400 meters, that Inca tradition says was founded around 1200 CE and that served as the capital of the Inca Empire until the Spanish took it in 1533.
search: cusco cusco is a city in the andes of southern peru, at about 3,400 meters, that inca tradition says was founded around 1200 ce and that served as the capital of the inca empire until the spanish took it in 1533. cusco lies at about 3,400 meters in the peruvian andes; inca tradition credits its founding to manco cápac around 1200, but archaeology shows that the killke culture lived in the region from about 900 to 1200 and that the city grew slowly before pachacuti. under pachacuti, whose reign is traditionally dated from 1438, and his successors, cusco was the center of the inca empire, with the coricancha (temple of the sun) at its ritual heart and the fortress of sacsayhuamán above the city. spanish accounts, notably bernabé cobo's in the 17th century, describe 41 lines called ceques radiating from the coricancha and linking about 328 shrines (huacas). some writers say the city was laid out in the shape of a puma, a claim that remains debated. francisco pizarro's force entered cusco on 15 november 1533, and manco inca besieged the spanish there for about ten months in 1536 to 1537 without success. the spanish built churches and houses on inca foundations; an earthquake in 1650 destroyed almost all colonial buildings and one in 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures, while many inca walls remained standing. túpac amaru ii was executed in cusco's plaza de armas in 1781 during his rebellion against spanish rule. unesco inscribed cusco in 1983, and it had 428,450 residents in 2017.

title: Córdoba
sum: Córdoba is a city on the Guadalquivir River in Andalusia, southern Spain, founded by Rome in the 2nd century BCE and best known as the capital of Muslim Iberia and of the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (929 to 1031).
search: córdoba córdoba is a city on the guadalquivir river in andalusia, southern spain, founded by rome in the 2nd century bce and best known as the capital of muslim iberia and of the umayyad caliphate of córdoba (929 to 1031). córdoba, roman corduba, was founded in the 2nd century bce (169 or 152 bce, a contested date), became the colony colonia patricia in 46 to 45 bce and later the capital of the province of baetica. muslim forces took the city in 711 or 712, and in 716 it became the provincial capital of al-andalus. abd al-rahman i, an umayyad prince who escaped the dynasty's overthrow by the abbasids in 750, took power in 756; abd al-rahman iii declared himself caliph in 929, and the caliphate ended in 1031 when hisham iii was expelled. the great mosque was begun in 785 to 786 and enlarged into the 10th century, and the palace-city of madinat al-zahra, begun about 936, was sacked in the civil war of the early 11th century. estimates of córdoba's population around 1000 ce range from about 100,000 to 1,000,000, and medieval accounts credit its libraries with very large collections. muslims, christians and jews lived in the city under muslim rule, non-muslims with a protected but unequal legal status, and historians debate how far the term "convivencia" (coexistence) fits; ibn rushd (averroes) and moses maimonides were both born in córdoba in the 12th century. ferdinand iii of castile took the city on 29 june 1236 and the mosque became a cathedral; from 1523 a cathedral nave was built inside it. unesco inscribed the mosque-cathedral in 1984 and extended the listing to the whole historic center in 1994.

title: Doggerland
sum: Doggerland was a lowland region of hunter-gatherers that connected Britain to continental Europe and lay where the North Sea is today until it was gradually flooded by rising seas.
search: doggerland doggerland was a lowland region of hunter-gatherers that connected britain to continental europe and lay where the north sea is today until it was gradually flooded by rising seas. after the last ice age, sea level rose as ice sheets melted, and the land now under the southern north sea was progressively submerged. it was largely underwater by around 6000 bce, though a 2020 study argues that remnant islands survived for centuries after the tsunami and that the last land was submerged about a thousand years later. the storegga slide, a huge submarine landslide off norway, produced a tsunami around 6200 bce that struck the coasts of the region. fishing vessels have dredged up animal bones and worked bone points from the seabed, and surveys have mapped submerged river valleys. its inhabitants were mesolithic hunter-gatherers.

title: Elmina Castle
sum: Elmina Castle is a fortress on the coast of Ghana built by the Portuguese in 1482 as São Jorge da Mina, the first European fort on the Gulf of Guinea, and later a holding place for people sold into the Atlantic slave trade.
search: elmina castle elmina castle is a fortress on the coast of ghana built by the portuguese in 1482 as são jorge da mina, the first european fort on the gulf of guinea, and later a holding place for people sold into the atlantic slave trade. elmina castle stands at the town of elmina in ghana's central region; the portuguese built it in 1482 by agreement with local rulers, to trade for gold, and named it são jorge da mina ("saint george of the mine"). in the 16th century the portuguese also brought enslaved people to elmina from elsewhere on the african coast and exchanged them for gold with african traders. the dutch captured elmina in 1637, and portugal ceded its claims in 1642; under dutch rule the castle became a base of the dutch west india company, whose trade came to include large-scale export of enslaved people to the americas. enslaved people were held in dungeons in the castle before being shipped across the atlantic; the total number who passed through elmina is unknown. britain took over the dutch gold coast possessions in 1872, and ghana became independent in 1957. unesco inscribed the forts and castles of ghana, including elmina, in 1979. elmina castle is now a museum and memorial, and ghana's "year of return" in 2019 drew large numbers of visitors from the african diaspora.

title: Forbidden City
sum: The Forbidden City is the former imperial palace complex at the center of Beijing, China, built from 1406 to 1420 for the Ming dynasty and used as the residence and ceremonial center of Ming and Qing emperors until 1924.
search: forbidden city the forbidden city is the former imperial palace complex at the center of beijing, china, built from 1406 to 1420 for the ming dynasty and used as the residence and ceremonial center of ming and qing emperors until 1924. the forbidden city was built under the yongle emperor from 1406 to 1420, as part of his move of the ming capital from nanjing to beijing. twenty-four emperors, 14 ming and 10 qing, lived and ruled there. the forbidden city covers about 72 hectares, is surrounded by walls about 8 meters high and a moat, and has roughly 980 surviving buildings arranged along a north-south axis. commoners were barred from entering, and yellow glazed roof tiles were reserved for imperial use. puyi, the last qing emperor, abdicated in 1912 after the xinhai revolution but was allowed to remain in the inner court until 1924, when he was expelled; the palace museum opened in 1925. part of the palace collection was moved south from 1933 to escape japanese advances, and some of it was taken to taiwan in 1948 and 1949, where it forms the core of the national palace museum in taipei. unesco inscribed the imperial palaces of beijing in 1987.

title: Ganges River
sum: The Ganges River (Ganga) is a river of northern India and Bangladesh about 2,525 kilometers long, flowing from the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal, whose plain has supported some of South Asia's densest populations and which is sacred in…
search: ganges river the ganges river (ganga) is a river of northern india and bangladesh about 2,525 kilometers long, flowing from the himalaya to the bay of bengal, whose plain has supported some of south asia's densest populations and which is sacred in hinduism. the ganges rises at the gangotri glacier in the himalaya and crosses the northern indian plain to the bay of bengal, where together with the brahmaputra and meghna it forms the world's largest delta; its basin supports several hundred million people. farming communities occupied the middle ganges plain from at least the 2nd millennium bce, and the river became the axis of the later vedic states and of 1st-millennium bce kingdoms such as magadha. in hinduism the river is worshiped as the goddess ganga; ashes of the dead are immersed in it, pilgrims bathe at sites such as varanasi, and the kumbh mela at prayagraj, where the ganges meets the yamuna, draws tens of millions of people. sewage and industrial waste pollute long stretches of the river; india launched the ganga action plan in 1985 and the namami gange program in 2014, and water quality remains poor in many stretches. the farakka barrage, completed in 1975, diverts water and has been a source of dispute between india and bangladesh, and a treaty of 1996 governs the sharing of the river's dry-season flow. in 2017 a high court in uttarakhand declared the ganges and yamuna to be legal persons, and the supreme court of india stayed the ruling.

title: Giza Necropolis
sum: The Giza Necropolis, near Cairo, holds three large pyramids built for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure in the 26th century BCE, along with the Great Sphinx.
search: giza necropolis the giza necropolis, near cairo, holds three large pyramids built for the pharaohs khufu, khafre, and menkaure in the 26th century bce, along with the great sphinx. the great pyramid of khufu was originally about 146.6 meters high. it was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years. workers were organized labor teams and were fed and housed by the state. it is the only one of the seven wonders of the ancient world still largely standing.

title: Gorée Island
sum: Gorée Island is a small island off Dakar, Senegal, held in turn by the Portuguese, Dutch, British and French from the 15th century, and a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade, though historians debate how many enslaved people left from it.
search: gorée island gorée island is a small island off dakar, senegal, held in turn by the portuguese, dutch, british and french from the 15th century, and a symbol of the atlantic slave trade, though historians debate how many enslaved people left from it. gorée island lies about 3 kilometers off dakar; the portuguese landed in 1444, the dutch took the island in 1617, and the french took it in 1677, after which it changed hands several times between britain and france until 1817. gorée was a trading post for goods such as gum and hides and for enslaved people; a community of afro-european merchant women, called signares, ran trade and property on the island, and some owned enslaved people. the house of slaves, built in 1776 and having a doorway to the sea called the "door of no return", is a pilgrimage site for visitors. many historians argue that gorée was a modest embarkation point compared with larger ports on the atlantic coast and that the house of slaves did not hold the numbers often claimed, while others stress its symbolic importance; the debate is unresolved. african merchants and rulers took part in the trade alongside european ones. visitors to gorée include nelson mandela in 1991, pope john paul ii in 1992 and us president barack obama in 2013. unesco inscribed the island of gorée in 1978.

title: Great Wall of China
sum: The Great Wall of China is a series of walls, ditches, towers and forts built across northern China by successive states and dynasties from about the 7th century BCE to the 17th century CE, mainly to control movement between farming…
search: great wall of china the great wall of china is a series of walls, ditches, towers and forts built across northern china by successive states and dynasties from about the 7th century bce to the 17th century ce, mainly to control movement between farming societies and the steppe. the great wall began as separate walls built by warring states kingdoms such as qi, yan, zhao and qin from about the 7th century bce (the dating of the earliest walls is uncertain); after unifying china in 221 bce, qin shi huang linked and extended walls in the north. the han dynasty extended walls and signal towers far to the northwest along the gansu corridor, to protect the routes westward and to counter the xiongnu. the best-known standing sections, in brick and stone, date to the ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), and building intensified after mongol forces captured the ming emperor zhengtong at tumu in 1449. a chinese government survey published in 2012 reported about 21,000 kilometers of walls, trenches and natural barriers built across all dynasties, of which about 8,850 kilometers are ming. soldiers, conscripted laborers and convicts built the wall; how many died is unknown, and the large figures in later stories are not documented. unesco inscribed the great wall in 1987. the claim that it is visible to the naked eye from the moon is false.

title: Great Zimbabwe
sum: Great Zimbabwe was a large stone-walled capital city in southeastern Africa, occupied from about the 11th to 15th century CE, ancestral to the Shona-speaking peoples.
search: great zimbabwe great zimbabwe was a large stone-walled capital city in southeastern africa, occupied from about the 11th to 15th century ce, ancestral to the shona-speaking peoples. its great enclosure has dry-stone walls up to about 11 meters high. older estimates gave 10,000 to 20,000 people; more recent modeling suggests the population did not exceed about 10,000. it traded gold and ivory with the swahili coast and beyond. the modern country zimbabwe is named after it.

title: Göbekli Tepe
sum: Göbekli Tepe is a Pre-Pottery Neolithic site in southeastern Turkey with large carved T-shaped stone pillars, dating to about 9500 to 8000 BCE.
search: göbekli tepe göbekli tepe is a pre-pottery neolithic site in southeastern turkey with large carved t-shaped stone pillars, dating to about 9500 to 8000 bce. pillars stand up to about 5.5 meters tall and are carved with animals. it was built by people who were, at the time, foragers or early farmers. excavations led by klaus schmidt began in 1995. it was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 2018.

title: Harappa
sum: Harappa is an archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan, on a dry bed of the Ravi River, occupied from about 3300 BCE and a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization until its urban phase declined after about 1900 BCE.
search: harappa harappa is an archaeological site in punjab, pakistan, on a dry bed of the ravi river, occupied from about 3300 bce and a major city of the indus valley civilization until its urban phase declined after about 1900 bce. harappa was occupied from about 3300 bce, and its urban "mature harappan" phase ran from about 2600 to 1900 bce, with population estimates of about 20,000 to 40,000. harappa had planned streets, brick drains and standardized weights, and its bricks followed a common size ratio used at other indus sites. harappa's seals, carved with animals and signs in a script that has not been deciphered, are found in many indus cities, and indus objects such as seals and carnelian beads have been found in mesopotamian cities. daya ram sahni began excavations at harappa in 1921, after british engineers had taken bricks from the site in the 1850s for railway ballast. the city's urban phase declined after about 1900 bce, and occupation continued at a smaller scale; proposed causes include changes in monsoon rainfall and river courses, and the causes are debated.

title: Hattusa
sum: Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, at Boğazkale in central Turkey, made the royal seat in about 1650 BCE and abandoned around 1200 BCE, and it preserved an archive of about 30,000 clay tablets.
search: hattusa hattusa was the capital of the hittite empire, at boğazkale in central turkey, made the royal seat in about 1650 bce and abandoned around 1200 bce, and it preserved an archive of about 30,000 clay tablets. hattusa lies at boğazkale in çorum province, turkey; a hattian settlement existed there earlier, and king hattusili i made it the hittite capital in about 1650 bce. hattusa was ringed by walls with monumental gates, including the lion gate and the sphinx gate, and had a great temple and a nearby rock sanctuary at yazılıkaya. the capital moved briefly to tarhuntassa under muwatalli ii and returned to hattusa under mursili iii. excavators, beginning with hugo winckler in 1906, found about 30,000 clay tablets in the royal archives, written in hittite, akkadian, luwian, hurrian and other languages and holding treaties, rituals and letters, including a version of the treaty with egypt made after the battle of kadesh. bedřich hrozný identified hittite as an indo-european language in 1915. hattusa was abandoned around 1200 bce, during the bronze age collapse; its central buildings burned, though whether the city was abandoned before or after the fire is debated. unesco inscribed hattusha in 1986.

title: Havana
sum: Havana is the capital of Cuba, on the island's northwest coast, established on its present harbor site in 1519 and long the assembly point for Spanish treasure fleets crossing the Atlantic.
search: havana havana is the capital of cuba, on the island's northwest coast, established on its present harbor site in 1519 and long the assembly point for spanish treasure fleets crossing the atlantic. havana was founded as san cristóbal de la habana; the settlement moved twice and was established on its present harbor site in 1519. from the 1560s spanish fleets carrying silver from mexico and peru assembled at havana for the crossing to spain, and the city was fortified with la real fuerza (built 1558 to 1577) and el morro (built 1589 to 1630). britain captured havana after a siege in 1762 during the seven years' war and returned it to spain in 1763 in exchange for florida; spain then built the la cabaña fortress. sugar and coffee plantations, worked by enslaved people, expanded cuba's economy from the late 18th century; hundreds of thousands of enslaved africans arrived in cuba, many through havana, and slavery there was abolished in 1886. the us battleship maine exploded in havana harbor on 15 february 1898, killing about 260 crew, an event that helped lead to the spanish-american war. since 1959 havana has been the capital of a socialist state, and the cuban missile crisis of 1962 placed cuba at the center of the cold war. unesco inscribed old havana and its fortifications in 1982.

title: Hegra
sum: Hegra, also called Mada'in Salih, is an archaeological site in the AlUla region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, the second major city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, known for 111 monumental rock-cut tombs.
search: hegra hegra, also called mada'in salih, is an archaeological site in the alula region of northwestern saudi arabia, the second major city of the nabataean kingdom after petra, known for 111 monumental rock-cut tombs. hegra lies north of the alula oasis on a caravan route between southern arabia and the mediterranean, and was part of the nabataean kingdom from about the 1st century bce. unesco records 111 monumental tombs cut into sandstone outcrops, 94 of them with decorated facades, along with dozens of wells; it inscribed hegra in 2008, the first unesco site in saudi arabia. many tombs bear nabataean inscriptions naming the owner and family, forbidding sale or reuse, and threatening penalties or curses; dated inscriptions fall mostly in the 1st century ce. after rome annexed the nabataean kingdom in 106 ce, hegra became part of the province of arabia, and roman inscriptions record a military presence there in the 2nd century. islamic tradition associates the site with the people of thamud mentioned in the quran, and travelers traditionally avoided it. the ottoman hejaz railway built a station at mada'in salih in 1907 to 1908.

title: Hiroshima
sum: Hiroshima is a city on the delta of the Ōta River in western Honshu, Japan, founded as a castle town in 1589 and, on 6 August 1945, the first city struck by a nuclear weapon.
search: hiroshima hiroshima is a city on the delta of the ōta river in western honshu, japan, founded as a castle town in 1589 and, on 6 august 1945, the first city struck by a nuclear weapon. hiroshima was founded as a castle town in 1589 by the daimyo mōri terumoto and grew into a military and port center; its population before the bombing was about 350,000. at 8:15 a.m. on 6 august 1945 the us b-29 enola gay dropped a uranium bomb, "little boy", which exploded about 600 meters above the city. about 70,000 to 80,000 people are estimated to have been killed immediately, and total deaths by the end of 1945 are estimated at 90,000 to 166,000, from burns, injuries and radiation. the dead included civilians, soldiers, korean forced laborers and a small number of allied prisoners of war. survivors, called hibakusha, faced radiation illness, increased cancer risks and discrimination; the atomic bomb casualty commission began long-term studies of them in 1947, continued by the radiation effects research foundation. a second atomic bomb was dropped on nagasaki on 9 august, and japan announced its surrender on 15 august 1945; whether the bombings were necessary to end the war remains debated among historians. the ruined genbaku dome was preserved as a memorial within the peace memorial park, and unesco inscribed it in 1996.

title: Hispaniola
sum: Hispaniola is the second-largest island of the Caribbean, in the Greater Antilles, divided between Haiti in the west and the Dominican Republic in the east, and the site of the first lasting European settlement in the Americas.
search: hispaniola hispaniola is the second-largest island of the caribbean, in the greater antilles, divided between haiti in the west and the dominican republic in the east, and the site of the first lasting european settlement in the americas. hispaniola covers about 76,000 square kilometers; its features include pico duarte, at 3,098 meters the highest peak in the caribbean, and lake enriquillo, a saline lake about 40 meters below sea level. the earliest evidence of human presence on hispaniola is dated by many archaeologists to about 4000 bce, though estimates vary; by 1492 the island was home to taíno societies organized into several chiefdoms, and spanish chroniclers report the names ayiti, quisqueya and bohío for it. columbus reached hispaniola in december 1492, and the spanish founded la navidad (destroyed in 1493), la isabela (1493) and santo domingo (1496). the taíno population of hispaniola declined sharply after 1492 under forced labor, violence and disease. in 1697 spain ceded the western third of hispaniola to france, which developed the sugar and slave colony of saint-domingue; the haitian revolution (1791 to 1804) ended slavery and french rule there. the dominican republic became independent in 1844, after haitian rule over the whole island from 1822.

title: Isfahan
sum: Isfahan is a city on the Zayande River in central Iran, a Seljuk capital from 1051 and the capital of the Safavid Empire from 1598, when Shah Abbas I rebuilt its center around the great square Naqsh-e Jahan.
search: isfahan isfahan is a city on the zayande river in central iran, a seljuk capital from 1051 and the capital of the safavid empire from 1598, when shah abbas i rebuilt its center around the great square naqsh-e jahan. isfahan stands on the zayande river on the iranian plateau and was settled long before islam; it became a seljuk capital in 1051, and its friday mosque reflects more than a thousand years of mosque architecture (unesco inscribed it in 2012). after a revolt in 1387, timur's forces killed a large part of isfahan's population; chroniclers give figures of tens of thousands. shah abbas i moved the safavid capital from qazvin to isfahan in 1598 and built the naqsh-e jahan (imam) square, the shah and sheikh lotfollah mosques, the ali qapu palace and covered markets. estimates by 17th-century european visitors put isfahan's population at several hundred thousand, and a persian saying called the city "half the world". in 1604 to 1605 shah abbas forcibly moved many armenians from julfa on the aras river into safavid territory, and many died on the way; the survivors founded new julfa, an armenian quarter of isfahan, in about 1606. afghan forces under mahmud hotak besieged isfahan in 1722, and the resulting famine killed many tens of thousands of its inhabitants; the fall of the city was a decisive blow to safavid rule. isfahan ceased to be the capital in the 18th century, and unesco inscribed meidan emam, esfahan in 1979.

title: Issyk-Kul
sum: Issyk-Kul is a large mountain lake in the northern Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan, at about 1,600 meters above sea level, on the routes between the steppe and the oases and near cemeteries whose graves have been linked to an early stage of the…
search: issyk-kul issyk-kul is a large mountain lake in the northern tian shan of kyrgyzstan, at about 1,600 meters above sea level, on the routes between the steppe and the oases and near cemeteries whose graves have been linked to an early stage of the black death. issyk-kul has an area of about 6,200 square kilometers, a maximum depth of about 668 meters and no outlet; the lake is slightly saline and does not freeze in winter, and its name means "warm lake" in kyrgyz. saka burial mounds around the lake date from the 1st millennium bce; the saka were iranian-speaking pastoralists related to the scythians. underwater surveys have reported settlement remains and objects from the shallows, dated variously from the bronze age to the middle ages; interpretations vary. routes across the tian shan connecting the steppe with the oases of central asia passed near the lake. gravestones in cemeteries at kara-djigach and burana, in the region of issyk-kul, record deaths from pestilence in 1338 to 1339. a 2022 study reported yersinia pestis dna from graves at kara-djigach and concluded that the strain was close to the ancestor of the lineage that caused the black death; some researchers question whether this locates the origin of the pandemic.

title: Jack Hills Zircons
sum: The Jack Hills zircons are tiny crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, some dated to about 4.4 billion years, the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust.
search: jack hills zircons the jack hills zircons are tiny crystals from the jack hills of western australia, some dated to about 4.4 billion years, the oldest known pieces of earth's crust. the zircon grains occur in ancient sedimentary rock in the narryer terrane of western australia, reworked into rocks that are themselves about 3 billion years old. the oldest grains are dated by uranium-lead decay to roughly 4.4 billion years, only about 150 million years after earth formed. oxygen-isotope ratios in some grains have been interpreted as evidence that their parent magma had interacted with liquid water, though this reading is contested. the grains survive because zircon is chemically tough and resists weathering and remelting. no rock of comparable age is known on earth; the grains are the only direct samples of hadean crust.

title: Jamestown
sum: Jamestown, on the James River in Virginia, USA, was founded in 1607 as the first permanent English settlement in North America and was the capital of the Virginia colony until 1699.
search: jamestown jamestown, on the james river in virginia, usa, was founded in 1607 as the first permanent english settlement in north america and was the capital of the virginia colony until 1699. jamestown was founded in may 1607 by about 105 english men and boys sent by the virginia company of london, on land within a paramount chiefdom of many algonquian-speaking communities led by wahunsenacawh, whom the english called powhatan. in the winter of 1609 to 1610, known as the starving time, hunger and disease reduced the colony from a few hundred people (commonly given as about 500) to about 60, and accounts and archaeological evidence record cannibalism. john rolfe's tobacco, first harvested successfully in 1614, gave the colony an export crop and increased the colonists' demand for land and labor. in july 1619 the first representative assembly in english america met at jamestown; in late august an english privateer, the white lion, landed about 20 africans at point comfort, downriver, who had been taken from a portuguese slave ship, and they were traded for food, and some were brought to jamestown; their legal status is debated. a powhatan attack on 22 march 1622 killed more than 300 colonists, about a third of the english population, and years of war followed; powhatan deaths from war and introduced disease are poorly recorded. jamestown was burned in 1676 during bacon's rebellion, and the capital moved to middle plantation, renamed williamsburg, in 1699 after the statehouse burned in 1698. archaeologists found the remains of the 1607 fort in 1996, after it had long been thought lost to river erosion.

title: Jericho
sum: Jericho, at Tell es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements, with permanent occupation beginning around 9000 BCE.
search: jericho jericho, at tell es-sultan in the jordan valley, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements, with permanent occupation beginning around 9000 bce. the site lies in the west bank, about 250 meters below sea level, near a perennial spring. excavations by kathleen kenyon in the 1950s found a stone wall and a large stone tower dated to roughly 8000 bce. the purpose of the wall, defense against attack or protection from floods and mudflow, is debated. houses in the later pre-pottery neolithic b period contained skulls with facial features modeled in plaster, dated to around 7000 bce. jericho is often described as one of the world's oldest towns.

title: Jerusalem
sum: Jerusalem is a city in the Judean hills of the southern Levant, settled since about the 4th millennium BCE and holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, whose political status is disputed today.
search: jerusalem jerusalem is a city in the judean hills of the southern levant, settled since about the 4th millennium bce and holy to jews, christians and muslims, whose political status is disputed today. settlement on the spur above the gihon spring dates from about the 4th millennium bce, and jerusalem is named in egyptian texts of the early 2nd millennium bce and in the amarna letters of the 14th century bce. according to the hebrew bible, king david captured the city about 1000 bce and his son solomon built the first temple; archaeologists debate the size of jerusalem in the 10th century bce, and the city grew markedly by the 8th century bce. babylonian forces destroyed jerusalem and the first temple in 586 bce and deported part of its population; the second temple was dedicated in 516 bce. roman forces destroyed the city and the second temple in 70 ce; after the bar kokhba revolt (132 to 135 ce) the romans refounded it as aelia capitolina and barred jews from entering. the church of the holy sepulchre was built in the 4th century under constantine; muslim forces took the city in 637 to 638, and the umayyad caliph abd al-malik completed the dome of the rock in 691 to 692. crusaders captured jerusalem in 1099 and killed many of its muslim and jewish inhabitants, with estimates of the dead varying widely; saladin retook it in 1187, and it was under ottoman rule from 1517 to 1917. unesco inscribed the old city of jerusalem and its walls in 1981. the city was divided between israel and jordan in 1948 and has been under israeli control since 1967, and its status remains disputed between israelis and palestinians.

title: Karakorum
sum: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire in the Orkhon Valley of central Mongolia, built from 1235 under Ögedei Khan, and it was damaged and razed by Ming forces in the 1370s and 1380s.
search: karakorum karakorum was the capital of the mongol empire in the orkhon valley of central mongolia, built from 1235 under ögedei khan, and it was damaged and razed by ming forces in the 1370s and 1380s. karakorum stood in the orkhon valley; chinggis khan is reported to have set up a camp there around 1220, and his son ögedei ordered a walled city built from 1235. craftsmen and captives from conquered lands, including china, central asia and europe, were settled at karakorum to work as artisans. william of rubruck, a flemish franciscan sent by louis ix of france, visited karakorum in 1254 and described temples of several traditions, mosques, a christian church, and a silver tree that dispensed drinks, made by the french goldsmith guillaume boucher. after kublai khan took power in 1260 and shifted the center of the empire to northern china, karakorum declined. ming forces damaged the city in 1372 and razed it in 1380, and one passage dates the destruction of the permanent palace to 1388; the buddhist monastery of erdene zuu was built nearby from 1585, partly with stone from the ruins. the ruins of karakorum were identified in the 19th century and excavated by a soviet-mongolian expedition in 1948 and 1949; unesco inscribed the orkhon valley cultural landscape, which includes the site, in 2004.

title: Karnak
sum: Karnak is a vast temple complex at Thebes, near modern Luxor in Egypt, dedicated mainly to the god Amun-Ra and built and enlarged over about 2,000 years from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period.
search: karnak karnak is a vast temple complex at thebes, near modern luxor in egypt, dedicated mainly to the god amun-ra and built and enlarged over about 2,000 years from the middle kingdom to the ptolemaic period. karnak's earliest surviving structures date to the reign of senusret i, around 1970 bce, and kings added to the complex until the ptolemaic period. the great hypostyle hall at karnak, begun by seti i and completed by ramesses ii in the 13th century bce, has 134 columns in 16 rows, the tallest about 21 meters high. the walls of karnak carry royal inscriptions, including annals of the campaigns of thutmose iii, reliefs of the battle of kadesh, and a relief of the campaign of shoshenq i in canaan. hatshepsut's obelisk at karnak stands about 30 meters high; images and inscriptions of hatshepsut were later removed from many monuments, and the motives are debated. papyri of the 12th century bce record large estates and tens of thousands of dependents attached to the temples of amun. kings of the kushite 25th dynasty added to karnak in the 8th and 7th centuries bce. an avenue of sphinxes about 2.7 kilometers long linked karnak with luxor temple, and its restored length was reopened in 2021; unesco inscribed ancient thebes with its necropolis, including karnak, in 1979.

title: Kilwa Kisiwani
sum: Kilwa Kisiwani is an island town off the coast of southern Tanzania that was a leading Swahili port from about the 12th to the 15th century, trading gold from the interior for goods carried across the Indian Ocean.
search: kilwa kisiwani kilwa kisiwani is an island town off the coast of southern tanzania that was a leading swahili port from about the 12th to the 15th century, trading gold from the interior for goods carried across the indian ocean. kilwa kisiwani was occupied from about the 9th century ce, and its great mosque dates from the 11th or 12th century and was enlarged in the 14th. the kilwa chronicle, written in the 16th century, traces the ruling dynasty to a founder from shiraz in persia; archaeological and linguistic evidence indicates that kilwa's society was rooted in african coastal communities that took part in indian ocean trade. from about the 13th century kilwa controlled the gold trade from sofala, in the south, whose gold came from the interior of zimbabwe, and the town minted its own coins, among the earliest in sub-saharan africa. sultan al-hasan ibn sulaiman built the palace and market complex of husuni kubwa in the early 14th century. the traveler ibn battuta visited kilwa in about 1331 and described it as one of the most beautiful and well-constructed towns. portuguese forces attacked kilwa in 1505 and built a fort; the town later came under omani influence and was involved in the trade in enslaved people in the 18th and 19th centuries. unesco inscribed the ruins of kilwa kisiwani and songo mnara in 1981.

title: Knossos
sum: Knossos is an archaeological site near Heraklion on the Greek island of Crete, occupied from about 7000 BCE and the site of the largest palace of the Minoan civilization, built from about 1900 BCE.
search: knossos knossos is an archaeological site near heraklion on the greek island of crete, occupied from about 7000 bce and the site of the largest palace of the minoan civilization, built from about 1900 bce. knossos was occupied by farmers by about 7000 bce, and the first palace was built about 1900 bce; an earthquake destroyed it about 1700 bce and a larger palace was built after it. the palace held storerooms for oil, grain and wine, workshops and frescoes, including bull-leaping scenes, and clay tablets in linear a, a script that has not been deciphered. tablets in linear b, which was deciphered by michael ventris in 1952 as an early form of greek, show that mycenaean greeks controlled knossos by about 1450 bce. the palace was destroyed by fire; the date is debated, with proposals from about 1375 to about 1200 bce. arthur evans excavated knossos from 1900 and rebuilt parts of it with concrete columns and repainted frescoes; the reconstructions are controversial among archaeologists. the name "minoan" is a modern term drawn from the legendary king minos, and later greek myth placed the minotaur and its labyrinth at knossos; whether the palace inspired the myth is uncertain. estimates of the population of knossos vary widely.

title: Kolyma
sum: Kolyma is a remote region of northeastern Siberia, Russia, that from 1932 until the 1950s held the Soviet Union's largest system of forced-labor camps, where prisoners mined gold and other metals in extreme cold and many died.
search: kolyma kolyma is a remote region of northeastern siberia, russia, that from 1932 until the 1950s held the soviet union's largest system of forced-labor camps, where prisoners mined gold and other metals in extreme cold and many died. kolyma lies along the kolyma river in the far northeast of siberia, where winter temperatures fall below minus 40 degrees celsius. gold was found on the kolyma river in the late 1920s, and in 1931 the soviet state created dalstroy, a state trust that developed the region with prisoners from the gulag system, the first of whom arrived in 1932. prisoners included people convicted of ordinary crimes and of political offenses, and many were sent during the great terror of 1937 to 1938; hundreds of thousands of people passed through the kolyma camps. estimates of deaths in the kolyma camps range from more than 100,000 to several hundred thousand, from hunger, cold, disease, overwork and executions; the full toll is uncertain. prisoners built the kolyma highway between magadan and yakutsk, known as the "road of bones" because of the deaths among its builders. varlam shalamov, who was imprisoned in the kolyma camps, wrote the short stories known as the kolyma tales about them. dalstroy was dissolved in 1957, and a memorial, the mask of sorrow, was unveiled in magadan in 1996.

title: Kuk Early Agricultural Site
sum: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site in the highlands of Papua New Guinea preserves drainage ditches and gardens showing that people cultivated wetlands there for at least 7,000 years.
search: kuk early agricultural site the kuk early agricultural site in the highlands of papua new guinea preserves drainage ditches and gardens showing that people cultivated wetlands there for at least 7,000 years. the site is in the wahgi valley of papua new guinea and was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 2008. it is reported to show agricultural use for at least 7,000 years, possibly beginning as early as 10,000 years ago. excavations show a gradual shift from exploiting taro and yam on wetland margins about 7,000 years ago to organized cultivation of bananas on drained ground about 4,000 years ago. it is one of the few places worldwide widely regarded as an independent center of plant domestication. the highlands of new guinea were settled by people descended from those who reached sahul more than 50,000 years ago.

title: Kyoto
sum: Kyoto is a city on the Japanese island of Honshu, founded in 794 CE as the imperial capital Heian-kyō and the seat of the emperor until 1868 to 1869.
search: kyoto kyoto is a city on the japanese island of honshu, founded in 794 ce as the imperial capital heian-kyō and the seat of the emperor until 1868 to 1869. kyoto was founded in 794 by emperor kanmu as heian-kyō, on a grid plan modeled on chinese capitals such as chang'an. under the heian court (794 to 1185) kyoto was the center of court culture, including the novel the tale of genji, written in the early 11th century by murasaki shikibu. the ashikaga shogunate ruled from kyoto from 1336 to 1573, and the onin war (1467 to 1477) destroyed much of the city. under the tokugawa shogunate (1603 to 1868) political power lay in edo, while kyoto remained the imperial seat and a center of crafts and buddhist institutions. the emperor moved to tokyo (formerly edo) in 1868 to 1869 after the meiji restoration, ending kyoto's role as capital. in 1945 kyoto was removed from the list of possible atomic-bomb targets at the urging of us secretary of war henry stimson, who is traditionally said to have cited its cultural significance. unesco inscribed 17 "historic monuments of ancient kyoto" in 1994.

title: L'Anse aux Meadows
sum: L'Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological site on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, where Norse people from Greenland built a small settlement of sod buildings around 1000 CE, the only widely accepted Norse site in North America.
search: l'anse aux meadows l'anse aux meadows is an archaeological site on the northern tip of newfoundland, canada, where norse people from greenland built a small settlement of sod buildings around 1000 ce, the only widely accepted norse site in north america. l'anse aux meadows lies at the northernmost tip of newfoundland; helge and anne stine ingstad found it in 1960 with the help of a local resident, george decker, and excavated it in the 1960s. the site has eight buildings of sod over wooden frames, including an iron smithy, a carpentry workshop and a boat-repair area, and more than 800 norse objects were found. radiocarbon dates place activity between about 990 and 1050 ce; a 2021 study of tree rings, using a solar-storm signal in the year 993, dated felled timber cut with metal tools to 1021 ce. the occupation was short, perhaps about 20 years, though this is debated, and no burials or signs of farming were found, so the site appears to have been left in an orderly way; the date_end of 1030 is a rough placeholder. butternuts found at the site grow farther south, so norse travelers reached or traded with regions beyond newfoundland. the icelandic sagas, written down in the 13th century, describe voyages to a land called vinland, and whether l'anse aux meadows is that place or a base for voyages farther south is debated. unesco inscribed l'anse aux meadows in 1978.

title: Lake Baikal
sum: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in southern Siberia, Russia, the deepest and oldest lake on Earth and the largest by volume of fresh water, with people living around it for many thousands of years and a UNESCO listing since 1996.
search: lake baikal lake baikal is a rift lake in southern siberia, russia, the deepest and oldest lake on earth and the largest by volume of fresh water, with people living around it for many thousands of years and a unesco listing since 1996. lake baikal lies in a rift valley, is about 636 kilometers long, has a maximum depth of 1,642 meters, and holds about 20 percent of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water. the baikal rift basin is estimated to be 25 to 30 million years old, which makes the lake the oldest on earth; this geologic age is far older than any human presence. more than 1,700 species of plants and animals live in and around lake baikal, about two thirds of them found nowhere else, including the baikal seal, a freshwater seal. hunter-fisher-gatherers of the kitoi culture buried their dead around the lake from about the 5th millennium bce, and much older paleolithic sites, such as mal'ta, lie nearby. russian explorers reached lake baikal in the 1640s, beginning russian settlement among the buryat and evenki peoples. a pulp and paper mill on the southern shore discharged waste into the lake from 1966 until it closed in 2013, and it was one of the earliest targets of organized environmental protest in the soviet union. unesco inscribed lake baikal in 1996.

title: Lake Titicaca
sum: Lake Titicaca is a large high-altitude lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia, sacred to the Inca as the birthplace of their first rulers and long settled by farming and fishing communities of the Andean highlands.
search: lake titicaca lake titicaca is a large high-altitude lake on the border of peru and bolivia, sacred to the inca as the birthplace of their first rulers and long settled by farming and fishing communities of the andean highlands. the lake lies at about 3,812 meters elevation, with a surface area of about 8,372 square kilometers, and is often called the world's highest navigable lake for commercial craft. communities around the lake farmed and fished from at least the mid-2nd millennium bce; the date_start of -1500 marks the period conventionally associated with early settled use of the basin, and older human presence in the andes belongs to a different brief. the tiwanaku civilization, centered south of the lake, built a temple on the island of the moon by about 650 to 1000 ce and left pottery and stonework recovered from the islands. inca tradition holds that the first inca ruler, manco cápac, and his sister-wife mama ocllo, emerged from the lake or its island of the sun by order of the sun god inti; the sacred rock on the island of the sun is linked in tradition to manco cápac's remains. the uros people build and live on floating islands made from layers of totora reed; about 1,200 uros lived on some 60 such islands as of 2011. a 2011 united nations report found high concentrations of cadmium, arsenic and lead in parts of the lake, and its water level fell 81 centimeters between april and november 2009, attributed to shorter rainy seasons and glacier melt in its tributaries.

title: Library of Alexandria
sum: The Library of Alexandria was a major research library in Ptolemaic Egypt, founded in the early 3rd century BCE as part of the Mouseion, and its decline was gradual rather than a single catastrophe.
search: library of alexandria the library of alexandria was a major research library in ptolemaic egypt, founded in the early 3rd century bce as part of the mouseion, and its decline was gradual rather than a single catastrophe. it was founded under the first ptolemaic rulers, in the 3rd century bce. scholars associated with it include eratosthenes, who estimated the circumference of the earth, and callimachus, who compiled a catalog of works. euclid is traditionally said to have worked in alexandria, though details of his life are uncertain. julius caesar's fire in 48 bce damaged some holdings, but the institution continued. its decline resulted from reduced funding, political upheaval, and the loss of scholars over several centuries.

title: London
sum: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, on the Thames River, founded as the Roman town of Londinium in about 47 CE and grown into a leading center of trade, finance and empire and, in the 19th century, the largest city in the world.
search: london london is the capital of the united kingdom, on the thames river, founded as the roman town of londinium in about 47 ce and grown into a leading center of trade, finance and empire and, in the 19th century, the largest city in the world. londinium was founded by the romans in about 47 ce near a crossing of the thames; boudica's revolt destroyed it in 60 or 61, and it later became the capital of roman britain, until roman rule ended around 410. william i was crowned at westminster in 1066 and began the tower of london in about 1078. the black death of 1348 to 1349 killed a large share of london's people, and the great plague of 1665 killed tens of thousands; the great fire of 1666 destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches. london was probably the largest city in the world from the 1830s to the 1920s, and the world's first underground railway opened there in 1863. during the 1854 cholera outbreak in soho, john snow mapped deaths by address and linked them to a water pump; the "great stink" of 1858 led to the building of a sewer system by joseph bazalgette. london was a major center of shipping, insurance and finance for the atlantic slave trade and for british colonial trade, and the capital of the british empire. the german air raids of 1940 to 1941 killed about 20,000 londoners or more.

title: Machu Picchu
sum: Machu Picchu is a stone citadel built about 1450 in the Peruvian Andes, probably as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.
search: machu picchu machu picchu is a stone citadel built about 1450 in the peruvian andes, probably as a royal estate for the inca ruler pachacuti. it sits at about 2,430 meters above sea level. it was abandoned around the time of the spanish conquest. local people knew of it; hiram bingham brought it to international attention in 1911. it was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 1983.

title: Marajó Island
sum: Marajó Island, at the mouth of the Amazon River in Pará, Brazil, was home to the Marajoara culture, which built earthen mounds and made elaborate pottery from about 400 BCE until its decline after European contact in the 16th century.
search: marajó island marajó island, at the mouth of the amazon river in pará, brazil, was home to the marajoara culture, which built earthen mounds and made elaborate pottery from about 400 bce until its decline after european contact in the 16th century. marajó, with a land area of about 40,100 square kilometers, is the second-largest island in south america, comparable in size to switzerland. the marajoara culture existed from about 400 bce to around 1600 ce; people lived in houses with tamped-earth floors, organized in matrilineal clans, and made large ceremonial pottery, including burial urns. archaeologist betty meggers argued the culture was founded by migrants from the andes and declined from about 1400 due to poor soil; anna roosevelt's later research argued instead that marajoara society developed independently in the amazon, with intensive farming and large-scale earthworks, and estimated a peak population of more than 100,000. european contact in the 16th century brought epidemic disease, and an estimated 90 percent of the island's indigenous population died from introduced illnesses to which they had no immunity. the island's economy today rests partly on introduced water buffalo, whose herds, numbering about 450,000, outnumber the roughly 400,000 human residents; lumber and açaí palm are also produced there.

title: Marib
sum: Marib is a city in Yemen on the edge of the Ramlat al-Sabatayn desert, east of Sanaa, which was the capital of the Kingdom of Saba from about the 8th century BCE and the site of a great dam that irrigated the oasis.
search: marib marib is a city in yemen on the edge of the ramlat al-sabatayn desert, east of sanaa, which was the capital of the kingdom of saba from about the 8th century bce and the site of a great dam that irrigated the oasis. marib appears in sabaean inscriptions from about the 8th century bce and was the capital of the kingdom of saba, whose wealth came from the incense trade. the great dam of marib, first built in about the 8th century bce, diverted seasonal floods from wadi adhanah into irrigation canals and was raised and repaired over many centuries; an inscription records a repair in 542 to 543 ce. the dam failed for the last time around the 6th century ce; the quran refers to a flood that ended the prosperity of saba, which tradition connects with the dam. marib has temples of almaqah, the chief god of saba, including the oval awwam temple, which local tradition calls mahram bilqis. a modern dam at marib, built in the 1980s with funding from the united arab emirates, replaced the ancient system. since 2015 marib has been a frontline city in the yemeni civil war and has taken in large numbers of people displaced by the fighting.

title: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang
sum: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is the burial complex of the first emperor of unified China, near Xi'an in Shaanxi, begun in 246 BCE and known for the Terracotta Army of clay soldiers buried in pits east of the tomb mound.
search: mausoleum of qin shi huang the mausoleum of qin shi huang is the burial complex of the first emperor of unified china, near xi'an in shaanxi, begun in 246 bce and known for the terracotta army of clay soldiers buried in pits east of the tomb mound. construction of the mausoleum began in 246 bce, when ying zheng became king of qin; he took the title qin shi huang ("first emperor") after unifying china in 221 bce and died in 210 bce. sima qian, writing about a century later, reports that 700,000 laborers worked on the tomb and palace, a figure that cannot be verified. farmers digging a well found the terracotta army in 1974. the pits hold life-size clay soldiers, horses, chariots and bronze weapons, estimated at about 8,000 figures in total, of which more than 2,000 have been excavated. the figures were assembled from molded parts, finished by hand and originally painted in bright colors, which mostly faded after exposure to air. other pits hold figures of officials, acrobats and musicians, and bronze waterbirds. the burial mound has not been excavated; soil around it has elevated mercury levels, consistent with sima qian's account of mercury in the tomb. sima qian also reports that childless women of the palace and workers who knew the tomb's secrets were sealed inside after the burial; archaeology has not confirmed this account. unesco inscribed the mausoleum in 1987.

title: Mecca
sum: Mecca is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, about 70 kilometers inland from the Red Sea, the birthplace of Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam, whose sanctuary around the Kaaba is the destination of the annual Hajj…
search: mecca mecca is a city in the hejaz region of western saudi arabia, about 70 kilometers inland from the red sea, the birthplace of muhammad and the holiest city of islam, whose sanctuary around the kaaba is the destination of the annual hajj pilgrimage. the date of mecca's first settlement is unknown, and the identification of mecca with the place macoraba in ptolemy's 2nd-century geography is disputed. muslim sources written after muhammad's time describe a sanctuary town governed by the quraysh in the century before islam. islamic tradition places muhammad's birth in mecca about 570 ce, his move to medina in 622, and mecca's passing under muslim control in 630 with little fighting. the hajj is one of the five pillars of islam, required once in a lifetime of muslims able to make the journey; saudi authorities have reported annual attendance in the low millions in recent decades. historians disagree about mecca's importance in long-distance trade before islam; some describe it as a regional sanctuary and market town rather than a hub of the incense and spice trades. mecca was ruled locally by the sharifs under successive overlords, including the ottomans from 1517, until the saudi conquest of 1924 to 1925. non-muslims are barred from entering the city. in the crush at mina, near mecca, during the 2015 hajj, the saudi authorities reported 769 deaths, while counts compiled from other governments' figures exceeded 2,000.

title: Medina
sum: Medina is a city in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, known before Islam as Yathrib, to which Muhammad migrated in 622 CE and where he is buried; it is the second holiest city of Islam.
search: medina medina is a city in the hejaz region of western saudi arabia, known before islam as yathrib, to which muhammad migrated in 622 ce and where he is buried; it is the second holiest city of islam. medina was an oasis settlement called yathrib before islam, inhabited by arab tribes, chiefly the aws and khazraj, and by jewish tribes; its earlier history is poorly documented. muhammad and his followers migrated there from mecca in 622 (the hijra), the year from which the islamic calendar counts; muhammad died and was buried there in 632. the constitution of medina, a document preserved in later sources, sets out obligations among muslim, jewish and other groups; its date and authenticity are debated. traditional islamic sources report that two jewish tribes, banu qaynuqa and banu nadir, were expelled from medina, and that the men of a third, banu qurayza, were executed in 627, with figures reported from about 400 to 900; some modern historians question details of these accounts. medina was the capital of the first caliphs until 656, when ali moved to kufa; the umayyad caliphs later ruled from damascus. the prophet's mosque in medina, first built in 622, was enlarged by the umayyad caliph al-walid i in the early 8th century and repeatedly since; non-muslims are barred from the central sanctuary area.

title: Mekong River
sum: The Mekong River is a river of Asia about 4,350 kilometers long, rising on the Tibetan Plateau and flowing through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam, whose annual flood supports rice farming and one of the world's…
search: mekong river the mekong river is a river of asia about 4,350 kilometers long, rising on the tibetan plateau and flowing through china, myanmar, laos, thailand, cambodia and vietnam, whose annual flood supports rice farming and one of the world's largest inland fisheries. the mekong rises on the tibetan plateau and flows through china, along the borders of myanmar, laos and thailand, and through cambodia and vietnam into the south china sea, where it forms a large delta. rice-farming and fishing communities lived along the middle and lower mekong from about the 3rd to 2nd millennia bce, and the early port of oc eo in the delta, part of the state called funan, traded from about the 1st century ce. the tonlé sap, a lake in cambodia joined to the mekong, changes its direction of flow with the season: floodwater flows into it in the wet season and back out in the dry season, supporting a major fishery. the lower basin has about 60 million people, and the river is among the world's most productive inland fisheries. a french exploration commission in 1866 to 1868 found that rapids made the mekong unnavigable as a route to china, and the mekong delta was a major area of fighting in the vietnam war. china has built a cascade of dams on the upper mekong since the 1990s, and laos began operating the xayaburi dam on the lower river in 2019; the mekong river commission, formed in 1995, coordinates the lower-basin countries, and the effects of the dams on fish, sediment and flood timing are debated.

title: Merv
sum: Merv was a major oasis city on the Silk Roads in what is now Turkmenistan, a city of the Achaemenid Persians, a capital of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and of the Seljuk sultans, and sacked by the Mongols in 1221.
search: merv merv was a major oasis city on the silk roads in what is now turkmenistan, a city of the achaemenid persians, a capital of the abbasid caliph al-ma'mun and of the seljuk sultans, and sacked by the mongols in 1221. merv lies in the murghab delta oasis near the modern city of mary; bronze age towns of the region, such as gonur depe, date to about 2000 bce, and the walled city of erk kala dates from the achaemenid period, from about the 6th century bce. arab forces took merv in 651, after the last sasanian king, yazdegerd iii, was killed near it. abu muslim launched the abbasid revolution from merv in 747, and the caliph al-ma'mun ruled from merv from about 813 to 818 before moving to baghdad. merv was a seljuk capital, notably under sultan sanjar (reigned 1118 to 1157), whose mausoleum survives, and some estimates suggest it was among the largest cities in the world in the 12th century. the geographer yaqut, who visited in 1219, described its libraries. the mongol army took merv in 1221; persian chronicles report hundreds of thousands to over a million killed, figures that modern historians regard as greatly exaggerated but that reflect a severe massacre and destruction. merv was rebuilt on a smaller scale in the 15th century and was finally abandoned in the late 18th century. unesco inscribed ancient merv in 1999.

title: Mesa Verde
sum: Mesa Verde is a plateau in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, USA, where Ancestral Puebloan farmers lived from about 550 CE until about 1300 and built the cliff dwellings of the late 12th and 13th centuries.
search: mesa verde mesa verde is a plateau in the four corners region of southwestern colorado, usa, where ancestral puebloan farmers lived from about 550 ce until about 1300 and built the cliff dwellings of the late 12th and 13th centuries. mesa verde lies in montezuma county, colorado; people used the area for thousands of years before farming communities settled the mesa, and they lived there continuously for about 700 years until the late 13th century. by the end of the 12th century residents began building cliff dwellings in sandstone alcoves beneath the mesa rim; the park holds more than 5,000 archaeological sites, including about 600 cliff dwellings, and cliff palace is among the largest cliff dwellings in north america. tree-ring records show a severe drought from 1276 to 1299, and drought, resource depletion and overpopulation are all proposed as causes of instability; the last residents left by about 1300. pueblo peoples such as the hopi, zuni and acoma regard the ancestral puebloans as their ancestors, and many pueblo people prefer "ancestral puebloan" to the older term "anasazi". the ranchers richard wetherill and charlie mason reached cliff palace on 18 december 1888, artifact collecting followed, and the site was protected as a national park in 1906. unesco inscribed mesa verde in 1978.

title: Mexico City
sum: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, built by the Spanish after 1521 on the site of Tenochtitlan in the former Lake Texcoco, and today one of the largest cities in the Americas.
search: mexico city mexico city is the capital of mexico, built by the spanish after 1521 on the site of tenochtitlan in the former lake texcoco, and today one of the largest cities in the americas. mexico city was rebuilt by the spanish on the ruins of tenochtitlan after the conquest of 1521, with a municipality founded in 1524 as méxico tenochtitlán, and it became the capital of the viceroyalty of new spain, established in 1535. the metropolitan cathedral, begun in the 1570s and completed in 1813, stands beside the main square, and the buried templo mayor of tenochtitlan was uncovered in excavations after workers found the coyolxauhqui stone in 1978. the lakes were drained by canals and tunnels from the 17th century in response to floods, and the city now covers much of the old lakebed; parts of it have sunk as much as nine meters and some areas still sink by nearly 50 centimeters a year. silver and goods moved through the capital in the spanish trade system, and the manila galleons linked new spain to asia through the pacific port of acapulco. mexican independence was secured in september 1821, with mexico city as the capital of the new state. the soft lakebed amplifies earthquakes: the quake of 19 september 1985 (magnitude about 8) killed about 10,000 people by official counts, with some estimates several times higher, and the quake of 19 september 2017 (magnitude 7.1) killed more than 300. the 2020 census counted 9,209,944 people in mexico city and 21,804,515 in greater mexico city, and unesco inscribed the historic centre and xochimilco in 1987.

title: Mogao Caves
sum: The Mogao Caves are a complex of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff near Dunhuang, in Gansu, China, begun by tradition in 366 CE and decorated with murals and sculptures over about a thousand years at a crossroads of the Silk Roads.
search: mogao caves the mogao caves are a complex of buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff near dunhuang, in gansu, china, begun by tradition in 366 ce and decorated with murals and sculptures over about a thousand years at a crossroads of the silk roads. the mogao caves lie near the oasis of dunhuang at the edge of the desert, where silk road routes met; han china had established a commandery at dunhuang in the late 2nd century bce. by tradition the first cave was dug in 366 ce by the monk yuezun, and work continued into the 14th century; the site has roughly 735 caves, about 490 of which hold murals or painted sculptures, with murals covering about 45,000 square meters. the art shows indian, central asian and chinese influences, and donors, including officials, merchants and local rulers, are painted into many caves. dunhuang was under tibetan rule from about 786 to 848, was governed by a local regime from 848, and passed to the tangut state of western xia in about 1036. the "library cave" (cave 17), sealed around the early 11th century, was opened in 1900 by wang yuanlu, a daoist priest who guarded the caves; it held tens of thousands of manuscripts in chinese, tibetan, sanskrit, sogdian, khotanese and other languages, including a printed diamond sutra dated 868. aurel stein in 1907, paul pelliot in 1908 and others obtained large numbers of these manuscripts, now held in london, paris and elsewhere; the removals are described in china as theft and by the acquiring institutions as purchases. unesco inscribed the mogao caves in 1987, and the dunhuang academy has conserved them since 1944.

title: Mohenjo-daro
sum: Mohenjo-daro was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization in present-day Pakistan, occupied from about 2500 to 1900 BCE.
search: mohenjo-daro mohenjo-daro was a major city of the indus valley civilization in present-day pakistan, occupied from about 2500 to 1900 bce. it had a grid layout with brick-lined drains and wells. the 'great bath' is a large water tank at the center of its citadel. it may have held tens of thousands of people. it was declared a unesco world heritage site in 1980.

title: Monte Alban
sum: Monte Alban was the hilltop capital of the Zapotec people in the Oaxaca Valley of Mexico, founded around 500 BCE and abandoned by about 800 CE.
search: monte alban monte alban was the hilltop capital of the zapotec people in the oaxaca valley of mexico, founded around 500 bce and abandoned by about 800 ce. the site sits on a leveled mountaintop overlooking three valleys. carved stones known as danzantes, dated to the early centuries of the city, show figures with glyphs, part of an early mesoamerican writing tradition. the city grew to a population of well over ten thousand in its classic period. it maintained relations with teotihuacan, and depictions at teotihuacan show zapotec visitors. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1987.

title: Monte Verde
sum: Monte Verde is an archaeological site in southern Chile that, for decades, was considered the best evidence that people lived in South America about 14,500 years ago, before the Clovis culture of North America; its age is now debated.
search: monte verde monte verde is an archaeological site in southern chile that, for decades, was considered the best evidence that people lived in south america about 14,500 years ago, before the clovis culture of north america; its age is now debated. excavations led by tom dillehay from the 1970s exposed wooden hut foundations, leather, rope, and plant remains preserved in a peat bog. in 1997 a panel of archaeologists inspected the site and accepted an age of about 14,500 years. the site helped overturn the 'clovis-first' model; see  peopling of the americas . a recent study has proposed a much younger age for the site; specialists dispute this, and the question is unsettled.

title: Nalanda
sum: Nalanda is an archaeological site in Bihar, India, of a Buddhist monastic university founded in about the 5th century CE that drew students from across Asia until it was sacked around 1200.
search: nalanda nalanda is an archaeological site in bihar, india, of a buddhist monastic university founded in about the 5th century ce that drew students from across asia until it was sacked around 1200. nalanda was founded in about the 5th century ce, traditionally under the gupta ruler kumaragupta i, and grew into a large monastic university. the chinese pilgrim xuanzang studied at nalanda in the 630s and 640s and reported about 10,000 residents; another chinese pilgrim, yijing, described it in 675. students and visitors came from china, tibet, korea, central asia and southeast asia, and in the 9th century a ruler of srivijaya funded a monastery at nalanda. nalanda taught buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine. forces under bakhtiyar khalji sacked nalanda around 1200; later traditions say its library burned for months, and historians debate how completely it was destroyed and whether its decline began earlier. unesco inscribed the archaeological site of nalanda mahavihara in 2016, and a new nalanda university opened in 2014.

title: Nan Madol
sum: Nan Madol is a ruined city of artificial stone islets built in a lagoon off Pohnpei, in the Federated States of Micronesia, the ceremonial and political center of the Saudeleur dynasty from about the 12th century until around 1628.
search: nan madol nan madol is a ruined city of artificial stone islets built in a lagoon off pohnpei, in the federated states of micronesia, the ceremonial and political center of the saudeleur dynasty from about the 12th century until around 1628. nan madol consists of about 92 artificial islets built from stacked basalt columns and coral fill, linked by tidal canals, over a core area of about 1.5 by 0.5 kilometers. human activity at the site dates from as early as the 1st or 2nd century ce, islet construction began in the 8th or 9th century, and the megalithic stonework that gives the site its present form was built from about 1180 to 1200. tradition holds that the saudeleur dynasty ruled pohnpei from nan madol, uniting an estimated population of about 25,000 on the island, though the number of people living at nan madol itself was probably under 1,000. around 1628 a warrior named isokelekel is said in tradition to have invaded and ended saudeleur rule; some scholars also point to population decline as a contributing cause of the site's abandonment. unesco inscribed nan madol as a world heritage site in 2016.

title: Nara
sum: Nara is a city in Japan's Kansai region that was the capital, then called Heijō-kyō, from 710 to 784 CE, a period in which the Japanese court adopted Chinese models of city planning, writing and state Buddhism.
search: nara nara is a city in japan's kansai region that was the capital, then called heijō-kyō, from 710 to 784 ce, a period in which the japanese court adopted chinese models of city planning, writing and state buddhism. heijō-kyō was established as the capital in 710 under empress genmei, on a grid plan modeled on the tang capital chang'an. court scholars compiled the chronicles kojiki (712) and nihon shoki (720) at nara, written with chinese characters. a smallpox epidemic in 735 to 737 is estimated by some historians to have killed a quarter to a third of japan's population, though the figure is uncertain. in 743 emperor shōmu ordered a giant bronze buddha, which was dedicated at tōdai-ji in 752; the statue is about 15 meters tall. the shōsōin storehouse at tōdai-ji preserves objects from the 8th-century court, including items that reflect trade along the silk roads. the court moved to nagaoka in 784 and to heian-kyō (kyoto) in 794, a move often attributed in part to the political influence of buddhist institutions at nara. unesco inscribed the historic monuments of ancient nara in 1998.

title: Nazca Lines
sum: The Nazca Lines are a group of geoglyphs in the desert of southern Peru, made between about 400 BCE and 500 CE by the Paracas and Nazca cultures, showing animal, plant and geometric shapes and hundreds of straight lines visible mainly from…
search: nazca lines the nazca lines are a group of geoglyphs in the desert of southern peru, made between about 400 bce and 500 ce by the paracas and nazca cultures, showing animal, plant and geometric shapes and hundreds of straight lines visible mainly from the air. the lines lie in the nazca desert between the towns of nazca and palpa, about 400 kilometers south of lima, and cover about 50 square kilometers. they were made by removing a top layer of reddish, iron-oxide-coated pebbles to expose lighter ground beneath; the lines and figures cut roughly 10 to 15 centimeters deep. the combined lines run more than 1,300 kilometers, and the largest figures, such as a 134-meter condor and a 93-meter hummingbird, reach lengths of tens to a few hundred meters. peruvian archaeologist toribio mejía xesspe noted the lines on foot in 1927; american historian paul kosok observed them from the air in 1940 to 1941 and proposed astronomical alignments, a theory developed further by maria reiche; researchers gerald hawkins and anthony aveni concluded in 1990 that the evidence did not support a systematic astronomical purpose. other proposed purposes include ritual paths connected to water and fertility, walked in ceremony, and markers tied to underground water sources; no single explanation is agreed on. unesco inscribed the lines and geoglyphs of nazca and pampas de jumana in 1994. the site has been damaged by squatters, a limestone quarry, a 2014 greenpeace protest that left marks near one geoglyph, and a 2018 truck crossing, and erosion and off-road vehicles remain ongoing threats.

title: Newgrange
sum: Newgrange is a large passage tomb in the Boyne Valley of County Meath, Ireland, built about 3200 BCE by Neolithic farmers and aligned so that the winter solstice sunrise lights its inner chamber.
