search: newgrange newgrange is a large passage tomb in the boyne valley of county meath, ireland, built about 3200 bce by neolithic farmers and aligned so that the winter solstice sunrise lights its inner chamber. newgrange is a mound about 12 meters high and roughly 80 meters across, with a passage about 19 meters long leading to a cross-shaped chamber, and radiocarbon dates place its construction about 3200 bce, older than the great pyramid of giza. a "roof box" above the entrance admits sunlight along the passage for about 17 minutes around sunrise at the winter solstice. kerbstones around the base carry carved designs, including spirals, and cremated remains of a small number of people were found in the chamber. the white quartz wall at the front was reconstructed in the 1970s, and whether it originally looked like that is debated. newgrange was used again in later periods, and roman coins and other offerings have been found there; later irish tradition associated the boyne complex with legendary figures. newgrange lies with the nearby passage tombs at knowth and dowth, and unesco inscribed the brú na bóinne complex in 1993.

title: Nile River
sum: The Nile River is a river of northeastern Africa about 6,650 kilometers long, flowing north to the Mediterranean, whose annual flood supported farming and the states of Egypt and Nubia from about the 6th millennium BCE.
search: nile river the nile river is a river of northeastern africa about 6,650 kilometers long, flowing north to the mediterranean, whose annual flood supported farming and the states of egypt and nubia from about the 6th millennium bce. the nile flows north from the highlands of east and central africa to the mediterranean; its two main branches, the white nile from the lake victoria region and the blue nile from lake tana in ethiopia, meet at khartoum, and the ethiopian highlands supply most of the seasonal flood. farming communities are documented in the nile valley and the fayum from about the 6th millennium bce, and the summer flood deposited silt that kept the valley fertile. egyptian officials measured the flood on nilometers, and in later periods taxation was tied to its height. the states of egypt, after the unification of egypt, and of kush, upstream in nubia, grew along the river. the aswan high dam, completed in 1970, ended the annual flood in egypt and created lake nasser; about 100,000 nubians were relocated, and monuments such as abu simbel were moved. eleven countries share the nile basin. a 1959 agreement between egypt and sudan allocated most of the river's measured flow to those two states, and ethiopia's grand ethiopian renaissance dam on the blue nile, begun in 2011 and filled in stages from 2020, is a subject of dispute over water with egypt and sudan.

title: Paris
sum: Paris is the capital of France, on the Seine River, which grew from a settlement of the Gaulish Parisii on the Île de la Cité in about the 3rd century BCE into a Roman town, a medieval capital, a center of revolutions and one of Europe's…
search: paris paris is the capital of france, on the seine river, which grew from a settlement of the gaulish parisii on the île de la cité in about the 3rd century bce into a roman town, a medieval capital, a center of revolutions and one of europe's largest cities. paris grew from a settlement of the parisii on the île de la cité in about the 3rd century bce; rome took the area in 52 bce and built the town of lutetia. clovis made paris his capital in about 508, and the capetian kings made it the center of the french kingdom from 987; notre-dame was begun in 1163, and the university of paris had developed by about 1200. paris had perhaps 200,000 inhabitants around 1300, among the largest cities in europe, and lost a large share of its people to the black death in 1348. the bastille fell on 14 july 1789 during the french revolution, and thousands of people were executed in paris in the reign of terror of 1793 to 1794. baron haussmann rebuilt central paris in the 1850s and 1860s with wide boulevards, sewers and parks. the suppression of the paris commune in 1871 killed many thousands of people in a week of fighting and executions, with estimates of about 10,000 to 20,000. germany occupied paris from june 1940 to august 1944; in july 1942 french police arrested about 13,000 jews in the vel' d'hiv roundup, most of whom were later deported to auschwitz. unesco inscribed paris, banks of the seine, in 1991.

title: Pasargadae
sum: Pasargadae was the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in about 550 BCE on the plateau of Fars in present-day Iran, and the site of his tomb.
search: pasargadae pasargadae was the first capital of the achaemenid persian empire, founded by cyrus the great in about 550 bce on the plateau of fars in present-day iran, and the site of his tomb. pasargadae lies in fars province, southwestern iran, about 90 kilometers northeast of persepolis. cyrus the great founded pasargadae after defeating the median king astyages, in about 550 bce, and it served as a royal seat until darius i and his successors developed persepolis and susa. pasargadae has an audience hall, residential palaces, a gate with a relief of a winged figure, and a formal garden with water channels that is regarded as an early example of the persian garden. stonemasons from other parts of the empire, including lydia and ionia in western anatolia, contributed to its masonry, and its architecture combines persian, elamite, mesopotamian and anatolian elements. the tomb of cyrus, a stepped base topped by a gabled stone chamber, stands at the site; greek writers report that alexander visited it and ordered its restoration after it had been robbed. inscriptions naming cyrus appear at pasargadae, though some scholars argue that they were added under darius i. unesco inscribed pasargadae in 2004.

title: Persepolis
sum: Persepolis was a ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire in southwestern Iran, begun around 518 BCE under Darius I and burned by Alexander the Great's army in 330 BCE.
search: persepolis persepolis was a ceremonial capital of the achaemenid empire in southwestern iran, begun around 518 bce under darius i and burned by alexander the great's army in 330 bce. construction began under darius i around 518 bce and continued under his successors. the apadana reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts. alexander's army burned the palace in 330 bce; ancient sources give conflicting motives, including revenge and drunken impulse. thousands of elamite tablets, the persepolis fortification tablets, record rations and administration. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1979.

title: Petra
sum: Petra is a rock-cut city in the mountains of southern Jordan that served as the capital of the Nabataean kingdom from about the 2nd century BCE until Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE.
search: petra petra is a rock-cut city in the mountains of southern jordan that served as the capital of the nabataean kingdom from about the 2nd century bce until rome annexed the kingdom in 106 ce. petra lies in a basin among sandstone mountains, entered through a gorge about 1.2 kilometers long known as the siq. greek writers describe an expedition against the nabataeans in 312 bce and their rock refuge, which is sometimes identified with petra, though the identification is doubtful. petra's carved facades, including al-khazneh ("the treasury"), date mostly from about the 1st century bce to the 1st century ce. most facades are thought to be tombs, though the use of some, including the treasury, is debated. petra was supplied by dams, channels, ceramic pipes and cisterns in a desert climate, and its wealth is generally attributed to the caravan trade in incense and other goods. estimates of its peak population are uncertain, with about 20,000 commonly cited and some figures as high as 30,000. after roman annexation in 106 ce, petra became part of the province of arabia. an earthquake in 363 ce destroyed many buildings and the city declined afterward; the swiss traveler johann ludwig burckhardt brought it to european attention in 1812. unesco inscribed petra in 1985.

title: Pompeii
sum: Pompeii was a Roman town on the Bay of Naples in Italy, founded in about the 7th century BCE, that was buried under volcanic ash and pumice when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE.
search: pompeii pompeii was a roman town on the bay of naples in italy, founded in about the 7th century bce, that was buried under volcanic ash and pumice when mount vesuvius erupted in 79 ce. pompeii was founded in about the 7th century bce by the oscans, came under greek and etruscan influence, and became a roman colony in 80 bce. an earthquake in 62 or 63 ce damaged the town, and repairs were still under way when vesuvius erupted in 79 ce. pompeii's population is estimated at about 11,000, with estimates ranging from about 10,000 to 20,000. the eruption buried pompeii under pumice and ash, and pyroclastic surges killed people who had stayed; about 1,100 bodies have been found in the excavated town, and many inhabitants are thought to have fled. the traditional date of the eruption is 24 august, but a charcoal inscription found in 2018 suggests a later date, possibly in october. excavations began in 1748, and in 1863 giuseppe fiorelli began pouring plaster into voids left by decayed bodies to produce casts of victims; graffiti, shop signs and election notices survive on the walls. unesco inscribed the archaeological areas of pompeii, herculaneum and torre annunziata in 1997.

title: Port Royal
sum: Port Royal was an English port town at the tip of the Palisadoes spit at the entrance to Kingston Harbour, Jamaica, which grew after 1655 as a base for privateers and traders and lost about two-thirds of its area to an earthquake on 7 June…
search: port royal port royal was an english port town at the tip of the palisadoes spit at the entrance to kingston harbour, jamaica, which grew after 1655 as a base for privateers and traders and lost about two-thirds of its area to an earthquake on 7 june 1692. england took jamaica from spain in 1655, and port royal was fortified from 1656; english governors issued commissions to privateers, who used the port as a base to attack spanish ships and towns. henry morgan, a privateer who later became lieutenant governor of jamaica, led raids from the colony, including the sack of panama in 1671. port royal was a trading port for the island's goods and a landing and sale point for enslaved africans; it had about 6,500 residents in 1692. on 7 june 1692 an earthquake, and the liquefaction of the sandy ground beneath the town, sank about two-thirds of port royal into the harbor. about 2,000 people are estimated to have died in the quake and its immediate aftermath, and several thousand more died of injury and disease in the following weeks. some contemporary accounts read the earthquake as divine judgment. survivors founded kingston across the harbor, a fire in 1703 destroyed much of what remained of port royal, and the royal navy used the town as a base into the early 20th century. underwater archaeology from the 1950s, and again from the 1980s, has recovered buildings and household objects from the submerged area.

title: Potosi
sum: Potosi is a mining city in the Bolivian Andes, founded in 1545 beside the silver mountain Cerro Rico, whose output supplied Spanish and world trade for centuries.
search: potosi potosi is a mining city in the bolivian andes, founded in 1545 beside the silver mountain cerro rico, whose output supplied spanish and world trade for centuries. silver was discovered at cerro rico in 1545. by around 1600 potosi was one of the largest cities in the americas, with population estimates around 150,000. the spanish organized labor through the mita, a forced-labor draft adapted from an inca system. the mercury amalgamation process introduced in the 1570s increased silver output. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1987.

title: Poverty Point
sum: Poverty Point is a large earthwork complex in Louisiana built by hunter-gatherer-fishers between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, with concentric ridges and huge mounds.
search: poverty point poverty point is a large earthwork complex in louisiana built by hunter-gatherer-fishers between about 1700 and 1100 bce, with concentric ridges and huge mounds. the site has six concentric earthen ridges and several mounds, the largest about 22 meters high. it was built by a society without agriculture, according to current evidence. stone and other materials were brought from across the mississippi valley, some from hundreds of kilometers away. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 2014. the site was abandoned around 1100 bce.

title: Rapa Nui
sum: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is a remote Pacific island settled by Polynesians around 1200 CE, famous for nearly a thousand monumental stone statues called moai.
search: rapa nui rapa nui (easter island) is a remote pacific island settled by polynesians around 1200 ce, famous for nearly a thousand monumental stone statues called moai. the island lies in the southeastern pacific, thousands of kilometers from the nearest large land. estimates for the arrival of the polynesian settlers range from as early as about 300 ce, based on contested early radiocarbon dates, to about 1200 ce, the date favored by many recent studies. about 400 moai (397 in one count) lie in the quarry of rano raraku in various stages of completion, and about 95 percent of the island's monolithic statues were carved from its volcanic tuff. published counts of the total number of moai differ. the popular story of self-inflicted ecological collapse is contested. researchers point to introduced rats, which may have been the main cause of deforestation, and to disease and slave raids. in december 1862 peruvian slavers captured about 1,000 islanders, and reports put the total taken in 1862 to 1864 at more than 1,400. most of the captives died in peru, and a smallpox epidemic that followed the return of a few survivors in 1863 reportedly killed about a thousand more. these figures come from popular summaries and vary between accounts. rapa nui national park was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1995.

title: Robben Island
sum: Robben Island is a small island in Table Bay, about 7 kilometers off Cape Town, South Africa, used from the 17th century to 1996 as a place of banishment, a leprosy colony and a prison, and best known for the political prisoners held there…
search: robben island robben island is a small island in table bay, about 7 kilometers off cape town, south africa, used from the 17th century to 1996 as a place of banishment, a leprosy colony and a prison, and best known for the political prisoners held there under apartheid, including nelson mandela. robben island lies in table bay about 7 kilometers from cape town and covers about 5 square kilometers; its name comes from the dutch word for seals. the dutch east india company began using robben island as a place of banishment in the 1650s; among those sent there was the khoikhoi interpreter autshumato, in 1658. a leprosy colony operated on the island from 1846 to 1931, and it served as a military base in the second world war. from 1961 to 1996 robben island was a maximum-security prison where the apartheid state held political prisoners, including nelson mandela (imprisoned on the island for 18 of his 27 years, from 1964), robert sobukwe, walter sisulu and govan mbeki. prisoners worked in a limestone quarry, and the glare damaged mandela's eyes; prisoners organized study and debate among themselves, and the prison was nicknamed a "university". the last political prisoners were released in 1991 and the prison closed in 1996. unesco inscribed robben island in 1999, and former prisoners lead tours of the island today.

title: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
sum: The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela are eleven churches carved down into volcanic rock in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, traditionally attributed to King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty in the early 13th century and still in use for…
search: rock-hewn churches of lalibela the rock-hewn churches of lalibela are eleven churches carved down into volcanic rock in the highlands of northern ethiopia, traditionally attributed to king lalibela of the zagwe dynasty in the early 13th century and still in use for worship. lalibela lies at about 2,500 meters in the amhara region of ethiopia and has eleven monolithic churches, in two main groups and one separate cross-shaped church, bete giyorgis. the churches are traditionally attributed to king lalibela, who reigned around the late 12th and early 13th centuries; some scholars propose that some churches are older. builders first cut trenches into the rock and then carved the exterior and interior of each church from the block left standing, joining the churches by trenches and tunnels and cutting drainage channels. lalibela is presented in tradition as a "new jerusalem", with features named after places in the holy land, such as a stream called the jordan; the link with the loss of jerusalem to saladin in 1187 is traditional and is not documented in contemporary sources. the churches remain in active use, and large numbers of pilgrims come at major festivals. unesco inscribed the rock-hewn churches of lalibela in 1978.

title: Rome
sum: Rome, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, grew from a small city on the Tiber to the capital of an empire and remains a major city today.
search: rome rome, traditionally founded in 753 bce, grew from a small city on the tiber to the capital of an empire and remains a major city today. rome had roughly a million inhabitants in the first two centuries ce, by many estimates. the colosseum was completed in 80 ce. the city was sacked in 410 and 455 ce. it later became the seat of the papacy.

title: Samarkand
sum: Samarkand is a city in present-day Uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of Central Asia and a leading crossroads of the Silk Roads.
search: samarkand samarkand is a city in present-day uzbekistan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of central asia and a leading crossroads of the silk roads. the ancient city (afrasiab) is thought to date from the 7th century bce or earlier. it was known to the greeks as maracanda and was taken by alexander the great in 329 bce. it was a major sogdian city, was sacked by genghis khan in 1220, and became timur's capital in the 1370s. unesco inscribed 'samarkand - crossroad of cultures' in 2001.

title: Santo Domingo
sum: Santo Domingo is the capital of the Dominican Republic, on the south coast of Hispaniola, founded by Spain in 1496 and commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the Americas.
search: santo domingo santo domingo is the capital of the dominican republic, on the south coast of hispaniola, founded by spain in 1496 and commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited european-founded city in the americas. santo domingo was founded in 1496 by bartholomew columbus on the east bank of the ozama river, and governor nicolás de ovando moved it to the west bank in 1502 after storm damage. santo domingo became the seat of spanish administration in the caribbean, with the first real audiencia in the americas (created by royal decree in 1511, with its start of operation dated differently by sources), a cathedral begun in the 1510s and completed in 1540, and a university founded in 1538. expeditions to puerto rico, cuba and the mainland were organized from hispaniola under this colonial administration. the taíno population of hispaniola fell sharply under forced labor, violence and disease, including a smallpox epidemic beginning in 1518. estimates of the pre-contact population range from tens of thousands to over a million, and a spanish count in 1514 recorded about 26,000 taíno on the island. enslaved africans were brought to hispaniola from the early 1500s; in december 1521 enslaved africans rebelled on a sugar estate near the city, an uprising commonly described as the first of its kind in the americas. unesco inscribed the colonial city of santo domingo in 1990.

title: Sarai
sum: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the western part of the Mongol Empire, on the lower Volga River in present-day southern Russia, founded around 1250 by Batu Khan and sacked by Timur in 1395.
search: sarai sarai was the capital of the golden horde, the western part of the mongol empire, on the lower volga river in present-day southern russia, founded around 1250 by batu khan and sacked by timur in 1395. batu khan, a grandson of chinggis khan, founded sarai (persian for "palace") about 1250 on the lower volga, near selitrennoye in present-day astrakhan oblast; a second city, sarai berke, was built upstream, near present-day volgograd, and the chronology of the two is debated. rus' princes traveled to sarai to pay tribute and receive a yarlyk (charter) confirming their rule, and an orthodox bishopric of sarai was established in 1261. öz beg khan (reigned 1313 to 1341) adopted islam as the horde's state religion. the traveler ibn battuta visited in the 1330s and described a large city with markets and people of many nations. plague reached the black sea port of caffa in 1346 during a siege by golden horde forces and spread from there through mediterranean ports; the horde's role in its spread is debated. timur sacked sarai in 1395 in his war with khan tokhtamysh, and the city did not recover its former status.

title: Stonehenge
sum: Stonehenge is a monument of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, begun as a circular earthwork around 3000 BCE and rebuilt in stone over the next several centuries.
search: stonehenge stonehenge is a monument of standing stones on salisbury plain in southern england, begun as a circular earthwork around 3000 bce and rebuilt in stone over the next several centuries. the first phase was a circular ditch and bank, around 3000 bce. the large sarsen stones, of which the biggest weigh around 25 tons, were sourced from around 25 kilometers away, according to a 2020 study identifying west woods as the source. the smaller bluestones were brought from the preseli hills in wales, more than 200 kilometers away. a 2024 study reported that the altar stone came from northern scotland, roughly 750 kilometers away. the site was used for burials, with cremated remains from early in its history, and its axis aligns with the solstice sunrise and sunset.

title: Taj Mahal
sum: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum in Agra, built from about 1632 to 1653 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.
search: taj mahal the taj mahal is a white marble mausoleum in agra, built from about 1632 to 1653 by the mughal emperor shah jahan for his wife mumtaz mahal, who died in 1631. mumtaz mahal died in 1631 while giving birth. construction began in 1632, with the main tomb largely finished by about 1643 and the complex by 1653. commonly cited estimates give around 20,000 workers. ustad ahmad lahori is often named as its chief architect, though attribution is debated. it was inscribed on the unesco world heritage list in 1983.

title: Tenochtitlan
sum: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 and destroyed after a siege in 1521.
search: tenochtitlan tenochtitlan was the capital of the aztec empire, founded on an island in lake texcoco in 1325 and destroyed after a siege in 1521. population estimates for 1519 range from about 100,000 to 400,000, with 200,000 often cited, making it one of the largest cities in the world. causeways and canals connected it to the mainland; chinampas provided food. the templo mayor was its main temple. mexico city was built over its ruins.

title: Teotihuacan
sum: Teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the Valley of Mexico that flourished from about 100 BCE to 550 CE, home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon.
search: teotihuacan teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the valley of mexico that flourished from about 100 bce to 550 ce, home to the pyramids of the sun and moon. at its peak, around 450 to 500 ce, it may have had 125,000 to 200,000 inhabitants. the city was laid out on a grid along the 'avenue of the dead'. it had wide trade and political links, including with maya cities. the aztecs later gave it its name, meaning roughly 'place where the gods were created'.

title: Tikal
sum: Tikal is a large Maya city in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, with traces of farming from about 1000 BCE, a dominant Classic-period kingdom whose rulers left inscriptions from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and a city almost deserted…
search: tikal tikal is a large maya city in the rainforest of northern guatemala, with traces of farming from about 1000 bce, a dominant classic-period kingdom whose rulers left inscriptions from the 3rd to the 9th century ce, and a city almost deserted after about 950. tikal, called yax mutal in inscriptions and the seat of a kingdom called mutul, lies in the petén region of guatemala; traces of farming date to about 1000 bce, and monumental building began about 400 to 300 bce. inscriptions record that in january 378 a warlord named siyaj k'ak' arrived from the west and tikal's king died the same day; a new king linked to teotihuacan was then installed, and scholars debate whether the event was a conquest or an alliance. in 562 tikal was defeated by calakmul and caracol and its king was apparently captured and sacrificed; in 695 jasaw chan k'awiil i defeated calakmul, and tikal revived. estimates of tikal's peak population range from about 10,000 to 90,000 for the city, with far higher numbers proposed for its surrounding region, and archaeologists debate them. the last dated monument was set up in 869, and after about 950 tikal was almost deserted, during the wider classic maya collapse. modesto méndez and ambrosio tut visited in 1848, alfred maudslay documented the site in 1881 to 1882, and the university of pennsylvania excavated it from 1956 to 1970; guatemala made it a national park in 1955 and unesco inscribed it in 1979.

title: Timbuktu
sum: Timbuktu is a city in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara that became a hub of the trans-Saharan trade and of Islamic scholarship.
search: timbuktu timbuktu is a city in mali on the southern edge of the sahara that became a hub of the trans-saharan trade and of islamic scholarship. it was founded around 1100 ce as a seasonal camp. salt from the sahara and gold from the south were traded there. the sankore mosque and madrasa were centers of learning. it holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts and was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 1988.

title: Troy
sum: Troy is an archaeological site at Hisarlık in northwestern Turkey, occupied from about 3000 BCE into the Byzantine era in nine main layers, and identified by many scholars as the city of Homer's Iliad.
search: troy troy is an archaeological site at hisarlık in northwestern turkey, occupied from about 3000 bce into the byzantine era in nine main layers, and identified by many scholars as the city of homer's iliad. troy stands at hisarlık, near the dardanelles in çanakkale province, turkey; excavators distinguish nine main settlement layers, troy i to troy ix, beginning around 3000 bce. heinrich schliemann began excavations at troy in 1870, and later excavators included wilhelm dörpfeld, carl blegen and manfred korfmann. schliemann's "treasure of priam" came from troy ii, about 2500 bce, far older than any trojan war; he took it out of the ottoman empire, it disappeared from berlin in 1945 and resurfaced in moscow in the 1990s. troy vi (about 1700 to 1300 bce) was a large fortified city, and troy viia was destroyed by fire around 1180 bce and is often proposed as the city of the trojan war, if the war has a historical basis. hittite texts mention a land called wilusa in western anatolia, whose name is often linked to ilios, a greek name for troy; the identification is debated. whether a trojan war took place is unknown; the iliad was composed in greek around the 8th century bce, centuries after the events it describes. greeks and romans later built the city of ilion at the site, and unesco inscribed troy in 1998.

title: Uluru
sum: Uluru is a large sandstone inselberg in central Australia, sacred to the Anangu people, who have been associated with the site for more than 10,000 years and hold traditional custodianship of it today.
search: uluru uluru is a large sandstone inselberg in central australia, sacred to the anangu people, who have been associated with the site for more than 10,000 years and hold traditional custodianship of it today. uluru rises 348 meters above the surrounding plain (863 meters above sea level) and lies about 335 kilometers southwest of alice springs; it is composed of arkose sandstone whose lack of internal jointing has left it largely free of scree slopes. archaeological evidence shows human presence in the area for more than 10,000 years; the date_start of -8000 is a round figure within that range, and older evidence for the peopling of the surrounding region belongs to a different brief. the anangu, whose pitjantjatjara and yankunytjatjara traditions call the rock's stories tjukurpa, hold that ancestral beings shaped the landscape, and some tracks and sites at uluru carry restrictions tied to gender and ceremony. surveyor william gosse named the formation ayers rock on 19 july 1873; the government returned ownership to the local pitjantjatjara people on 26 october 1985, under a 99-year lease-back and joint management arrangement, and dual naming (later reordered to uluru / ayers rock in 2002) followed in 1993. the uluru-kata tjuta national park board voted in 2017 to end recreational climbing, which had long concerned the anangu as crossing a sacred track and as a safety risk; the ban took effect on 26 october 2019. unesco inscribed uluru-kata tjuta national park in 1987.

title: Upano Valley Settlements
sum: The Upano Valley settlements are a network of ancient urban centers in the Ecuadorian Amazon, documented by lidar and reported in 2024, occupied from about 500 BCE for many centuries.
search: upano valley settlements the upano valley settlements are a network of ancient urban centers in the ecuadorian amazon, documented by lidar and reported in 2024, occupied from about 500 bce for many centuries. the network spans roughly 300 square kilometers (about 115 square miles) and includes some 15 urban centers. more than 6,000 rectangular earthen platforms, probably house and civic foundations, are linked by roads and drainage canals. the valley probably held at least 10,000 farmers, and possibly many more, about 2,000 years ago. the population began to leave between about 300 and 600 ce; the reasons are unknown.

title: Ur
sum: Ur was a Sumerian city in southern Iraq, occupied from about 3800 BCE and abandoned around 500 BCE, known for its Great Ziggurat, its royal cemetery, and its role as the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2100 BCE.
search: ur ur was a sumerian city in southern iraq, occupied from about 3800 bce and abandoned around 500 bce, known for its great ziggurat, its royal cemetery, and its role as the capital of the third dynasty of ur about 2100 bce. ur lies at tell el-muqayyar in dhi qar governorate, southern iraq, near the euphrates; it was occupied by the late ubaid period and grew into a city in the 3rd millennium bce. leonard woolley excavated ur from 1922 to 1934 and found a royal cemetery dated to about 2600 to 2500 bce, with graves holding gold and lapis lazuli jewelry, lyres and, in some, the bodies of many attendants placed with the dead; how the attendants died is debated. enheduanna, a daughter of sargon of akkad and high priestess of the moon god nanna at ur about 2300 bce, is the earliest named author known. ur-nammu (reigned about 2112 to 2095 bce) founded the third dynasty of ur, built the great ziggurat for nanna, and is credited with the earliest surviving law code. ur fell to elamite forces about 2004 bce and later became a smaller city; it was abandoned around 500 bce, and proposed causes include a shift in the euphrates and drier conditions. the biblical "ur of the chaldees", birthplace of abraham, is often identified with ur, but the identification is debated. unesco included ur in the "ahwar of southern iraq" listing in 2016.

title: Uruk
sum: Uruk was a Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 BCE.
search: uruk uruk was a sumerian city in southern mesopotamia and one of the first large cities in the world, at its peak around 3200 to 2900 bce. it has yielded some of the earliest known writing, on clay tablets from the eanna temple precinct. by about 2900 bce a wall about 9 kilometers long enclosed roughly 600 hectares (6 square kilometers), with an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 residents. uruk is the legendary city of gilgamesh. the modern site is called warka, in iraq.

title: Valley of the Kings
sum: The Valley of the Kings is a valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, in Egypt, where pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 BCE.
search: valley of the kings the valley of the kings is a valley on the west bank of the nile opposite thebes, in egypt, where pharaohs of the new kingdom were buried in rock-cut tombs from about 1500 to 1070 bce. the valley of the kings served for royal burials of the 18th to 20th dynasties, from about 1500 bce until about 1070 bce, and holds more than 60 tombs cut into limestone hills. the rulers chose hidden rock-cut tombs in place of the pyramids of earlier periods, such as those at giza. most tombs were robbed in antiquity; records of trials of tomb robbers survive from the 20th dynasty, and priests later moved royal mummies to hidden caches. the workmen's village of deir el-medina yielded ration accounts and an account of a strike over unpaid rations in about 1157 bce, often described as one of the earliest recorded labor strikes. howard carter found the tomb of tutankhamun (kv62) in november 1922, largely intact and holding thousands of objects. unesco inscribed ancient thebes with its necropolis, including the valley of the kings, in 1979.

title: Varanasi
sum: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, continuously settled since about the 8th century BCE and the most important Hindu pilgrimage and cremation center.
search: varanasi varanasi, also called benares or kashi, is a city on the ganges in uttar pradesh, india, continuously settled since about the 8th century bce and the most important hindu pilgrimage and cremation center. varanasi lies on the left bank of the ganges in uttar pradesh, and excavations at rajghat show settlement from about the 8th century bce. hindu tradition holds that dying at varanasi and being cremated beside the ganges gives release from the cycle of rebirth, so families bring their dead from across india to cremation sites such as manikarnika, and more than 80 bathing and cremation steps (ghats) line the river. the buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon at sarnath, near varanasi, in about the 5th century bce; sarnath has an ashokan pillar and gupta-period sculpture. varanasi has been a center of sanskrit learning, and banaras hindu university was founded in 1916; the city is also known for silk weaving. the kashi vishwanath temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times, and the present temple dates from 1780; the adjacent gyanvapi mosque and the history of the site are the subject of continuing legal disputes. varanasi had about 1.2 million people at the 2011 census.

title: Venice
sum: Venice is a city on islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century CE and, as an independent republic until 1797, a leading maritime and trading power of the…
search: venice venice is a city on islands in a lagoon at the head of the adriatic sea in northeastern italy, settled from about the 5th to 6th century ce and, as an independent republic until 1797, a leading maritime and trading power of the mediterranean. tradition dates venice's founding on lagoon islands to 25 march 421, but no surviving records deal with it directly; the date_start of 500 is a round placeholder for settlement in the 5th to 6th centuries. nominally under byzantine authority, venice became self-governing under elected doges, dated by tradition from 697 and by historians from the early 8th century; about 810 the ducal seat moved to the rialto. in 1204 a crusade fleet supplied by venice under doge enrico dandolo sacked constantinople, and venice took a large share of the byzantine lands, including crete; wars with the ottoman empire later cost it negroponte (1470), cyprus (1570 to 1573) and crete (1669). venice opened a plague hospital on the island of santa maria di nazareth in 1423, regarded as the first permanent lazaretto, and a second, lazzaretto nuovo, in 1468, and its isolation of arriving people and goods became an early model of quarantine. in 1516 the republic required its jewish residents to live in an enclosed district called the ghetto, whose name later spread to other cities. the great council voted to end the republic on 12 may 1797, as french forces approached; austria received venice under the treaty of campo formio, and it joined the kingdom of italy in 1866. unesco inscribed venice and its lagoon in 1987; the historic center's population fell from about 175,000 in the 1950s to under 50,000, and the mose flood barriers were first raised in october 2020.

title: Xingu Garden Cities
sum: The Xingu garden cities are pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu region of Brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 CE, whose plazas, roads, and ditches were mapped by the anthropologist Michael Heckenberger with the Kuikuro people.
search: xingu garden cities the xingu garden cities are pre-columbian settlements in the upper xingu region of brazil, dating from about 1200 to 1600 ce, whose plazas, roads, and ditches were mapped by the anthropologist michael heckenberger with the kuikuro people. researchers documented about 28 towns, villages, and hamlets, which may have supported up to about 50,000 people. larger towns had ditches about 3 meters deep and 10 meters wide, plazas up to 150 meters across, and roads aligned with the summer solstice. surrounding fields grew manioc, and earthen dams and ponds supported fish farming. population estimates are debated, and the descendants of the builders still live in the region.

title: Yellow River
sum: The Yellow River (Huang He) is a river of northern China, about 5,460 kilometers long, whose loess-laden floodplain was a center of early farming and of the Shang and Zhou states, and whose floods and course changes have shaped Chinese…
search: yellow river the yellow river (huang he) is a river of northern china, about 5,460 kilometers long, whose loess-laden floodplain was a center of early farming and of the shang and zhou states, and whose floods and course changes have shaped chinese history. the yellow river rises in the bayan har mountains of qinghai and flows through northern china to the bohai sea. farming communities growing millet are documented in the yellow river basin from about the 7th to 6th millennia bce, and the shang and zhou states arose in its middle and lower reaches. the yellow river carries a heavy load of loess sediment from the loess plateau, which has raised its bed above the surrounding plain in the lower reaches and made dikes necessary; records list many breaches and several major changes of course. from 1128 (some sources give 1194) until 1855 the river mostly ran south of the shandong peninsula into the yellow sea, until a breach around 1851 to 1855 returned it to a northern course. a flood in 1887 is estimated to have killed between about 900,000 and 2 million people. in 1938, during the second sino-japanese war, nationalist forces breached dikes at huayuankou to slow the japanese advance; several hundred thousand people died, with published estimates up to about 900,000, and millions were displaced.

title: Çatalhöyük
sum: Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement in central Turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE, with houses packed together and entered from the roof.
search: çatalhöyük çatalhöyük was a large neolithic settlement in central turkey, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 bce, with houses packed together and entered from the roof. it held several thousand people at its height. walls bore paintings, and the dead were buried under house floors. it had no streets; people walked across roofs. it was inscribed as a unesco world heritage site in 2012.

title: Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands
sum: The Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands are the forests, river systems, and savannas east of the Andes, home to Indigenous societies whose scale and complexity are being rediscovered through aerial laser survey.
search: amazon basin and south american lowlands the amazon basin and south american lowlands are the forests, river systems, and savannas east of the andes, home to indigenous societies whose scale and complexity are being rediscovered through aerial laser survey. lidar surveys over the past decade have revealed large networks of earthworks, roads, and settlements beneath the forest; see  casarabe culture ,  upano valley settlements , and  xingu garden cities . indigenous land management, including soil enrichment, shaped much of the forest; see  amazonian urbanism and dark earths . scientists dispute whether the dark earths (terra preta) were largely made by people or arose from natural processes that people then used. european contact after 1492 brought severe population loss from epidemic disease and forced labor. it is debated whether this caused widespread forest regrowth: a 2021 study of 39 fossil pollen records found no synchronized regrowth after european arrival, and found that at most sites land abandonment and regrowth began about 300 to 600 years earlier. the researchers bush and mcmichael argue that populations probably peaked and declined well before 1492. alexander koch and colleagues, who proposed the regrowth hypothesis for the americas as a whole, reply that amazonia may have been less affected than mexico, central america, and the andes. the region is the setting of the  marajoara culture  and, at its edges, of many peoples never ruled by the  inca empire .

title: Andes
sum: The Andes are the mountain spine of western South America. Highland and coastal societies developed complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system.
search: andes the andes are the mountain spine of western south america. highland and coastal societies developed complex states without wheeled transport or a conventional writing system. the  inca empire  became the largest pre-columbian state in the americas. potatoes and llamas were domesticated in the andes. the inca recorded information on knotted cords called quipu. the site of  machu picchu  dates to the 15th century.

title: Arabian Peninsula
sum: The Arabian Peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. It was a corridor for trade and the origin of Islam.
search: arabian peninsula the arabian peninsula is a large, largely arid peninsula between the red sea and the persian gulf. it was a corridor for trade and the origin of islam. incense and spice caravans linked southern arabia with the mediterranean. islam emerged in the hejaz in the early 7th century; see  rise of islam  and  muhammad . monsoon-driven sea trade connected the peninsula with east africa and south asia.

title: Caribbean and Atlantic World
sum: The Caribbean and Atlantic World is the Caribbean basin together with the Atlantic coasts of the Americas, Europe, and Africa that were linked by shipping, trade, and forced migration from the 15th century.
search: caribbean and atlantic world the caribbean and atlantic world is the caribbean basin together with the atlantic coasts of the americas, europe, and africa that were linked by shipping, trade, and forced migration from the 15th century. the caribbean islands were settled by indigenous peoples, including the taino and kalinago, several thousand years before 1492. columbus reached the caribbean in 1492; indigenous populations collapsed within decades through disease, violence, and forced labor. sugar plantations worked by enslaved africans made the region among the most valuable in the early modern world. it was the setting of the  haitian revolution .

title: Central Asian Oases
sum: The Central Asian Oases are the river valleys and oasis cities between the steppe and the Iranian plateau, including Samarkand and Bukhara, which served as hubs of the Silk Roads.
search: central asian oases the central asian oases are the river valleys and oasis cities between the steppe and the iranian plateau, including samarkand and bukhara, which served as hubs of the silk roads. the region, known in antiquity as sogdiana and transoxiana, was home to the  sogdians . it was conquered by  alexander's conquests  and later brought into the islamic world in the early 8th century. it was the center of the  timurid empire , with its capital at  samarkand . scholars such as  ulugh beg  made it a center of astronomy in the 15th century.

title: Central Asian Steppe
sum: The Central Asian Steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern Eurasia. Mounted pastoralists there shaped the history of every neighboring civilization.
search: central asian steppe the central asian steppe is the vast grassland belt across northern eurasia. mounted pastoralists there shaped the history of every neighboring civilization. horse domestication and mounted warfare developed on the western steppe. the  mongol empire  came from the eastern steppe in the 13th century. the steppe was a corridor for the  opening of the silk roads  and for the  indo-european language spread .

title: East Asia
sum: East Asia includes China, Korea, Japan and neighboring regions. China's centralized state tradition is among the longest continuous political traditions.
search: east asia east asia includes china, korea, japan and neighboring regions. china's centralized state tradition is among the longest continuous political traditions. farming of millet and rice began independently in the yellow and yangtze river basins. the first unified empire was created in 221 bce; see  unification of china under qin . major inventions include  paper ,  gunpowder , the  magnetic compass  and printing. major states included the  shang dynasty ,  han dynasty  and  song dynasty .

title: Europe
sum: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia. It hosted early farming societies, the Roman Empire's northern provinces, and later the technologies and empires of the early modern and industrial periods.
search: europe europe is the western peninsula of eurasia. it hosted early farming societies, the roman empire's northern provinces, and later the technologies and empires of the early modern and industrial periods. farming spread into europe from anatolia over several thousand years. the  norse  traveled from scandinavia across the atlantic and through eastern rivers. the  scientific revolution  and  industrial revolution  began here, drawing on knowledge from many regions. the continent was the main theater of  world war i  and  world war ii .

title: Iranian Plateau
sum: The Iranian Plateau is the highland region between Mesopotamia and South Asia. It was the heartland of Persian empires and a link on overland routes across Eurasia.
search: iranian plateau the iranian plateau is the highland region between mesopotamia and south asia. it was the heartland of persian empires and a link on overland routes across eurasia. the  achaemenid persians  built a vast empire from here in the 6th century bce. the plateau sits on the routes of the  opening of the silk roads . it was later incorporated into the  abbasid caliphate  and the  mongol empire .

title: Levant and Anatolia
sum: The Levant and Anatolia are the eastern Mediterranean coast and the Turkish peninsula. They are a crossroads between Africa, Asia, and Europe and a center of early farming.
search: levant and anatolia the levant and anatolia are the eastern mediterranean coast and the turkish peninsula. they are a crossroads between africa, asia, and europe and a center of early farming. early farming and monumental building appear here, including  göbekli tepe  and  çatalhöyük . the  phoenicians  developed a widely copied alphabet; see  alphabet . later,  constantinople  stood at the junction of europe and asia. the region saw the collapse of many bronze age states; see  bronze age collapse .

title: Mediterranean Basin
sum: The Mediterranean Basin is the sea and its surrounding coasts. It was one of history's most connected zones of trade, cultural exchange, and conflict.
search: mediterranean basin the mediterranean basin is the sea and its surrounding coasts. it was one of history's most connected zones of trade, cultural exchange, and conflict. the sea connects europe, africa, and asia. seafaring cultures included the  minoans ,  phoenicians ,  ancient greeks  and  romans . rome eventually ruled the entire coastline; see  rome . the basin saw both the  bronze age collapse  and the  fall of the western roman empire .

title: Mesoamerica
sum: Mesoamerica is the cultural region from central Mexico to Central America. It developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a sophisticated calendar independently of the Old World.
search: mesoamerica mesoamerica is the cultural region from central mexico to central america. it developed farming (maize, beans, squash), monumental cities, writing, and a sophisticated calendar independently of the old world. early complex societies included the  olmecs . the  maya  developed a full writing system and precise astronomy. major cities included  teotihuacan  and  tenochtitlan . the  aztec empire  was conquered by spain in 1519 to 1521.

title: Mesopotamia
sum: Mesopotamia is the land between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in present-day Iraq and parts of neighboring countries. It is a birthplace of cities and writing.
search: mesopotamia mesopotamia is the land between and around the tigris and euphrates rivers, in present-day iraq and parts of neighboring countries. it is a birthplace of cities and writing. irrigated farming supported some of the world's first cities, such as  uruk . cuneiform writing appeared here about 3400 to 3200 bce; see  invention of writing . early societies included the  sumerians , later joined by akkadian, babylonian and assyrian states. the region later became the center of the  abbasid caliphate .

title: Nile Valley
sum: The Nile Valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the Nile River through northeastern Africa, home to one of the earliest states.
search: nile valley the nile valley is the narrow, fertile corridor of the nile river through northeastern africa, home to one of the earliest states. the nile floods annually, depositing silt that supported dense farming in a desert setting. egypt was unified about 3100 bce; see  unification of egypt . nile valley peoples included the  ancient egyptians  and, to the south, nubian kingdoms. monuments such as  giza necropolis  date from the third millennium bce.

title: North America
sum: North America north of Mexico was settled by peoples who arrived at least 15,000 years ago and who developed diverse societies, from mobile hunters to farming towns and confederacies.
search: north america north america north of mexico was settled by peoples who arrived at least 15,000 years ago and who developed diverse societies, from mobile hunters to farming towns and confederacies. the  peopling of the americas  began during the last ice age. regional societies included the mound-building cultures of the mississippi valley and ancestral puebloans. the  haudenosaunee confederacy  was a political union of five (later six) nations. european colonization from the 16th century changed the continent through disease and conquest.

title: Oceania
sum: Oceania includes Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands. It holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside Africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans.
search: oceania oceania includes australia, new guinea, and the pacific islands. it holds both the oldest continuing cultures outside africa and the last large landmasses settled by humans. humans reached australia at least 50,000 years ago; see  aboriginal australians . new guinea was an independent center of agriculture. polynesian navigators settled the remote pacific; see  polynesians  and  polynesian settlement of the pacific . aotearoa new zealand was among the last habitable lands settled, around 1250 to 1300 ce.

title: Planet-wide

search: planet-wide planet-wide is the region tag for events and processes that affect the whole earth, or that have no single location, such as mass extinctions, climate shifts, and global exchange networks. used as the  region  value for deep-time events and for global human phenomena. earth's surface is about 510 million square kilometers, of which about 71 percent is ocean.

title: Siberia and the Arctic
sum: Siberia and the Arctic are the northern lands of Asia from the Urals to the Pacific, and the Arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past.
search: siberia and the arctic siberia and the arctic are the northern lands of asia from the urals to the pacific, and the arctic coasts beyond, where cold and permafrost shaped both human ways of life and the preservation of the past. some of the oldest known human genomes come from siberia; see  mal'ta and the ancient north eurasians . permafrost and ice preserved frozen tombs of the  scythians  in the altai. the yakut (sakha), evenki, chukchi, and many other peoples developed herding, hunting, and fishing economies; see  yakut (sakha) . russia expanded across siberia to the pacific between 1582 and 1639; see  russian expansion into siberia .

title: South Asia
sum: South Asia is the Indian subcontinent. It is home to one of the earliest urban civilizations and to major religious and mathematical traditions.
search: south asia south asia is the indian subcontinent. it is home to one of the earliest urban civilizations and to major religious and mathematical traditions. the  indus valley civilization  flourished about 2600 to 1900 bce; see  mohenjo-daro . hindu, buddhist, jain and sikh traditions originated here; see  siddhartha gautama  and  ashoka . the decimal place-value system developed in india and spread outward. monsoon winds shaped indian ocean trade.

title: Southeast Asia
sum: Southeast Asia is the mainland and island region between India and China. It was a hub of maritime trade and hosted powerful states influenced by Indian and Chinese culture.
search: southeast asia southeast asia is the mainland and island region between india and china. it was a hub of maritime trade and hosted powerful states influenced by indian and chinese culture. the  khmer empire  built  angkor  between the 9th and 15th centuries ce. austronesian-speaking peoples spread from here into the pacific; see  polynesian settlement of the pacific . spice trade from the malay archipelago drew traders from across eurasia.

title: Sub-Saharan Africa
sum: Sub-Saharan Africa is the region south of the Sahara. It is the birthplace of the hominin lineage and of Homo sapiens, and it holds the greatest human genetic and linguistic diversity.
search: sub-saharan africa sub-saharan africa is the region south of the sahara. it is the birthplace of the hominin lineage and of homo sapiens, and it holds the greatest human genetic and linguistic diversity. fossil evidence places the origins of  homo sapiens  in africa about 300,000 years ago. the  bantu expansion  spread bantu languages across much of central, eastern and southern africa. major states included  kingdom of aksum ,  mali empire , and the builders of  great zimbabwe . trans-saharan and indian ocean trade linked the region to eurasia; see  timbuktu .
