title: Anomalocaris
sum: Anomalocaris was a large swimming Cambrian animal with spiny grasping appendages, a round mouth ringed by plates, and large compound eyes. It lived about 515 to 505 million years ago, is known from Canada and Australia, and is a stem-group…
search: anomalocaris anomalocaris was a large swimming cambrian animal with spiny grasping appendages, a round mouth ringed by plates, and large compound eyes. it lived about 515 to 505 million years ago, is known from canada and australia, and is a stem-group relative of arthropods. anomalocaris is securely known from the burgess shale of british columbia (about 505 million years old) and the emu bay shale of south australia (about 515). chinese fossils once assigned to it have mostly been moved to other genera. its appendages were described in 1892 as a crustacean tail, its mouth as a jellyfish, and its body as a sea cucumber. harry whittington and derek briggs showed in 1985 that they belonged to one animal. complete burgess specimens are about 20 to 25 cm long. estimates of 35 to 50 cm include appendages and tail, and a claim of about 1 m rests on fragments. compound eyes from the emu bay shale, up to 3 cm long, preserve at least 16,000 lenses, comparable to the sharpest-sighted living arthropods. the mouth looks too weak to crush trilobite shells, and studies propose suction feeding or soft prey. whether it was the top predator of its seas is debated.

title: Archaea
sum: Archaea are single-celled organisms without a nucleus that form one of the three domains of life, with Bacteria and eukaryotes. Recognized as separate only in 1977, they may date to about 3.5 billion years ago, though no fossil archaeon…
search: archaea archaea are single-celled organisms without a nucleus that form one of the three domains of life, with bacteria and eukaryotes. recognized as separate only in 1977, they may date to about 3.5 billion years ago, though no fossil archaeon has been identified with confidence. in 1977 carl woese and george fox used ribosomal rna sequences to show that methane-producing microbes were as distinct from bacteria as from eukaryotes. in 1990 the three domains were named bacteria, archaea, and eucarya. archaea were first known from hot springs, salt lakes, and methane-rich mud, but they also live in soils, deep sediments, and the open ocean, where in one pacific study they made up about 39 percent of the smallest plankton at depth. the earliest evidence is indirect. methane in australian rocks about 3.5 billion years old was read in 2006 as microbial, but nonliving processes can give similar isotope values. molecular clocks range from 3.5 to 4.1 billion years, and are also disputed. asgard archaea, first found in 2015, carry genes for proteins otherwise known only in eukaryotes. some researchers therefore place eukaryotes inside archaea, which would leave two primary domains, not three. no archaeon is established as a human pathogen.

title: Archaeopteryx
sum: Archaeopteryx was a feathered, winged dinosaur about the size of a raven, known from Late Jurassic limestone in Bavaria, Germany, about 150 million years old.
search: archaeopteryx archaeopteryx was a feathered, winged dinosaur about the size of a raven, known from late jurassic limestone in bavaria, germany, about 150 million years old. fossils come from the solnhofen limestone of bavaria, germany. it combined bird-like features, such as feathers and wings, with reptile-like ones, including teeth, clawed fingers, and a long bony tail. the first skeleton was found in 1861, two years after darwin published on the origin of species, and was quickly cited as a transitional form. feathered non-avian dinosaurs found in china from the 1990s onward strengthened the link between birds and theropod dinosaurs. birds are the living descendants of theropod dinosaurs.

title: Australopithecus afarensis
sum: Australopithecus afarensis was an early hominin that lived in East Africa about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago and walked upright, and is best known from the fossil 'Lucy'.
search: australopithecus afarensis australopithecus afarensis was an early hominin that lived in east africa about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago and walked upright, and is best known from the fossil 'lucy'. 'lucy' was found in hadar, ethiopia, in 1974 and is about 3.2 million years old. footprints at laetoli, tanzania (about 3.66 million years old), record upright walking. it had a small brain (estimates range from about 380 to 550 cubic centimeters) and long arms adapted to climbing. it is often considered close to the ancestry of the genus homo.

title: Barley
sum: Barley is a cereal grass domesticated in the Fertile Crescent from around 9000 BCE, one of the earliest crops farmed by humans and, in ancient Mesopotamia, a staple used as food, drink and even a standard of value.
search: barley barley is a cereal grass domesticated in the fertile crescent from around 9000 bce, one of the earliest crops farmed by humans and, in ancient mesopotamia, a staple used as food, drink and even a standard of value. barley was domesticated from wild barley in the fertile crescent, with early domesticated forms recorded in the jarmo region of modern iraq from about 9000 to 7000 bce; grinding stones with starch traces from wild barley at ohalo ii, near the sea of galilee, show it was eaten well before domestication, by about 23,000 bce. domestication produced grain heads that hold together instead of shattering, making the plant far easier to harvest but dependent on deliberate replanting. barley was likely among the first grains brewed into beer, one of the earliest alcoholic drinks made by neolithic farmers. in mesopotamia, barley served as a de facto currency, with the shekel functioning as a standard unit of its weight, and cuneiform records from around 2350 bce, under the ruler urukagina, describe monthly barley rations issued to adults. by about 2000 bce barley had spread across eurasia, reaching finland by about 4200 bce, the indus civilization region between roughly 5,700 and 3,300 years ago, and the korean peninsula by about 1500 to 850 bce. global production reached about 146 million tonnes in 2023, the fourth largest cereal harvest after maize, rice and wheat; about 70 percent goes to animal feed and about 30 percent to malting for beer and whisky.

title: Cacao
sum: Cacao, the source of chocolate, was first domesticated in the Amazon basin of South America by at least 3300 BCE and later became a ritual drink and currency in Mesoamerica before Spanish traders carried it to Europe in the 16th century.
search: cacao cacao, the source of chocolate, was first domesticated in the amazon basin of south america by at least 3300 bce and later became a ritual drink and currency in mesoamerica before spanish traders carried it to europe in the 16th century. cacao's native range is the amazon rainforest, and genetic and archaeological evidence places its earliest domestication at the santa ana-la florida site in present-day ecuador, by the mayo-chinchipe culture, at least 5,300 years ago, before it reached mesoamerica. chemical residue on pottery from puerto escondido, honduras, shows cacao products were being consumed there between about 1500 and 1400 bce, with the sweet pulp around the beans likely valued before the beans themselves. across mesoamerica before the spanish conquest, cacao beans served as a currency for everyday purchases, and olmec and maya elites drank cacao in spiritual ceremonies; a spanish chronicler recorded that the aztec ruler moctezuma ii drank only chocolate, reportedly consuming dozens of servings a day from a golden goblet. spanish traders introduced chocolate to europe, and it became a popular drink there by the mid-17th century; the spanish also spread cacao cultivation to their colonies in the west indies and the philippines. ivory coast and ghana together grow most of the world's cacao today, and reporting on the industry has documented large-scale child labor: an estimated 2.1 million children were involved in cocoa harvesting in the two countries as of 2017, often exposed to pesticides and hazardous tasks; a 2021 lawsuit against major chocolate companies over forced child labor was dismissed for lack of a traceable link to specific plantations. global cacao production reached about 5.8 million tonnes in 2022, with ivory coast alone supplying about 38 percent.

title: Cassava
sum: Cassava is a starchy root crop domesticated in south-central Brazil, likely within the last 10,000 years, that requires processing to remove natural toxins and that Portuguese and Spanish traders carried to Africa and Asia in the 16th…
search: cassava cassava is a starchy root crop domesticated in south-central brazil, likely within the last 10,000 years, that requires processing to remove natural toxins and that portuguese and spanish traders carried to africa and asia in the 16th century, where it became a staple for hundreds of millions of people. cassava was domesticated from wild relatives centered in west-central brazil; the date of domestication is imprecise, likely within the last 10,000 years, and cassava pollen appears in gulf of mexico lowland sediment by about 4600 bce, with the oldest direct evidence of cultivation coming from the maya site of joya de cerén in el salvador, about 1,400 years old. raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds, linamarin and lotaustralin, that release toxic hydrogen cyanide; bitter varieties can carry up to 1,000 milligrams of cyanide per kilogram of fresh root, and communities developed soaking and fermentation methods, some reducing cyanide content by 85 to 99 percent, to make the crop safe to eat. portuguese traders introduced cassava from brazil to west africa in the 16th century, and portuguese and spanish traders also carried it to their colonies in goa, malacca, eastern indonesia, timor and the philippines; it reached east africa by about 1850 through arab and european traders. cassava is now a primary food staple for an estimated 500 million to 800 million people, particularly in sub-saharan africa, and it ranks as the tropics' third-largest carbohydrate source after rice and maize, valued for growing on poor soils with little rainfall. global cassava production reached about 330 million tonnes in 2022, with nigeria the largest producer and thailand the largest exporter of cassava starch.

title: Cattle
sum: Cattle are large grazing animals domesticated from the wild aurochs in southwestern Asia about 10,500 years ago, and with over 940 million animals today they are among the most numerous and heaviest livestock on Earth.
search: cattle cattle are large grazing animals domesticated from the wild aurochs in southwestern asia about 10,500 years ago, and with over 940 million animals today they are among the most numerous and heaviest livestock on earth. domestic cattle descend from the aurochs (bos primigenius), a wild ox that once ranged across europe, north africa and much of asia; humans hunted aurochs long before domestication, and that older history is outside this note. taurine cattle were domesticated about 10,500 years ago in a zone spanning central anatolia, the levant and western iran, and mitochondrial dna suggests the taurine line may descend from as few as about 80 aurochs tamed in upper mesopotamia. a separate domestication on the indian subcontinent produced the humped zebu cattle. cattle are kept for meat, milk and leather and as draft animals that pull carts and farm implements; taurine cattle spread across europe and temperate asia and were later carried by europeans to the americas and australia. more than 940 million cattle lived in the world in 2022, led by india (about 307 million), brazil (about 194 million) and china (about 102 million); by one estimate they have the largest biomass of any animal species, about 650 million tonnes. cattle farming accounts for about 7 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, mostly methane from digestion, and overgrazing has reduced biodiversity in some rangelands. cattle are sacred in hinduism, and slaughter of cows is forbidden by law in several indian states and in nepal.

title: Chicken
sum: The chicken descends from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, was carried across the Pacific and the Old World, and is now the most numerous bird on Earth, with more than 26 billion alive in 2023; the timing of its domestication is…
search: chicken the chicken descends from the red junglefowl of southeast asia, was carried across the pacific and the old world, and is now the most numerous bird on earth, with more than 26 billion alive in 2023; the timing of its domestication is uncertain. chickens descend from the red junglefowl (gallus gallus), native to southeast asia, and still interbreed with it. genomic studies estimate that chickens were domesticated about 8,000 years ago in southeast asia, but the earliest bones judged probably chicken come from ban non wat in central thailand, about 3,250 years old, and older claims from china are debated; the date_start of -1250 marks that earliest secure evidence, not the beginning of domestication. one proposal holds that wild junglefowl were drawn to rice seeds and nested nearby, and another that chickens were kept first for cockfighting and only later for food; researchers dispute both. chickens spread with austronesian-speaking voyagers across island southeast asia, micronesia, melanesia, polynesia and madagascar, and reached egypt from the middle east about 1400 bce, becoming widely bred there by about 300 bce. whether chickens reached the americas before european contact is debated: bones from chile's arauco peninsula were dated as pre-columbian and linked by dna to polynesian birds, but further study cast doubt on the result. more than 26.5 billion chickens were alive in 2023 and more than 50 billion were produced annually for food; about 74 percent of the world's poultry meat and 68 percent of eggs come from factory farming. a modern broiler may weigh about 1.8 kilograms at 35 days against about 1.05 kilograms for a heritage bird, and the life expectancy of commercial laying hens falls from around seven years to under two.

title: Coffee
sum: Coffee is a shrub whose beans, first documented as a drink among Sufi communities in Yemen by the late 15th century, spread through the Ottoman Empire and Europe and were then grown on slave and colonial plantations across the tropics.
search: coffee coffee is a shrub whose beans, first documented as a drink among sufi communities in yemen by the late 15th century, spread through the ottoman empire and europe and were then grown on slave and colonial plantations across the tropics. coffee's popular origin story, in which a 9th-century ethiopian goatherd named kaldi discovers the plant's effects on his flock, does not appear in writing before 1671 and is likely a later legend; there is no confirmed evidence of coffee as a drink before the 15th century, when it was well established among sufi communities in yemen. the first known coffeehouse opened in istanbul in 1555, and pope clement viii's declaration of coffee as an acceptable christian drink in 1600 helped it spread in catholic europe; the first european coffeehouse outside ottoman territory opened in venice in 1647. french naval officer gabriel de clieu brought coffee plants to martinique in the 1720s, and cultivation began in the french colony of saint-domingue (haiti) in 1734; by 1788 saint-domingue, worked by enslaved laborers, supplied roughly half the world's coffee, and the harsh conditions on its plantations were a contributing factor in the haitian revolution. coffee reached brazil in 1727, but large-scale cultivation there did not take off until after independence in 1822. coffee cultivation across its colonial-era expansion generally displaced and exploited indigenous and enslaved populations, a pattern recorded here as sustained harm rather than as an incidental cost of production. global coffee production reached about 11 million tonnes in 2023, with brazil producing about 31 percent and vietnam the second-largest share.

title: Cotton
sum: Cotton was domesticated independently in the Indus Valley of South Asia and in the Americas, and its later mechanized processing in Britain and the American South tied the plant directly to the Industrial Revolution and to the expansion of…
search: cotton cotton was domesticated independently in the indus valley of south asia and in the americas, and its later mechanized processing in britain and the american south tied the plant directly to the industrial revolution and to the expansion of slavery. cotton textile fragments and spindle whorls from mohenjo-daro in the indus valley date to the 3rd millennium bce, and the date_start of -3000 marks this firmly dated use; mineralized thread at mehrgarh, dated by some to the 6th millennium bce, would be earlier but is less certain. cotton was domesticated separately in the americas, with gossypium hirsutum in mexico dated to about 3400 to 2300 bce, bolls from a tehuacán cave dated to as early as 5500 bce, and a different species in use in peru by the 7th to 6th millennia bce. indian cotton textiles, especially from bengal and dhaka, were the most important manufactured goods in 18th-century world trade and held about a quarter of the global textile trade, until british colonial tariffs and policy suppressed indian exports and favored british cloth. processing a bale of cotton by hand took over 600 hours of labor until eli whitney's gin, patented in 1793, cut that to about a dozen hours; the gin made large-scale growing far more profitable and drove a rapid expansion of slavery in the american south, where cotton was the backbone of the regional economy by the mid-19th century. india is the largest cotton producer today and the united states has long been the largest exporter; world output is roughly 25 million tonnes a year on about 2.5 percent of the world's arable land. cotton needs an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 liters of water per kilogram of fiber worldwide and up to about 22,500 liters in drier regions of india, and conventional growing relies heavily on fertilizers and pesticides, though pest-resistant bt cotton has cut insecticide use in some regions.

title: Cyanobacteria
sum: Cyanobacteria are bacteria that perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis. Their activity led to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere.
search: cyanobacteria cyanobacteria are bacteria that perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis. their activity led to the oxygenation of earth's atmosphere. the earliest unambiguous cyanobacterial fossils are about 2.15 billion years old, and direct fossil evidence of photosynthetic membranes is about 1.75 billion years old. biomarker evidence once cited for 2.7 billion years was later shown to be younger contamination, so the 2.7-billion-year start date used for this note reflects an older, disputed estimate and is approximate. chloroplasts in plants and algae descend from cyanobacteria through endosymbiosis. they still live in oceans, lakes, and soils around the world. the  great oxidation event  followed their spread.

title: Denisovans
sum: Denisovans are an extinct human group known first from DNA in a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2010.
search: denisovans denisovans are an extinct human group known first from dna in a finger bone found in denisova cave in siberia in 2010. very few fossils are known, including a jaw from xiahe in tibet. some living populations, especially in oceania and east asia, carry denisovan dna. a gene variant helping tibetans adapt to high altitude came from denisovans. the harbin cranium (at least 146,000 years old, once nicknamed 'dragon man' and named homo longi) was linked to denisovans in 2025, using mitochondrial dna recovered from dental calculus and ancient protein evidence, in studies published in cell and science. it is the first denisovan skull identified.

title: Dinosaurs
sum: Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated land ecosystems for about 165 million years. Birds are living descendants of one dinosaur lineage.
search: dinosaurs dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated land ecosystems for about 165 million years. birds are living descendants of one dinosaur lineage. the earliest dinosaurs appeared roughly 233 million years ago in the triassic. non-avian dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to the largest land animals ever. many had feathers, and birds descend from small feathered theropods. non-avian dinosaurs died out in the  cretaceous-paleogene extinction .

title: Domestic Cat
sum: The domestic cat descends from the African wildcat and was first tamed in the Near East by Neolithic farmers, with the earliest evidence of a tamed wildcat buried near a human grave on Cyprus about 7500 to 7200 BCE.
search: domestic cat the domestic cat descends from the african wildcat and was first tamed in the near east by neolithic farmers, with the earliest evidence of a tamed wildcat buried near a human grave on cyprus about 7500 to 7200 bce. domestic cats descend from the african wildcat (felis lybica), and the earliest known sign of a tamed wildcat is a burial found close to a human neolithic grave at shillourokambos, southern cyprus, dated to about 7500 to 7200 bce. the leading explanation is that african wildcats were drawn to early farming settlements in the fertile crescent by rodents, especially the house mouse, and were tolerated and then tamed, a long relationship that lasted thousands of years. cats were venerated in egypt from about 3100 bce, and egyptian wildcats later contributed to the maternal gene pool of the domestic cat. as farming spread, so did cats: they reached greece about 1200 bce with traders, southern europe by the 5th century bce and northern germany by the 5th century ce. in the united states alone domestic cats are estimated to kill 1.3 to 4.0 billion birds and 6.3 to 22.3 billion mammals a year, and abandoned pets add to a global feral cat population that has driven declines of bird, mammal and reptile species.

title: Domestic Pig
sum: The domestic pig was bred from the wild boar in the Near East, in or around the Tigris basin, by about 9400 BCE, was domesticated again independently in China, and is now tied with chicken as the most commonly eaten meat in the world.
search: domestic pig the domestic pig was bred from the wild boar in the near east, in or around the tigris basin, by about 9400 bce, was domesticated again independently in china, and is now tied with chicken as the most commonly eaten meat in the world. domestic pigs descend from the wild boar (sus scrofa) and were first domesticated in the near east, in or around the tigris basin; pigs brought to cyprus more than 11,400 years ago imply domestication or close management on the mainland by then. pigs were domesticated separately in china starting some 8,000 years ago. pigs reached europe at least 8,500 years ago and over the next 3,000 years interbred with european wild boar until their genomes held less than 5 percent near eastern ancestry, a change that amounts to a further, local domestication. austronesian-speaking peoples carried pigs across island southeast asia and oceania beginning about 4,000 years ago, and most pigs from the philippines to hawai‘i descend from those introductions. spanish explorers including hernando de soto brought pigs to southeastern north america, where escaped animals became feral; feral pigs now damage crops and wildlife in the united states, new zealand, northern queensland and south america. eating pork is forbidden in islam and judaism, and pigs are sacred in some other religions. about 850 million pigs were alive in 2019, with china holding about 36.5 percent, and roughly 1.5 billion are slaughtered each year.

title: Donkey
sum: The donkey was domesticated from the African wild ass in northeastern Africa, probably by pastoralists in Nubia, some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, and became the main pack animal of early long-distance trade in Egypt and Southwest Asia.
search: donkey the donkey was domesticated from the african wild ass in northeastern africa, probably by pastoralists in nubia, some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, and became the main pack animal of early long-distance trade in egypt and southwest asia. donkeys descend from the african wild ass (equus africanus) and were domesticated in africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, probably by pastoral people in nubia; remains from the fourth millennium bce have been found at ma'adi in lower egypt, and the date_start of -4000 is the midpoint of that range. donkeys were vital to long-distance trade in egypt, and in the fourth dynasty (about 2675 to 2565 bce) wealthy individuals were known to own more than 1,000 of them, used as pack animals and in farming and for milk and meat. by the end of the fourth millennium bce donkeys had spread to southwest asia, the main breeding center had shifted to mesopotamia by about 1800 bce, and the greeks and romans later spread them through their empires. a male donkey crossed with a female horse produces a mule, and the reverse cross produces a hinny; mules are valued as working and riding animals in many countries. more than 40 million donkeys were alive in the early 2000s, about 96 percent of them in developing countries, where they are used mainly as pack animals or for draught work.

title: Dromedary and Bactrian Camels
sum: Two camel species were domesticated by about the middle of the third millennium BCE, the one-humped dromedary in southern Arabia or Somalia and the two-humped Bactrian camel in Central Asia, and together they made long-distance caravan…
search: dromedary and bactrian camels two camel species were domesticated by about the middle of the third millennium bce, the one-humped dromedary in southern arabia or somalia and the two-humped bactrian camel in central asia, and together they made long-distance caravan travel across deserts possible. the dromedary was domesticated in somalia or southern arabia during the third millennium bce, though a 2016 genetic study points to southeastern arabia. the bactrian camel was domesticated in central asia around 2500 bce, with evidence at shahr-e sukhteh in iran, and one analysis places its domestication east of the zagros mountains by the middle of the third millennium bce. the military arabian saddle developed in the 7th century bce, and between about 500 and 100 bce bactrian camels entered military use with new saddles placed over the humps. about 14 million camels were alive in 2010, roughly 90 percent of them dromedaries; the domestic bactrian numbers about 1.4 million, and the wild bactrian, a separate species, is reduced to about 1,000 animals and is still declining. frankincense and myrrh moved from southern arabia and the horn of africa to mediterranean and mesopotamian markets mostly by camel caravan, for well over a thousand years. more than a million dromedaries are estimated to be feral in australia, a population growing by about 8 percent a year that stood at about 700,000 in 2008.

title: Dunkleosteus
sum: Dunkleosteus was a large armored placoderm fish of the Late Devonian with bony blades in place of teeth. Its best-known species, D. terrelli, comes from the Cleveland Shale of Ohio; its size has been revised downward and its bite force is…
search: dunkleosteus dunkleosteus was a large armored placoderm fish of the late devonian with bony blades in place of teeth. its best-known species, d. terrelli, comes from the cleveland shale of ohio; its size has been revised downward and its bite force is under review. the genus is reported from the late devonian, about 382 to 359 million years ago, but d. terrelli is best documented from about 372 to 360 million years ago, chiefly in the cleveland shale of ohio. ten species have been named, and about four are widely accepted. older reconstructions gave lengths of 6 to 10 m. a 2023 study using the eye socket and cheek plate estimated about 3.4 m for typical adults and about 4.1 m for the largest. it has not been independently replicated. a 2007 study modeled the skull as a linked lever system and estimated a bite force of about 4,400 newtons at the tip and 5,400 at the blade edge, for an individual then thought to be 6 m long. a 2025 study argues that these figures need re-examination. the name was coined in 1956 by jean-pierre lehman to honor david dunkle. placoderms died out at the end-devonian hangenberg event, about 359 million years ago.

title: Ediacaran Biota
sum: The Ediacaran biota are the first large, complex, multicellular organisms in the fossil record, living in the sea in the last stretch of the Proterozoic, before the Cambrian.
search: ediacaran biota the ediacaran biota are the first large, complex, multicellular organisms in the fossil record, living in the sea in the last stretch of the proterozoic, before the cambrian. the ediacaran period spans about 635 to 538.8 million years ago. the biota are named after the ediacara hills of south australia and are known also from newfoundland, namibia, and the white sea coast of russia. many forms were soft-bodied and frond-, disc-, or quilt-shaped. the relationship of many ediacaran forms to living animal groups is unclear. the classic assemblages largely disappear near the start of the cambrian.

title: Eurypterids
sum: Eurypterids, or sea scorpions, were predatory arthropods that lived from the Ordovician to the Permian, about 467 to 252 million years ago. They were relatives of spiders and horseshoe crabs, not true scorpions, and included one of the…
search: eurypterids eurypterids, or sea scorpions, were predatory arthropods that lived from the ordovician to the permian, about 467 to 252 million years ago. they were relatives of spiders and horseshoe crabs, not true scorpions, and included one of the largest arthropods known, about 2.5 m in body length. the oldest well-described eurypterid, pentecopterus from iowa, is about 467 to 458 million years old. moroccan fragments reported in 2025 may be about 479 million years old but are tentatively assigned. all eurypterids are chelicerates, the group of spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs. a 2013 analysis placed them closer to arachnids than to horseshoe crabs, which remains debated. the largest, jaekelopterus rhenaniae of the early devonian of germany, was estimated in 2007 from a pincer fragment to have a pincer about 46 cm long and a body about 2.5 m long, without the extended pincers. another study argued for a smaller size. only the earliest eurypterids were strictly marine; many later forms lived in brackish or fresh water. a 6-m trackway in carboniferous sandstone in scotland has been attributed to a land-walking hibbertopterus, an inference. after the late devonian extinction only three families reached the carboniferous and permian. the last records are permian, about 254 to 252 million years old at the latest.

title: Flowering Plants
sum: Flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the fossil record in the Early Cretaceous, about 130 million years ago, and now make up most land plant species.
search: flowering plants flowering plants (angiosperms) appear in the fossil record in the early cretaceous, about 130 million years ago, and now make up most land plant species. the oldest widely accepted angiosperm pollen dates to the hauterivian and barremian ages of the early cretaceous, about 133 to 125 million years ago. the oldest well-preserved flowering-plant macrofossils, such as those from china, date to about 125 million years ago. some molecular-clock studies place their origin earlier, in the triassic or jurassic; this gap is debated. flowering plants radiated rapidly in the cretaceous alongside pollinating insects. cereals, legumes, fruits, and most other crops descend from this group.

title: Goat
sum: The domestic goat was bred from the wild bezoar ibex in southwestern Asia around 10,000 years ago, one of the first animals kept by farming communities, and it remains valued today for milk, meat and fiber, especially on marginal land…
search: goat the domestic goat was bred from the wild bezoar ibex in southwestern asia around 10,000 years ago, one of the first animals kept by farming communities, and it remains valued today for milk, meat and fiber, especially on marginal land unsuited to other livestock. domestic goats descend from the bezoar ibex, a wild goat still found in the zagros mountains of iran and formerly widespread in anatolia, and domestication is dated to about 10,000 years ago in southwest asia and eastern europe. the earliest clear archaeological evidence for goat domestication comes from ganj dareh in iran, with further early sites at jericho, choga mami, djeitun and çayönü dating domestication to between about 8,000 and 9,000 years ago. neolithic herders used goats for milk and meat and also made use of their dung as fuel and their bones, hair and sinew for tools, building materials and clothing. goats remain economically important today for dairy, providing about 2 percent of the world's total annual milk supply, and for fiber such as cashmere and mohair, valued in part for their hardiness on land too marginal for cattle or sheep. more than 1.1 billion goats were living worldwide as of 2022, of which about 150 million were in india, the largest single-country population; india was also the largest goat-milk producer that year, followed by bangladesh and south sudan.

title: Hallucigenia
sum: Hallucigenia is a small, worm-like Cambrian animal with paired back spines and clawed legs, known from the Burgess Shale of Canada and from China, about 510 to 505 million years ago. It is known for being reconstructed upside down in 1977…
search: hallucigenia hallucigenia is a small, worm-like cambrian animal with paired back spines and clawed legs, known from the burgess shale of canada and from china, about 510 to 505 million years ago. it is known for being reconstructed upside down in 1977 and for the 2015 discovery of its head. three species are named: h. sparsa from the burgess shale of british columbia, h. fortis from chengjiang and h. hongmeia from guanshan, both in yunnan, china. the burgess shale is about 505 million years old by fossil zones; chengjiang is at most 518. h. sparsa is about 3 cm long, though published maxima reach 5.5 cm, and it is rare, about 0.19 percent of specimens counted in the walcott quarry. in 1977 simon conway morris reconstructed it walking on stilt-like spines with tentacles along its back. work on chinese specimens in 1991 showed that the spines were on top and the "tentacles" were legs. in 2015 martin smith and jean-bernard caron showed that the supposed head was a decay stain. the true head has a pair of simple eyes, a mouth ringed with plates, and a toothed throat. its claws resemble those of living velvet worms, and it is placed among the lobopodians, stem relatives of that group. some analyses place it more basally among the panarthropods.

title: Homo erectus
sum: Homo erectus was an early human species that lived from about 1.9 million to roughly 110,000 years ago, the first known hominin to spread widely beyond Africa.
search: homo erectus homo erectus was an early human species that lived from about 1.9 million to roughly 110,000 years ago, the first known hominin to spread widely beyond africa. fossils have been found in africa, georgia (dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old), and east and southeast asia. it made acheulean handaxes and probably used fire; see  control of fire . its brain was about 900 cubic centimeters and its body proportions were similar to modern humans'. it may be the longest-lived human species.

title: Homo floresiensis
sum: Homo floresiensis, nicknamed 'the hobbit', was a small-bodied human species that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores. Its bones date to about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and stone tools attributed to it extend to about 50,000 years…
search: homo floresiensis homo floresiensis, nicknamed 'the hobbit', was a small-bodied human species that lived on the indonesian island of flores. its bones date to about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and stone tools attributed to it extend to about 50,000 years ago. it was discovered in 2003 at liang bua cave. adults stood about 1.1 meters tall, with a brain of about 400 cubic centimeters. it made stone tools and lived on an island isolated by deep water. whether it descended from h. erectus or an earlier ancestor is debated.

title: Homo habilis
sum: Homo habilis ('handy man') is an early member of the genus Homo that lived in Africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago.
search: homo habilis homo habilis ('handy man') is an early member of the genus homo that lived in africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago. it was named in 1964 from fossils at olduvai gorge in tanzania. its brain was roughly 500 to 700 cubic centimeters (estimates vary). it is associated with  oldowan stone tools , though the link is not certain. whether it is a distinct species or a variant of other early homo is debated.

title: Homo naledi
sum: Homo naledi is a small-brained human relative whose remains were found in the Rising Star cave system in South Africa in 2013, dated to about 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.
search: homo naledi homo naledi is a small-brained human relative whose remains were found in the rising star cave system in south africa in 2013, dated to about 335,000 to 236,000 years ago. fossils of at least 15 individuals were found deep in a cave. the brain size was about 500 cubic centimeters, yet the species lived at the same time as early homo sapiens. researchers have proposed deliberate burial and cave markings, but those claims are contested. its combination of primitive and modern features is unusual.

title: Homo neanderthalensis
sum: Neanderthals were a human species that lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago and interbred with Homo sapiens.
search: homo neanderthalensis neanderthals were a human species that lived in europe and western asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago and interbred with homo sapiens. they had large brains, robust bodies adapted to cold, and made mousterian stone tools. the neanderthal genome was first sequenced in 2010. non-african people today derive up to about 2 percent of their ancestry from neanderthals. evidence for burial, ornaments, and pigment use is debated but growing.

title: Homo sapiens
sum: Homo sapiens is the species of modern humans: the only living member of the genus Homo, which emerged in Africa about 300,000 years ago and now numbers about eight billion.
search: homo sapiens homo sapiens is the species of modern humans: the only living member of the genus homo, which emerged in africa about 300,000 years ago and now numbers about eight billion. modern humans have a brain of about 1,350 cubic centimeters. they are notable for language, symbolic thought, and cumulative culture. they have inhabited every continent and now live in cities, deserts, polar stations, and orbit. genetic diversity is relatively low compared with other apes.

title: Horse
sum: The domestic horse descends from a lineage that a 2021 genetic study traced to the Pontic-Caspian steppe by about 2200 BCE, and its use for riding and chariot traction transformed warfare, transport and steppe societies across Eurasia.
search: horse the domestic horse descends from a lineage that a 2021 genetic study traced to the pontic-caspian steppe by about 2200 bce, and its use for riding and chariot traction transformed warfare, transport and steppe societies across eurasia. a 2021 study of 264 ancient genomes traced modern domestic horses to a lineage that arose in the volga-don region of the pontic-caspian steppe by about 2200 bce; horses lived wild across much of the continent before then, and that older history is outside this note. the botai culture of kazakhstan (about 3700 to 3500 bce) left horse teeth with wear consistent with bits and traces of horse milking, but a 2018 study found modern domestic horses are not closely related to botai horses, whose feral descendants are the przewalski's horses, and some researchers hold that botai people hunted and managed wild horses without fully domesticating them. horse-drawn chariots appear in sintashta and petrovka graves dated about 2100 to 1700 bce; within perhaps 500 years chariot evidence appears in greece, egypt and mesopotamia, and within another 500 years in china. horse bones appear in mesopotamia from about 2000 bce, where horses began to replace hybrid equids in war, and in the iron age mounted cavalry rose and mounted archers eventually displaced chariots. columbus brought horses to hispaniola on his 1493 voyage and hernán cortés landed in mexico in 1519 with 16 horses; wild horses had vanished from the americas at least 10,000 years earlier. after the pueblo revolt of 1680, horses left by the spanish spread among pueblo, apache and comanche communities, and by the late 1700s most peoples of the western plains were mounted.

title: Last Universal Common Ancestor
sum: The last universal common ancestor, or LUCA, is the inferred population of cells from which all living Bacteria and Archaea, and so all life today, descend. It is reconstructed from the genes of living organisms, not from fossils, with age…
search: last universal common ancestor the last universal common ancestor, or luca, is the inferred population of cells from which all living bacteria and archaea, and so all life today, descend. it is reconstructed from the genes of living organisms, not from fossils, with age estimates from about 3.5 to 4.3 billion years ago. luca is not a named organism or a fossil. it is the last population ancestral to every cell alive today; other lineages living beside it left no descendants. a 2024 study dated luca to about 4.2 billion years ago (about 4.09 to 4.33, depending on the clock model), using gene duplications that predate luca. older estimates gave 3.5 to 3.8 billion years, and some researchers doubt a luca older than 4 billion years. the same study inferred an anaerobic cell with about 2,650 proteins. a 2016 study with stricter criteria traced only 355 protein families to luca and pictured a heat-loving cell of hydrothermal vents. the oldest widely accepted traces of life are stromatolites in western australia, about 3.43 to 3.48 billion years old. older claims, such as graphite in a 4.10-billion-year-old zircon from jack hills, are disputed. where the root of the tree of life lies is unresolved and shifts every reconstruction.

title: Llama and Alpaca
sum: The llama and the alpaca are South American camelids domesticated in the high Andes of Peru about 6,000 years ago from the guanaco and the vicuña, and they were the Inca Empire's only beasts of burden and a main source of fiber.
search: llama and alpaca the llama and the alpaca are south american camelids domesticated in the high andes of peru about 6,000 years ago from the guanaco and the vicuña, and they were the inca empire's only beasts of burden and a main source of fiber. dna analysis has confirmed that the guanaco is the wild ancestor of the llama and the vicuña is the wild ancestor of the alpaca. the earliest evidence of domestication comes from high-altitude puna sites in the peruvian andes between about 4,000 and 4,900 meters; at telarmachay, about 170 kilometers northeast of lima, animal remains suggest that early domestic llamas and alpacas were under human control by about 6,000 to 5,500 years ago and that a herding economy was established by about 5,500 years ago. llamas were the only beasts of burden in the inca empire, and they also supplied meat and fiber; llama figures and llamas themselves were placed in burials as offerings, and one scholar argues that widespread andean farming depended on llama dung as fertilizer. alpaca fiber is much finer than llama fiber, about 10 to 15 micrometers in diameter against 20 to 40 micrometers. a colonial-era writer estimated that as many as 300,000 llamas were employed hauling cargo from the mines of potosí alone, but after europeans introduced horses, mules and donkeys the llama's importance as a beast of burden greatly diminished. more than seven million llamas and alpacas lived in south america in 2007.

title: Maize
sum: Maize is a cereal grass domesticated from wild teosinte in the Balsas River valley of southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, and it became the staple crop and a central religious symbol across much of the pre-Columbian Americas before…
search: maize maize is a cereal grass domesticated from wild teosinte in the balsas river valley of southwestern mexico about 9,000 years ago, and it became the staple crop and a central religious symbol across much of the pre-columbian americas before spreading worldwide after 1492. maize was domesticated from balsas teosinte in the balsas river valley of mexico about 9,000 years ago; stone milling tools bearing maize residue found near iguala, guerrero, are about 8,700 years old. maize farming reached highland ecuador by at least 8,000 years ago and the colombian andes between roughly 7,000 and 6,000 years ago, and spread north into what is now new mexico and arizona by about 4,100 years ago, with large-scale adoption in eastern north america by about 900 ce. by 3,000 years ago maize was central to olmec culture, including its calendar and mythology, and later maya and aztec societies treated maize as a deity and processed it by nixtamalization, soaking and cooking it with an alkaline solution that improves its nutritional value. after 1492 spanish settlers carried maize to europe within decades, and it had become a common peasant food in southern europe by the 17th century, and it also reached west africa and the philippines. hybrid corn breeding, beginning with james reid's yellow dent in the 1860s and double-cross hybrids from about 1918 to 1922, made hybrid maize the dominant form grown from the 1940s onward. global maize production reached about 1.16 billion tonnes in 2020, led by the united states, china and brazil, and it is used mainly for animal feed, with the rest split between human food, starch and syrup production, and ethanol and other biofuels.

title: Pikaia
sum: Pikaia is a small, eel-like swimming animal from the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 505 million years old. Reinterpreted in 1979 as an early chordate, it is often cited as a relative of vertebrate ancestors, though not thought to…
search: pikaia pikaia is a small, eel-like swimming animal from the burgess shale of british columbia, about 505 million years old. reinterpreted in 1979 as an early chordate, it is often cited as a relative of vertebrate ancestors, though not thought to be one. pikaia gracilens is known only from the walcott quarry of the burgess shale, dated to about 505 million years ago by fossil zones, with no radiometric date and no later fossils. it is about 5 cm long and flattened from side to side, with about 100 muscle blocks, a bilobed head with short tentacles, a dorsal fin, and paired appendages. charles walcott described it in 1911 as a worm. in 1979 simon conway morris and harry whittington read it as a chordate, and a 2012 redescription of 114 specimens read a narrow strand as a notochord. a 2024 study argued that earlier reconstructions were upside down. older chordate-like animals from chengjiang, about 518 million years old, include haikouichthys, so pikaia is not the earliest known chordate. in wonderful life (1989), stephen jay gould used pikaia to argue that history is contingent. conway morris later argued that evolution converges on similar solutions.

title: Potato
sum: The potato is a tuber crop domesticated in the highlands of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, roughly 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, and it later reshaped diet and population growth across Europe after its…
search: potato the potato is a tuber crop domesticated in the highlands of southern peru and northwestern bolivia, near lake titicaca, roughly 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, and it later reshaped diet and population growth across europe after its introduction there in the 16th century. the potato was domesticated from wild relatives in the s. brevicaule species complex, in the region around lake titicaca in southern peru and northwestern bolivia, an estimated 7,000 to 10,000 years ago; the earliest verified tuber remains, from ancón on the central peruvian coast, date to about 2500 bce. andean farmers developed thousands of potato varieties adapted to different altitudes, and quechua and aymara communities traditionally made chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, to preserve the crop through the region's cold nights. in inca religious tradition the deity axomama was associated with the fertility of potatoes and the soil. spanish colonizers introduced the potato to europe in the second half of the 16th century; european farmers were initially slow to adopt it, but after about 1750 it became an important staple, and the crop is estimated to have driven roughly a quarter of old world population and urban growth between 1700 and 1900. potato blight, caused by the water mold phytophthora infestans, destroyed crops across ireland and parts of scotland from 1845, contributing to the great famine; estimates of irish deaths run from about 700,000 to over 1 million, alongside roughly 1 million more who emigrated, and ireland's population fell from about 8.4 million in 1844 to about 6.6 million by 1851. global potato production reached about 390 million tonnes in 2024, led by china, india and ukraine.

title: Rice
sum: Rice is a cereal grass domesticated from a wild ancestor in the Yangtze valley of China from about 9,000 years ago, and it is now the staple food of more than half the world's population.
search: rice rice is a cereal grass domesticated from a wild ancestor in the yangtze valley of china from about 9,000 years ago, and it is now the staple food of more than half the world's population. rice was domesticated from wild _oryza rufipogon_ by neolithic communities in the upper and lower yangtze valley, in what is now china, about 9,000 years ago. genetic evidence for the gene that stops rice grains from shattering is identical in the two main cultivated groups, japonica and indica, which points to a single original domestication event rather than two separate ones; indica rice is thought to have arisen later, when japonica reached india about 4,500 years ago and hybridized with a local wild or semi-wild rice. rice farming reached korea and japan between about 5,500 and 3,200 years ago, and island southeast asia and taiwan between about 5,500 and 4,000 years ago, carried in part by austronesian-speaking migrations, and mainland southeast asia by about 5,000 years ago. rice is the staple food of more than half the world's population, and china and india together consumed several hundred million tonnes of it in the early 2020s. the green revolution rice variety ir8 was bred in 1966 at the international rice research institute by crossing an indonesian and a chinese variety, producing a short, strong-stemmed plant that resisted falling over under heavy fertilizer use. global rice production reached about 800 million tonnes in 2023, with about 90 percent grown in asia, and less than 8 percent of the crop traded internationally.

title: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
sum: Sahelanthropus tchadensis is a roughly 7-million-year-old fossil ape from Chad, proposed as one of the earliest members of the human lineage.
search: sahelanthropus tchadensis sahelanthropus tchadensis is a roughly 7-million-year-old fossil ape from chad, proposed as one of the earliest members of the human lineage. the nearly complete skull, nicknamed toumai, was found in 2001. the position of the skull's base suggests possible upright walking. its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's. whether it is a hominin at all is debated.

title: Sheep
sum: The domestic sheep was bred from the wild mouflon in Mesopotamia between about 11,000 and 9000 BCE, first kept for meat, milk and skins, and only later selectively bred for wool, and it now numbers well over a billion animals worldwide.
search: sheep the domestic sheep was bred from the wild mouflon in mesopotamia between about 11,000 and 9000 bce, first kept for meat, milk and skins, and only later selectively bred for wool, and it now numbers well over a billion animals worldwide. sheep were domesticated from the mouflon, a wild sheep of southwestern asia, in an estimated window between 11,000 and 9000 bce in mesopotamia, and the practice had spread to mehrgarh in the indus valley by about 7000 bce. early domestic sheep were kept mainly for meat, milk and skins rather than fleece; archaeological evidence, including statuary from iran, suggests deliberate selection for woolly sheep began around 6000 bce, roughly two millennia after initial domestication, a shift sometimes called the secondary products revolution. the earliest known woven wool garments date to around 4000 bce, and neolithic farmers in what is now france, among the castelnovien people, were keeping domestic sheep by about 6000 bce. sheep are raised in large numbers today across australia, new zealand, the southern regions of south america, south africa and the british isles, and china and india also hold very large flocks by absolute count; the world's domestic sheep population was estimated at around 1.2 billion in 2019.

title: Sorghum
sum: Sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grass domesticated in eastern Sudan more than 5,000 years ago, and it remains a staple food across Africa, Central America and South Asia today.
search: sorghum sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grass domesticated in eastern sudan more than 5,000 years ago, and it remains a staple food across africa, central america and south asia today. sorghum bicolor was domesticated in eastern sudan, in the area of the atbara and gash rivers, more than 5,000 years ago; archaeological evidence near kassala, linked to the neolithic butana group culture, dates domestication to about 3500 to 3000 bce, and a piece of sorghum bread from predynastic egypt, about 5,100 years old, survives in the egyptian museum in turin. the crop spread to the indian subcontinent by about 4,000 years ago and reached west africa by about 3,000 years ago. during the medieval arab agricultural expansion, sorghum was carried across the arab world as far as al-andalus in spain. sorghum is highly drought- and heat-tolerant and efficient with nitrogen, which makes it valuable in arid and semi-arid regions, and it remains a food staple in africa, central america and south asia, ranking as the fifth most widely grown cereal crop in the world. global production reached about 57 million tonnes in 2023, led by the united states, mexico and ethiopia, and the grain is used for food, animal feed and biofuel, including ethanol, with an energy return comparable to sugarcane and higher than maize.

title: Soybean
sum: The soybean is a legume domesticated in the region between the Yellow and Huai rivers in China between roughly 9,000 and 6,000 years ago, long central to East Asian diets through foods such as tofu and soy sauce, and now grown worldwide…
search: soybean the soybean is a legume domesticated in the region between the yellow and huai rivers in china between roughly 9,000 and 6,000 years ago, long central to east asian diets through foods such as tofu and soy sauce, and now grown worldwide chiefly as animal feed and oil. the soybean was domesticated in north-central china, between the yellow river and the huai river, with earliest evidence from the site of jiahu in henan province dated to between about 9,000 and 7,800 years ago. chinese tradition credits the legendary emperor shennong, dated in myth to 2853 bce, with naming the soybean one of five sacred grains alongside rice, wheat, barley and millet. fermented soy foods such as soy sauce, fermented bean paste, natto and tempeh, along with tofu made from soy milk, developed over many centuries in east asia; the earliest japanese textual reference to soybeans appears in the kojiki, compiled in 712 ce. the soybean was introduced to the americas and europe in the 18th century, with the first recorded north american cultivation in 1765 on skidaway island, georgia, and the first french cultivation in 1779. genetically modified, herbicide-tolerant soybean varieties were introduced commercially in 1995 and made up about 8 percent of united states soybean acreage by 1997, rising to about 93 percent by 2010. in 2019 brazil, the united states and argentina were the largest producers, together accounting for roughly four-fifths of world output, and about 80 percent of the global soybean crop is used to feed livestock.

title: Sponges
sum: Sponges (phylum Porifera) are simple aquatic animals without true tissues or organs and among the earliest branches of the animal family tree. Unambiguous fossils begin in the earliest Cambrian, about 535 million years ago; older fossil…
search: sponges sponges (phylum porifera) are simple aquatic animals without true tissues or organs and among the earliest branches of the animal family tree. unambiguous fossils begin in the earliest cambrian, about 535 million years ago; older fossil and chemical claims are disputed. sponges have no true tissues or organs; flagellated cells drive water through a jelly-like body. about 9,900 valid species are described, over 90 percent of them demosponges. undisputed sponge spicules first appear about 535 million years ago in south china. sponge-like archaeocyaths were common from about 530 to 500 million years ago. a 2009 study read a rare sterol in rocks 635 million years old or older as a sponge biomarker. later work showed that algae or protists could make similar compounds. older body fossils, such as otavia in namibia (about 760 million years) and structures in 890-million-year-old canadian reefs, are read by critics as mineral grains or as unconfirmed. molecular clocks place the common ancestor of living animals roughly 830 to 650 million years ago. whether sponges or comb jellies branched off first is unresolved.

title: Stromatolites
sum: Stromatolites are layered rock structures built by communities of microbes trapping sediment and precipitating minerals; the oldest widely cited examples are about 3.48 billion years old.
search: stromatolites stromatolites are layered rock structures built by communities of microbes trapping sediment and precipitating minerals; the oldest widely cited examples are about 3.48 billion years old. stromatolites form when microbial mats, often including cyanobacteria, bind sediment into thin repeating layers. the oldest widely cited examples are in the dresser formation of the pilbara region of western australia, dated to about 3.48 billion years; some researchers dispute that they are biological. living stromatolites grow today in a few places, including shark bay in western australia. stromatolites were abundant in shallow seas for much of the precambrian. they declined later, a decline often attributed to grazing animals, though other causes have been proposed.

title: Sugarcane
sum: Sugarcane was domesticated in New Guinea and nearby parts of Southeast Asia around 6,000 years ago, spread through Asia and the Mediterranean world over the following millennia, and after 1492 became the crop most closely tied to slave…
search: sugarcane sugarcane was domesticated in new guinea and nearby parts of southeast asia around 6,000 years ago, spread through asia and the mediterranean world over the following millennia, and after 1492 became the crop most closely tied to slave labor in the americas. sugarcane was domesticated from the wild grass saccharum robustum in new guinea around 6,000 years ago; a related domestication of saccharum sinense by austronesian peoples in southern china and taiwan occurred by at least 5,500 years ago. austronesian traders carried sugarcane to china and india by about 3,000 years ago, and persian and greek writers encountered it in the 6th to 4th centuries bce; by the 8th century ce sugar was traded into the mediterranean world as an expensive luxury spice from india. christopher columbus brought sugarcane to hispaniola on his second voyage, and the first sugar harvest in the americas took place there in 1501; portuguese colonizers introduced the crop to brazil, where by 1540 the island of santa catarina alone held about 800 sugar mills. the atlantic sugar trade formed one side of a triangular trade linking european manufactured goods, enslaved africans, and new world sugar and other raw materials, and sugar plantations across the caribbean and brazil were worked overwhelmingly by enslaved labor; in louisiana, enslaved workers helped make the state responsible for nearly a quarter of the world's exportable sugar by 1853. global sugarcane production reached about 1.92 billion tonnes in 2022, with brazil producing about 38 percent and india about 23 percent.

title: Tea Plant
sum: The tea plant is native to the borderlands of southwestern China, northeastern India and northern Myanmar, drunk in China by at least the 2nd century BCE, and its later global trade helped provoke both British cultivation in colonial India…

title: Insulin

title: Steam Engine
sum: The steam engine converts heat into mechanical work. Thomas Newcomen built the first commercially successful engine in 1712, and James Watt's improvements from the 1760s made it far more efficient.
search: steam engine the steam engine converts heat into mechanical work. thomas newcomen built the first commercially successful engine in 1712, and james watt's improvements from the 1760s made it far more efficient. early engines pumped water out of coal mines. watt's separate condenser (patented 1769) greatly improved fuel economy. high-pressure engines (trevithick, 1802) made railways and steamships possible. steam power freed factories from dependence on rivers.

title: Stirrup
sum: The stirrup is a foot support hung from a saddle that aids mounting and balance. The earliest firm evidence is a single mounting stirrup on a Chinese figurine of about 302 CE, with paired stirrups following within decades.
search: stirrup the stirrup is a foot support hung from a saddle that aids mounting and balance. the earliest firm evidence is a single mounting stirrup on a chinese figurine of about 302 ce, with paired stirrups following within decades. a ceramic figurine from a western jin tomb near changsha, china, dated about 302 ce, shows a single stirrup meant only for mounting. the earliest known paired riding stirrups appear in an eastern jin tomb near nanjing, about 322 ce. the oldest surviving physical double stirrups come from the 415 ce tomb of the northern yan noble feng sufu. claims of earlier toe-loop mounting aids elsewhere are debated; firm dated evidence begins in china. stirrups spread from east asia through steppe peoples to byzantium and europe over later centuries. lynn white's 1962 "stirrup thesis," linking stirrups to european feudalism, was challenged from the 1970s on and is now largely rejected.

title: Telegraph and Submarine Cables
sum: The electric telegraph, first demonstrated commercially in the 1840s, and the submarine cables that followed, allowed messages to cross continents and oceans in minutes instead of weeks.
search: telegraph and submarine cables the electric telegraph, first demonstrated commercially in the 1840s, and the submarine cables that followed, allowed messages to cross continents and oceans in minutes instead of weeks. samuel morse sent the first public long-distance message, 'what hath god wrought', in 1844. a transatlantic cable was laid in 1858 but failed within weeks; a durable cable was completed in 1866. cables linked britain to india in the 1870s, and later most of the world. the telegraph changed news, markets, diplomacy, and warfare.

title: Telephone
sum: The telephone transmits speech as electrical signals over wire. Alexander Graham Bell received the first US telephone patent in 1876, amid competing claims from other inventors.
search: telephone the telephone transmits speech as electrical signals over wire. alexander graham bell received the first us telephone patent in 1876, amid competing claims from other inventors. bell's application, titled improvement in telegraphy, was filed on 14 february 1876; us patent 174,465 was granted on 7 march 1876. elisha gray filed a patent caveat for a similar device the same day; the dispute led to litigation. bell's notebook records intelligible speech to his assistant thomas watson on 10 march 1876. antonio meucci filed a caveat on 28 december 1871 for a voice-communication device; it lapsed after 1874. the us house passed a 2002 resolution honoring meucci; the senate did not, and its meaning is disputed. the first commercial exchange opened in new haven, connecticut, on 28 january 1878.

title: Telescope
sum: The telescope is an optical instrument using lenses to magnify distant objects, first documented in the Netherlands in 1608 and quickly turned toward the night sky.
search: telescope the telescope is an optical instrument using lenses to magnify distant objects, first documented in the netherlands in 1608 and quickly turned toward the night sky. hans lipperhey, a dutch spectacle-maker, filed the first known telescope patent application on 2 october 1608, in the hague. the states general denied the patent in december 1608, since similar devices were already known to others. jacob metius and sacharias janssen made rival claims around the same time; priority among the dutch makers remains disputed.  galileo galilei  heard of the device in 1609 and built improved telescopes with much higher magnification. galileo observed lunar mountains in late 1609 and four moons of jupiter in january 1610, publishing these findings in sidereus nuncius that march.

title: Terracotta Army
sum: The Terracotta Army is a buried set of life-size clay soldiers, horses, and chariots built for the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China, and found only in 1974.
search: terracotta army the terracotta army is a buried set of life-size clay soldiers, horses, and chariots built for the tomb of qin shi huang, first emperor of unified china, and found only in 1974. on 29 march 1974, farmers digging a well near lintong, outside xi'an, struck pottery fragments near the  mausoleum of qin shi huang . more than 2,000 figures have been excavated from three pits; estimates put the full total above 8,000, most still unexcavated. figures were individually finished, with distinct faces, hairstyles, and armor, and were originally painted in bright pigment that flakes away within minutes of air exposure. unesco inscribed the mausoleum of the first qin emperor, including the army, as a world heritage site in 1987. the army dates to the reign of qin shi huang (unified china 221 bce, died 210 bce); whether construction began at his accession in 246 bce or later is debated.

title: The Wheel
sum: Wheeled vehicles appear in the archaeological record around 3500 to 3000 BCE, in Mesopotamia, Europe, and the steppe.
search: the wheel wheeled vehicles appear in the archaeological record around 3500 to 3000 bce, in mesopotamia, europe, and the steppe. the oldest surviving wooden wheel, from the ljubljana marshes in slovenia, is about 5,150 years old (radiocarbon dated to roughly 5,100 to 5,350 years ago). pictographs from uruk show sleds and wheeled carts. the wheel arrived in east asia later, and was not used for transport in the americas before contact. potter's wheels used rotation for shaping clay.

title: Trans-Siberian Railway
sum: The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and largely completed by 1916, is a railway line of about 9,300 kilometers linking Moscow with the Pacific port of Vladivostok.
search: trans-siberian railway the trans-siberian railway, begun in 1891 and largely completed by 1916, is a railway line of about 9,300 kilometers linking moscow with the pacific port of vladivostok. construction began in 1891, with a ceremony at vladivostok attended by the future nicholas ii. the full line between moscow and vladivostok is about 9,289 kilometers. the bridge over the amur river at khabarovsk, completed in 1916, closed the last major gap. it led to the movement of millions of settlers into siberia. it is the longest continuous railway line in the world.

title: Vaccination
sum: Vaccination began in 1796 when Edward Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox, and it led to the eradication of smallpox in 1980.
search: vaccination vaccination began in 1796 when edward jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox, and it led to the eradication of smallpox in 1980. inoculation with smallpox material (variolation) was practiced earlier in asia, africa, and the middle east. smallpox killed about 300 million people in the 20th century alone before eradication. the world health organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. vaccines have since been developed against many diseases.

title: Variolation
sum: Variolation is deliberate exposure to smallpox material, by skin scratching or nasal insufflation of dried scab powder, to induce a milder infection and immunity, used before Jennerian vaccination.
search: variolation variolation is deliberate exposure to smallpox material, by skin scratching or nasal insufflation of dried scab powder, to induce a milder infection and immunity, used before jennerian vaccination. wan quan's douzhen xinfa (1549) is the oldest confirmed chinese text describing nasal-insufflation inoculation; claims of 10th-century origins are legendary and unverified. the practice was used independently in the ottoman empire, south asia, and parts of west africa before its documented adoption in western europe, though the earliest dates in each region are poorly attested. lady mary wortley montagu observed variolation in constantinople in 1717 and had her son inoculated there in 1718. montagu's advocacy and a 1721 london trial on condemned prisoners helped popularize variolation in england. variolation carried a real fatality risk, roughly 1 to 2 percent, and was largely replaced after edward jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccination.

title: Water Clock
sum: A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the steady flow of water into or out of a vessel. The oldest surviving example is the alabaster clepsydra from Karnak, made in the reign of Amenhotep III in the 14th century BCE, and a written…
search: water clock a water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the steady flow of water into or out of a vessel. the oldest surviving example is the alabaster clepsydra from karnak, made in the reign of amenhotep iii in the 14th century bce, and a written record points to an earlier egyptian origin. the karnak clepsydra was found in 1904 and is now in a cairo museum. its alabaster body has twelve columns of hour-marks, and water drips through a small hole in its base. a tomb inscription of the official amenemhet, from the 16th century bce, credits him with devising a water clock: earlier written evidence than the karnak vessel itself. as the water level fell, the flow slowed, so many designs used sloped sides or constant-level inflow to keep the rate steady. in athens, water clocks timed speeches in the law courts. chinese and islamic makers built elaborate water-driven clocks; su song's 1088 astronomical clock tower is the best known. see  mechanical clock .

title: Windmill
sum: The windmill converts wind into rotational mechanical power, historically used to grind grain and pump water. The earliest well-documented windmills are vertical-axis panemone mills in Sistan, on the Iranian Plateau, described by Islamic…
search: windmill the windmill converts wind into rotational mechanical power, historically used to grind grain and pump water. the earliest well-documented windmills are vertical-axis panemone mills in sistan, on the iranian plateau, described by islamic geographers in the 9th and 10th centuries ce. vertical-axis panemone windmills operated in sistan, on the iranian plateau, by the 9th to 10th century ce. the geographers al-masudi (writing 943 ce) and ibn hawqal (traveling 943-969 ce) both recorded sistan's wind-driven grain mills. the mills used vertical wooden-frame sails of cloth or reed matting in tall adobe towers, turned by strong seasonal winds. sistan mills ground grain and, in some structures, pumped water for irrigation, alongside the region's  qanat  system. a structurally distinct horizontal-axis windmill, the post mill, appears in europe from the 12th century ce, about three centuries later. whether the european design diffused from persian precedent or arose independently is debated, with no settled consensus.

title: Woodblock Printing
sum: Woodblock printing, carving a whole page into a block of wood, inked and pressed onto paper, was developed in East Asia by the 8th century CE.
search: woodblock printing woodblock printing, carving a whole page into a block of wood, inked and pressed onto paper, was developed in east asia by the 8th century ce. the diamond sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book. early printing was largely for buddhist texts and calendars. the technique spread to korea, japan, and vietnam. bi sheng invented movable type in china in about 1040.

title: X-ray Imaging
sum: X-rays are penetrating electromagnetic radiation identified in 1895 by Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen. Within months they let physicians see bones and foreign objects inside living bodies without surgery.
search: x-ray imaging x-rays are penetrating electromagnetic radiation identified in 1895 by wilhelm conrad roentgen. within months they let physicians see bones and foreign objects inside living bodies without surgery. on 8 november 1895, roentgen saw a glow on a fluorescent screen while working with cathode-ray tubes at the university of wurzburg. he called them x-rays because their nature was unknown, and published in december 1895 with an image of his wife's hand. photographs circulated from january 1896, and medical use began within weeks in europe and north america. early operators suffered skin burns and other injuries before the hazards were understood. henri becquerel reported radioactivity in uranium salts in 1896, following up on the new rays. roentgen received the first nobel prize in physics in 1901 and took no patent.

title: Zero and Place-Value Notation
sum: The decimal place-value system, in which zero serves as a digit and placeholder, developed in India in the first millennium CE and spread across the world.
search: zero and place-value notation the decimal place-value system, in which zero serves as a digit and placeholder, developed in india in the first millennium ce and spread across the world. the bakhshali manuscript, found in what is now pakistan, uses a dot as a placeholder zero. it is a composite of birch-bark leaves from different periods: oxford radiocarbon dating in 2017 gave 224 to 383 ce, 680 to 779 ce, and 885 to 993 ce for three folios, and a 2024 revision widened the overall range to 799 to 1102 ce and moved the oldest tested folio to 931 to 1032 ce. the claim that it holds the earliest zero is therefore contested. the indian mathematician brahmagupta gave rules for arithmetic with zero in 628 ce. scholars in the islamic world, including  al-khwarizmi , carried the system westward. fibonacci's 1202 book popularized it in europe.

title: Art and Ritual
sum: Art and ritual are symbolic and expressive practices: painting, carving, ornament, music and dance, storytelling, monumental building, and ceremony, including rites for the dead. They are found in all human societies and go back at least…
search: art and ritual art and ritual are symbolic and expressive practices: painting, carving, ornament, music and dance, storytelling, monumental building, and ceremony, including rites for the dead. they are found in all human societies and go back at least to the paleolithic, with engraved ochre, beads, and cave paintings from tens of thousands of years ago. the vault follows them from cave painting and prehistoric monuments, through the temple and court arts of ancient empires and medieval kingdoms, to renaissance and mughal building, and to objects taken in conquest, such as the benin bronzes. it treats art and ritual as evidence of what societies valued and of how they marked power, belonging, and mortality.

title: Earth Systems and Life
sum: Earth systems and life cover the physical planet, its climate, and the history of living things, from the formation of the Solar System about 4.57 billion years ago to the present. The vault follows the planet's changing atmosphere,…
search: earth systems and life earth systems and life cover the physical planet, its climate, and the history of living things, from the formation of the solar system about 4.57 billion years ago to the present. the vault follows the planet's changing atmosphere, oceans, continents, and ice; the origin and diversification of life, punctuated by mass extinctions; the evolution of hominins and humans through ice-age cycles; and the recent period in which human activity has become a major influence on the planet. human history sits inside this longer story and depends on it, on the warm and relatively stable climate of the holocene, on domesticated plants and animals, and on the diseases and environmental changes that societies met along the way. this hub also covers the scientific work that reconstructed this history.

title: Kinship and Society
sum: Kinship and society cover how people organize families, descent, marriage, households, communities, and social ranks, and how those arrangements scale from foraging bands to states and beyond. Kin relations are among the most variable…
search: kinship and society kinship and society cover how people organize families, descent, marriage, households, communities, and social ranks, and how those arrangements scale from foraging bands to states and beyond. kin relations are among the most variable features of human cultures. the vault traces them from the small mobile groups of the paleolithic, through farming villages, chiefdoms, cities, and empires, to the modern struggles over citizenship, equality, and status, and it includes the migrations and conquests that mixed populations along the way. it also covers gender, slavery and freedom, and the ways groups define who belongs.

title: Language and Writing
sum: Language and writing are the systems by which people communicate and store information: speech, writing systems, numerals, record-keeping devices such as knotted cords, and the media that copy and carry them. Spoken language is universal…
search: language and writing language and writing are the systems by which people communicate and store information: speech, writing systems, numerals, record-keeping devices such as knotted cords, and the media that copy and carry them. spoken language is universal and very old, though when it arose is uncertain; writing appeared much later, independently in a few places, and spread by contact, conquest, religion, and trade. the vault follows them from the symbolic behavior of early homo sapiens, through clay tablets, alphabets, paper, and printing, to the telegraph and digital networks, and it also covers the spread of language families across continents. it gives equal weight to peoples who kept records without alphabets.

title: Religion and Belief

search: religion and belief religion and belief cover the shared systems of ritual, story, and moral teaching that people use to explain the world, organize communities, and face death. they appear in every known human society, and the vault follows them from the burials and symbolic objects of the paleolithic and the monumental sites of the neolithic, through temple states, philosophical and prophetic traditions, and the world religions, to the secular creeds and religious movements of the modern era. the hub also covers political and civic ideologies that do similar work, since the line between religion and ideology is itself debated. it records what is known about how beliefs arose, spread, and shaped states, and it does not judge their truth claims.

title: Science
sum: Science is the systematic study of the natural world through observation, measurement, mathematics, and testing, together with the habits and institutions that let people check and extend one another's claims. Its practices run from the…

title: Technology
